PARTNER_TOMMASOCIUFFI_PALMARES:

Following these results, in 2019 he joined a factory team and won the Italian Two-Wheel Drive Championship with six victories and 63 fastest times. He was selected by ACI Team Italia in 2020 for a WRC3 programme, but after Rally Sweden the season was halted due to Covid.

In 2021 Tommaso returned to competition, stepping up to Rally2. His growth continued over two seasons: 6th overall in CIAR 2022, 3rd in Promozione with one win and several podiums. In 2023 he returned to gravel, for the first time in four-wheel drive, finishing 3rd in the Italian Gravel Rally Championship.

In 2024 he fought until the final round, ending 2nd, and set out immediately to try again in 2025. Tommaso received the Pegaso Sport Prize from the Tuscany Region in 2019 and the Giglio da Corsa from the City of Florence in 2021, which continues to support his sporting career today.

CARSETUP_ELECTRONIC_MAP_DESC:
<StyleBold>Active differential maps</> are electronically controlled settings that adjust how torque is distributed between wheels based on driving conditions.

Each map offers a unique characteristic and handling style by varying the differential locking behavior and torque transfer. Through sensors and an ECU, the system dynamically locks or unlocks the differential to optimize traction, stability, and cornering performance. Some maps increase lock on entry and exit of corners for stability and acceleration, while others allow more slip through the apex for better rotation.

Drivers select different maps to match varying road surfaces and driving styles. This sophisticated control improves speed and reduces sliding compared to mechanical differentials.
CARSETUP_ADDITIONAL_LIGHTS_DESC:
<StyleBold>Additional lights</> are powerful light components used to improve visibility during night stages and low visibility conditions in rally racing. While they can significantly enhance a driver's ability to see the road ahead, many cars only have them as optional equipment, and regulations often enforce their installation for night events.

These lights are delicate and positioned on the car’s front, making them vulnerable to damage from collisions. Because of their fragility, installing additional lights requires the car’s bodywork to be in good condition. <StyleBold>If the front bodywork is heavily damaged, it must be repaired</> before the lights can be securely fitted, ensuring both safety and functionality.
CARSETUP_ANGLE_OF_INCIDENCE_DESC:
<StyleBold>Adjustable wings</> allow fine-tuning of aerodynamic balance by changing the wing’s angle of incidence.

<StyleBold>Increasing</> the wing angle boosts downforce, improving grip, but only up to the stall limit, beyond which downforce drops sharply. Higher angles also increase drag, impacting your potential top speeds and can cause the front end to lift up whilst airborne.

<StyleBold>Decreasing</> the rear wing angle will produce less drag, improving the top speed of the car but at the cost of aerodynamic grip, making the car more prone to oversteer at higher speeds. Running too lower rear wing angle can also decrease the cars stability whilst airborne, making the car more likely to pitch forward.

CARSETUP_ANTIROLLBAR_STIFFNES_DESC:
<StyleBold>Anti-roll bars</> connect the wheels on the same axle to reduce body roll during cornering.
While this decreases roll and helps maintain better camber angles, it also increases load transfer between the tyres, which can reduce the overall grip of that axle.

Raising the anti-roll bar stiffness at the front generally moves the bias towards understeer. Increasing it at the rear tends to cause oversteer by allowing the rear to rotate more in the mid corner.

In rally cars, especially on loose surfaces with long suspension travel, it’s important to balance anti-roll bar settings. Too much stiffness causes excessive load transfer and tyre grip saturation, while too little roll can lead to poor camber control.
OPTION_CLUTCH_DESC:
<StyleBold>Automatic clutch</> control kicks in, without driver intervention, during gear changes, when starting off and when the engine revs are very low, preventing the car from stalling and ensuring that gear changes are correct.

<StyleBold>Manual clutch control</>, on the other hand, requires the driver to press the clutch when necessary.

Incorrect clutch management could slow down or prevent gear engagement, or cause the engine to stall after an accident or when starting off. Expert clutch control ensures better performance when starting off and when changing gear, while automatic clutch allows less experienced drivers to achieve adequate performance in any situation.

Manual clutch control is only selectable with manual transmission.
CARSETUP_CASTER_DESC:
<StyleBold>Caster angle</> refers to the tilt of the steering axis viewed from the side of a car, with positive caster being where the geometry leans backwards when drawing a line between the upper and lower tyre joints.  

<StyleBold>Higher positive caster</> angles increase the mechanical trail, making the steering feel heavier and improving steering returnability, which helps the wheels self-center after a turn.

Additionally, increased caster boosts dynamic camber gain during cornering, enhancing tyre grip and stability.

This balance between steering effort and handling responsiveness is crucial to maintain control and optimal performance.
PACENOTES_INSTRUCTIONS_DESC:
<StyleBold>Co-driver instructions</> are directives given to the driver to indicate actions to be taken or upcoming events. In these cases, the driver must simply follow these instructions to complete the stage and continue on the correct route.

<StyleTitle>End of race instructions</>
When approaching the finish line, the co-driver will announce the end of the stage with the instruction <StyleBold>FINISH</>. Upon receiving this indication, the driver knows the finish is near and must push to that point; once the stage end is reached, they can begin to slow down.
After crossing the finish line, the co-driver will indicate to the player the possible route to reach the marshals checkpoint. On this short section of the course, the driver must reduce speed to a minimum and stop at the marshals to conclude the event.

<StyleTitle>Course direction instructions</>
Along the route, there may be intersections or forks where the player will need to take a specific direction to continue on the correct test track. In these cases, the driver must simply follow the indicated direction: <StyleBold>GO LEFT</>, <StyleBold>STRAIGHT</>, or <StyleBold>RIGHT</>; otherwise, they might compromise the test or be forced to return to the correct course.
PACENOTES_OVERVIEW_DESC:
<StyleBold>Co-driver notes</> are a fundamental part of rally racing. Unlike circuit racing, the driver generally tackles each corner only once in a rally. Additionally, the use and layout of public roads often offers limited visibility of curves and hazards ahead. On top of this, unpredictable weather, changing light conditions, and irregular, variable road surfaces make it essential to have assistance to face these challenges.

This is where the co-driver comes in, sitting in the passenger seat during each rally stage and providing detailed information about the course ahead.

Co-driver notes include:
•	The difficulty and characteristics of the corners
•	Presence of straight sections and the distance to the next corner
•	Information about the sequences of corners and how they connect
•	Warnings of hazards on the road or specific points of the stage that require extra attention
•	Course details such as jumps or potholes
•	Race instructions and regulatory information

Moreover, the co-driver helps the driver understand what is happening with the car or the race by providing additional useful information such as:
•	The status of key vehicle components
•	Changes in weather or road surface
•	Unexpected events and mistakes
•	Support in maintaining focus and the proper level of attention

An example of a sequence of notes might be as follows (see image alongside):

<StyleBold>Caution, Right 6 into hairpin Left, Opens, and pothole, 80, Finish!</>

This sequence describes a complex part of the stage where the driver must be very attentive: immediately after a fairly fast right corner, there is a left hairpin which opens up toward the exit, followed by a pothole taking up the entire width of the road. Then comes a straight of about 80 meters leading to the stage finish.
CARSETUP_GEARSET_DESC:
<StyleBold>Each gearset</> consists of a pair of gearbox shafts (and, if available, a drop gear) equipped with fixed gears.

When selecting the ideal gearset for a rally stage, consider that closer lower ratios can provide better acceleration on high-traction surfaces, while wider lower ratios may be preferable on loose or slippery terrain to increase wheel torque and maintain control.

Increasing the gear set value selects wider lower ratios.
Decreasing the value selects closer lower ratios.

Choose the configuration that best matches the stage conditions to optimize performance.
<StyleBold>Different Gear set may have a different number of Gears.</>
CARSETUP_FAST_HEAVE_BUMP_DESC:
<StyleBold>Fast Heave Bump</> damping controls the high-speed resistance of the damper shaft during suspension compression in parallel motion caused by bumps in the road surface.

Increasing this setting raises the force opposing the Heave Spring compression, reducing wheel oscillations and improve control.
However, excessive damping can cause a pumping effect on rough surfaces, where the suspension barely moves and the tyre sidewall absorbs most impacts, reducing effective damping.

Typically, Heave Bump is set lower than Heave Rebound due to the spring force aiding compression. In softer springs, higher Heave Bump can help control longitudinal load transfer.
CARSETUP_FAST_HEAVE_REBOUND_DESC:
<StyleBold>Fast Heave Rebound</> damping regulates the high-speed resistance of the damper shaft extending during parallel suspension movement caused by bumps in the road surface.

Increasing this setting strengthens the force opposing suspension extension, which helps control wheel oscillations by slowing them down. This leads to better stability on smoother surfaces, but can reduce the time the tyre stays in contact with the ground on rougher surfaces.

Overall, fast heave rebound damping is crucial for managing suspension behavior during rapid wheel movements, balancing control and tyre contact on uneven terrain.
CARSETUP_FAST_BUMP_DESC:
<StyleBold>Fast bump</> damping controls the resistance force on the damper shaft during rapid suspension compression, in repsonse to suspension movement caused by the terrain.

Increasing this setting slows down the suspensions compression by adding more resistance, reducing oscillations and improving control. 

However, too high a fast bump setting can cause a pumping effect, where the suspension feels underdamped despite being overdamped, resulting in most compression being absorbed by the tyre sidewall, which offers minimal damping. It can also amplify the feeling of larger bumps on rougher terrain, by not allowing the suspension to compress quickly enough to absorb the impact.
Typically, bump damping is set lower than rebound damping because the spring force also opposes compression.
CARSETUP_FAST_REBOUND_DESC:
<StyleBold>Fast rebound</> damping controls the high-speed resistance of the damper shaft during extension and wheel droop, in response to suspension movement caused by the terrain.

Increasing this setting raises the force opposing suspension extension, which helps to slow down and better control wheel oscillations. This creates a firmer response, improving stability on smoother terrain, but can in turn reduce the wheel's contact time with the ground, potentially impacting grip on rougher surfaces.
GROUP_4WD_DESC: <StyleBold>Four-wheel-drive (4WD)</> cars provide excellent traction on all surfaces. On asphalt, they favor smooth driving, and on slippery surfaces, they require less countersteering than rear-wheel-drive cars.

CARSETUP_FRONT_TORQUE_DISTR_DESC:
<StyleBold>Front Torque Distribution</> in a 4WD rally car refers to the static distribution of torque sent to the front axle. This setting can be adjusted depending on the driver’s style and the surface conditions.

A higher front torque bias generally improves stability and grip on tarmac or solid surfaces, giving the car more predictable handling. Too much bias though can make the car understeer when on throttle and exiting corners.

Shifting the torque bias rearwards is more ideal on loose or slippery surfaces like gravel, where the lower grip levels require more oversteer and rotation to help with cornering. 

However, too much torque toward the rear on loose surfaces often results in reduced control and slower stage times, making it essential to balance torque distribution carefully for optimal performance.
GROUP_FWD_DESC: <StyleBold>Front-wheel-drive</> rally cars tend to understeer during acceleration and usually have a stiff rear to help rotating the car. In corners, lifting off the throttle causes instability, while applying gas makes them steer inward due to the limited-slip differential, demanding high focus when entering a turn.
HISTORY_80GROUPB_DESC:
<StyleBold>Group B</> rallying, active from <StyleBold>1982 to 1986</> in the World Rally Championship, is often hailed as the golden era of rally racing for its extraordinary blend of power, innovation, and sheer spectacle. Introduced by the <StyleBold>FIA</> with remarkably few design restrictions and lower homologation requirements, only 200 units, Group B allowed manufacturers unprecedented technical freedom, enabling them to create some of the most powerful and sophisticated rally cars ever built. These machines were typically lightweight but boasted turbocharged or supercharged engines producing over 500 horsepower, paired with advanced all-wheel-drive systems and cutting-edge aerodynamics. The result was blistering acceleration and top speeds well beyond 100 mph on narrow and unpredictable stages, thrilling fans and challenging drivers in ways unseen before.

This era attracted legendary drivers like <StyleBold>Walter Röhrl</>, <StyleBold>Ari Vatanen</>, and <StyleBold>Michèle Mouton</>, whose skill and daring matched the capabilities of their machines, creating intense rivalries and unforgettable moments. Iconic cars such as the Audi Quattro, Lancia 037 and Delta S4, Peugeot 205 T16, and Ford RS200 competed fiercely, each pushing the envelope of rally technology. The diversity of designs, from Audi's four-wheel drive to Lancia's rear-wheel-drive 037, made the competition even more compelling.

However, this freedom came at a cost. The cars were brutally fast, but <StyleBold>safety</> measures lagged behind. Both in car design and event management, with spectators often standing dangerously close to the racing action. Tragically, several catastrophic accidents included fatalities of both drivers and spectators. These incidents led the FIA to <StyleBold>ban</> Group B cars from the World Rally Championship starting in 1987, marking an <StyleBold>abrupt end</> to this thrilling but perilous chapter in motorsport history.

Despite its short life, Group B left a lasting legacy: it redefined what rally cars could be and is remembered with reverence by enthusiasts and casual fans alike for the unparalleled excitement and risk it embodied. Its influence persists in rally culture and motorsport engineering, and Group B cars remain icons of automotive performance and daring innovation.
COMPOUND_HARD_DESC:
<StyleBold>HARD tyres</> are the ultimate durability tyre compound, ideal for longer and multiple stages in a row.
Grip levels are lower than the two softer compounds, however it is better suited for hotter conditions and faster or more abrasive surfaces.
This tyre will struggle for grip in lower and cooler temperatures. 

<StyleBold>HARD tyres</> are best for long stages, hot conditions, or rally legs featuring multiple moderate to long length stages before being able to change tyres.
PARTNER_FABRICEGORDON_BIO:
<StyleBold>Hi, I'm Fabrice Gordon</>
I’m a professional French rally co-driver born on August 23, 1970. Throughout my career, I’ve built a reputation for being highly adaptable, navigating for various drivers across both modern and historic categories. Whether it’s a cutting-edge R5 or a legendary vintage machine, I know how to find the rhythm.
I’ve competed in <StyleBold>more than 290 rallies</> throughout my career, but if you want to know how it all really took off, I have one story I’ll never forget.
<StyleBold>The Ultimate "Right Place, Right Time" Moment</>
It was November 1997. I was on vacation with my wife and son in Sainte-Maxime, right in the middle of the <StyleBold>Rallye du Var</>. I was just sitting there, relaxing at a café terrace, when my phone rang.
It was Jean-Pierre Chiaroni and Dominique Savignoni. They asked if I was available to jump in because the legendary <StyleBold>Yves Loubet</> was stuck without a co-driver (Jean-Marc Andrié had fallen ill). 
My answer was instant: <StyleBold>"Yes."</> 
I met Yves right in the middle of a special stage. I jumped in the car and said, "Hi Yves, I'm Fabrice." He didn't skip a beat. He just pointed at the pace notes and said, "Coco, this is where we are." And just like that, we went flat out into the stage.
At the finish line, he asked for my license, sent it off to the team, and officially named me his co-driver for the rest of the event. We ended up taking the <StyleBold>victory in Group N.</>
That was the moment my career truly began.
CARSETUP_GEAR_DESC:
<StyleBold>Higher gear ratios</> in a car are designed to improve acceleration, allowing the vehicle to reach top speeds more quickly from a standstill. By favoring quicker engine revving and faster power delivery, these ratios provide an advantage during rapid changes in pace, such as tight corners or technical sections.

However, this comes with trade-offs. While acceleration is enhanced, the car’s top speed is reduced, limiting its maximum velocity on straights. Moreover, higher ratios can negatively affect traction, as increased torque at the wheels may lead to wheel spin, especially on loose or slippery surfaces.
COMPOUND_MEDIUM_DESC:
<StyleBold>MEDIUM tyres</> are a jack of all trades, capable of performing across a wide range of scenarios. The medium compound provides good amounts of cornering grip and traction off corners, and has a moderate amount of durability. 
They won't have quite as much bite as a soft tyre but will provide more grip than a hard. They perform better over longer distances than a soft, but wear out faster than a hard compound. 

<StyleBold>MEDIUM tyres</> are best for moderate length stages, fast flowing sections, and rally legs where you'll tackle multiple stages before being able to change tyres.
CARSETUP_MUD_FLAPS_DESC:
<StyleBold>Mud flaps</> are plastic fixtures mounted behind a rally car’s tyres. Typically they’re often mounted behind on the rear wheels, but some mud flaps behind all four. Their primary purpose is to minimize the spray of dirt, mud, and debris kicked up by the rotating tyres, helping to keep the car cleaner and improving visibility.
In rally racing, this can be crucial for maintaining traction and reducing damage from flying rocks.

However, in our specific case, the mud flaps serve mainly an <StyleBold>aesthetic role</>, enhancing the aggressive and rugged look of the vehicle without significantly impacting performance or dirt control.
OPTION_PACENOTETIMING_DESC:
<StyleBold>Pacenote Anticipation</> changes the timing of the co-driver's note call for a point on the stage. 

By setting to <StyleBold>Early</> the anticipation of the call, the co-driver will give instructions further away from the described point. By setting it to <StyleBold>(late)</> instead, the note will be given closer to the point of interest.
CARSETUP_PACKER_THICKNESS_DESC:
<StyleBold>Packers</> are thin, Teflon discs of varying <StyleBold>thickness</> positioned around the damper shaft, typically installed between the damper body and the bump stop. Their primary role is to limit bump travel by effectively acting as spacers.

In car suspension setups, especially on the front end, packers help control excessive aerodynamic diving during braking without significantly compromising spring rates. By fine-tuning together with the bump travel, they allow for better suspension response and improved handling characteristics.

Increasing the packer thickness will reduce the amount of travel allowed when the springs compress, making the car sharper in response. Decreasing the packer thickness will allow for more compression, giving better stability and control over rougher terrain.

This balancing act helps maintain vehicle stability and performance across rough terrain and high-speed maneuvers commonly encountered in rally racing.
COMPOUND_WET_DESC:
<StyleBold>RAIN tyres</> are the choice to go for in wet conditions. They feature more heavily tread blocks to disperse water from underneath the tyre, better maintaining contact between the tyre and road surface when it is wet providing more grip.
The compound is generally very soft, allowing it to generate heat quicker than a dry tyre and maintain grip in the cooler wet conditions.
This does however mean that a rain tyre will overheat easily if the surface is dry or abrasive, causing grip levels to drop sharply and rapidly increase tyre wear.

<StyleBold>RAIN tyres</> should only be used when wet conditions are forecasted, or there are more wet stages than dry in the next rally leg.
COMPOUND_SNOW_DESC:
<StyleBold>SNOW tyres</> are specific tyres designed for snowy stages, such as those of the Swedish rally.
Their narrow design and <StyleBold>7 millimeters studs</> allow the tyre to carve through the snow at higher speeds, whilst providing good amounts of grip whilst braking and cornering. 
Their built to work in extremely cold temperatures, and will therefore overheat and wear very quickly on tarmac and conditions above freezing.

<StyleBold>SNOW tyres</> are only available on full snow rally stages.
COMPOUND_SOFT_DESC:
<StyleBold>SOFT tyres</> offer superior grip due to their more pliable rubber, making it suitable for loose surfaces, gravel or cold/mild tarmac.
In these conditions, the SOFT compound provides better cornering grip, shorter braking zones, and better traction off corners compared to harder compounds.
However, they wear out faster than the harder compounds and are easier to overheat, especially on hot or abrasive roads.

<StyleBold>SOFT tyres</> are best for short, technical stages or cooler conditions where grip is prioritized over durability.
CARSETUP_SLOW_HEAVE_BUMP_DESC:
<StyleBold>Slow Heave Bump</> damping controls the low-speed resistance of the damper shaft, as the heave spring compresses during parallel suspension motion, from driver input.

Increasing this setting raises the force opposing suspension compression, slowing the dive or squat body movement but can cause a pumping effect. Pumping occurs when the suspension feels underdamped but is actually overdamped, causing most compression to come from the tyre sidewall, which offers little damping.

Decreasing this setting will allow the heave springs to compress faster, which can load the tyres quicker and shift the cars balance forwards or back faster, in response to heavy braking or acceleration.

Typically, Heave Bump is set lower than Heave Rebound because the heave spring also resists compression. However, with soft springs, higher Heave Bump can help reduce longitudinal load transfers.
CARSETUP_SLOW_HEAVE_REBOUND_DESC:
<StyleBold>Slow Heave Rebound</> damping regulates the low-speed resistance of the damper shaft as the wheel extends during parallel suspension movement, from driver input.

Increasing this setting raises the force opposing suspension extension, which helps to better control body motions by slowing down how quickly the car’s body responds to bumps and body roll.

However, higher damping increases the risk of wheel jacking, especially on rough terrain, as the suspension resists unloading too quickly.
CARSETUP_SLOW_BUMP_DESC:
<StyleBold>Slow bump</> damping controls the low-speed resistance of the damper shaft during suspension compression, in response to driver inputs.

Increasing slow bump damping strengthens the force opposing wheel bump, helping to slow down body movements for better control.

However, too high a setting can make the car feel less responsive to input, slowing the rate at which tyres load up in grip. It can also cause a pumping effect, where the suspension appears underdamped but is actually overdamped, relying mainly on tyre sidewall flex with minimal damping.
Typically, bump damping is set lower than rebound damping since the spring also resists compression. In softer springs, slightly higher bump damping can help reduce load transfer.
CARSETUP_SLOW_REBOUND_DESC:
<StyleBold>Slow rebound</> damping regulates the low-speed resistance of the damper shaft against the wheel’s downward movement, extension, or droop, caused by driver inputs.

Increasing this setting raises the force opposing suspension extension, which helps control body movements by slowing them down, resulting in improved stability and handling.

However, higher slow rebound damping can also prevent the suspension from extending quickly enough to maintain tyre grip in response to driver input.
COMPOUND_TARMACSNOW_DESC:
<StyleBold>TARMAC SNOW tyres</> are a more extreme version of the winter tyre, featuring <StyleBold>2 millimeters metal studs</> protruding from the rubber.
These provide great traction in very snowy and icey conditions, with the metal studs digging into the surface to provide more grip.
They however wear extremely quickly on exposed tarmac, as the studs grind down and break away on the solid surface.

The <StyleBold>TARMAC SNOW tyres</> is therefore only to be used on stages that are covered in compact snow and ice, with little exposed tarmac.
COMPOUND_TARMACWINTER_DESC:
<StyleBold>TARMAC WINTER tyres</> are a bespoke tyre compound suited for the variable conditions that the rallies like Monte-Carlo can produce.
Its foundation is a very soft compound, that is designed to work across conditions from very cold but dry, through to wet and into snowy conditions. Due to it's soft compound, it may start to overheat and wear quicker if the majority of the stage is dry tarmac.

The <StyleBold>TARMAC WINTER tyres</> are therefore best used when conditions are wet, or there is significant sections of the road covered in snow at some of the higher elevations on the Monte-Carlo stages.
PACENOTES_CAUTION_DESC:
<StyleBold>Warning</> notes highlight sections of the road where the driver must pay particular attention or perform specific maneuvers to ensure the best performance.
When the driver hears one of these warnings, they should pay extra attention to driving and make sure they fully understand every instruction given by the co-driver, so they can best face the hazard.

The warnings can be of various types; the most commonly used are:

<StyleTitle>CAUTION</>
The <StyleBold>CAUTION</> alert is by far the most used and is often found before a particularly complex sequence or before an element of the track that represents a danger to safety or to the successful completion of the stage. At a CAUTION alert, pay extra attention to the following notes and prepare for any kind of hazard by slowing down or focusing more on the road.

<StyleTitle>WARNING INSIDE/OUTSIDE</>
In some cases, the danger may be located on the <StyleBold>INSIDE</> or <StyleBold>OUTSIDE</> of a corner. In these situations, the driver must pay extra attention to that part of the road to avoid risks.

<StyleTitle>DON'T CUT</>
When there are hidden or obvious dangers inside a corner, the co-driver's notes generally indicate DO NOT CUT that corner. This means avoiding putting the wheels off the road, maintaining a certain safety margin from the edge, to prevent any danger that could damage or slow down the car.

<StyleTitle>CUT</>
In certain corners, the co-driver may suggest the driver to <StyleBold>CUT</> the inside of the corner to save time or simplify the approach.
Cutting means it is safe to take the wheels outside the road section without risking accidents or damage to the car and tyres.
Sometimes it may be indicated whether to cut a little or a lot, to better assist the driver in setting the corner.

<StyleTitle>BRAKE</>
The <StyleBold>BRAKE</> warning suggests the driver to apply the brakes and slow down the car at that specific point of the track.
This may precede a particularly difficult corner or serve to highlight the presence of hazards or especially complex sections.

<StyleTitle>HANDBRAKE</>
The use of the <StyleBold>HANDBRAKE</> is generally indicated before a hairpin or an extremely tight corner, signaling that using the hand brake will make the car change direction more quickly, facilitating the entry and exit of the corner.

<StyleTitle>KEEP IN/OUT or LEFT/MIDDLE/RIGHT</>
Similarly to the inside/outside warning, the co-driver can instruct the driver on how best to position the car on the road to avoid hazards or adapt to particular surface shapes.
For example, the note <StyleBold>KEEP IN</> suggests placing the car on the inside of the corner, while “KEEP RIGHT” suggests moving the car to the right side of the road, relative to the driver.

<StyleTitle>BAD CAMBER</>
The note <StyleBold>BAD CAMBER</> describes a section of the road where the slope is opposite to the direction of the corner.
For example, a right-hand corner that is counter-banked will be raised on the inside rather than the outside of the corner.
This can make it difficult to set the proper line and cause problems both entering and exiting the corner, destabilizing the car.

<StyleTitle>BLIND/HIDDEN</>
A <StyleBold>BLIND</> corner generally has an exit not visible to the driver, preventing them from setting the final line in advance.
A <StyleBold>HIDDEN</> corner, on the other hand, has an entry not visible to the driver, making it harder to set the initial trajectory correctly.

<StyleTitle>SLIPPERY</>
The note <StyleBold>SLIPPERY</> indicates a section of the road that is particularly slippery, where the driver must pay extra attention to avoid wheel lockup and the risk of going off the road.

<StyleTitle>MAYBE</>
The <StyleBold>MAYBE</> note is less common but can be useful in particular situations, especially before a jump. It indicates that, depending on speed or car setup, we might face a jump or simply a "significant" bump that does not cause the wheels to leave the surface.
CARSETUP_WHEEL_COVER_DESC:
<StyleBold>Wheel covers</> help managing brake temperature during intense rally stages. By fitting these covers over the wheels, they help channel airflow around the brake components, aiding in <StyleBold>heat dissipation</> from the wheel compartment. 

This improved ventilation reduces the risk of brake overheating, which can lead to decreased performance or brake failure if the brakes get too hot. However, using them on stages with little braking can cause the brakes too cool too much, reducing their effectiveness in stopping the car under initial brake application.

PARTNER_IKERACING_COMPANY:
<StyleTitle>IKE RACING: REVIVING A BEAST</>

<StyleBold>Driven by Passion. Fueled by Legend.</>

Born from the relentless mind of entrepreneur, 30 years’ experience driver and 3x FIA European Historic Rally Champion <StyleBold>Andrea "Zippo" Zivian, IKE Racing is bringing an icon back to life: the Peugeot 306 Maxi.</> 

A pure legend of the Kit Car era, this 300hp beast is back on the stages, roaring louder than ever and ready to thrill a new generation of fans.

<StyleBold>The Evolution of an Icon.</> We didn’t just rebuild it; we perfected it. Starting with chassis no. 90 -the legendary car driven by David Salanon to dominate the French Cup in 2010 and 2011 - IKE Racing has <StyleBold>combined original engineering with cutting-edge upgrades.</>
•	<StyleBold>Custom 7-Speed Gearbox: a full re-creation of the iconic original.</>
•	<StyleBold>Precision Performance:</> Thanks to improvements in reliability, safety, and comfort, every detail has been dialed in for top-level performance.
•	<StyleBold>The Global Hub:</> we aren't just racing; we’re becoming <StyleBold>the global destination for 306 Maxi parts and specialized engineering know-how</>
•	<StyleBold>The Ultimate Collaboration:</> This project is a "Who's Who" of motorsport excellence. We’ve united the legends of the past with the tech of the future:
•	<StyleBold>Matter Motorsport:</> The original 306 chassis masters.
•	<StyleBold>Mario Fornaris (Sportech Engineering):</> The mastermind behind the 306 Maxi’s birth.
•	<StyleBold>Mako Shark & Lettieri Technology:</> High-end composites and Inconel exhaust systems.
•	<StyleBold>RTR Project & Trico WRT:</> The heart of the gearbox and precision assembly.

The outcome? A car that honours its heritage. Rally legend François Delecour steered the IKE Racing machine to victory at the 2024 Rally Madeira Legend. Meanwhile, Andrea Zivian took the overall win at Rally Weiz 2025, the car’s full-spec debut.

This isn’t a comeback—it’s a takeover. And we’re just getting started.

GROUP_MINI_COOPERS_DESC: A 1960s icon and style legend, the <StyleBold>Mini Cooper S</> is a rally symbol with compact size, power, and advanced engineering. Its front-wheel drive and excellent handling make it ideal for beginners.
CARSETUP_PLATES_NUMBER_DESC:
A <StyleBold>limited-slip differential (LSD)</> in a rally car uses <StyleBold>friction plates</> to control torque distribution between the wheels. The number of friction plates in contact directly affects the locking force of the differential, influencing wheel slip in both coast and on-power situations.

<StyleBold>Increasing</> the number of plates amplifies the locking effect, making the LSD more aggressive by transmitting more torque to the wheel with better traction. This can shift the bias towards more stability through more understeer when coasting, but more oversteer when on power.

<StyleBold>Reducing</> the number of plates reduces the locking effect, allowing for freer wheel rotation. This shifts the bias towards more freer rotation and better cornering during coast, but more understeer when on power.

This adjustability enables fine-tuning of the LSD to match driving style and conditions, enhancing traction and vehicle control within various scenarios.
FORCEFEEDBACK_WHEELMINFEDBACK_DESC: A constant force applied to the wheel to help keep it centred. Also designed for less powerful wheels that produce lower forces, i.e. non-direct drive wheels, to provide force at low input levels to counter a steering deadzone.
WARNING_PRESET_NAME_ALREADY_TAKEN: A preset with the same name already exist, please change name.
CH_RWD_GRAVEL_TEST_124ABARTH_DESC: A rear-wheel drive car with modest power, like the 124 Abarth, allows the driver to take corners in a controlled drift. Any oversteer should be managed by careful throttle control and steering input, which in this model is relatively slow to respond.
CH_RWD_TARMAC_TEST_STARTOSHF_DESC: A rear-wheel-drive car with a mid-mounted engine and high power, like the Lancia Stratos HF, ensures excellent grip on asphalt stages. The traction is outstanding, and in the event of oversteer, quick corrections can prevent sudden mistakes.
CH_ELATIA_PART2_R_DESC: A special stage that is almost entirely downhill, leading to the outskirts of Elatia. The course is wide and fast, with a few sweeping hairpins. On these roads the cars’ power is fully exploited: drivers can carry high speeds in slides, negotiating direction changes quickly and dynamically.
GROUP_124ABARTH_DESC: A symbol of Fiat’s rally ambition, the <StyleBold>124 Abarth 16V</> proved small makers could compete. Made with ultralight materials, rear-wheel drive, and 200 hp, it delivered excellent performance, durability, and great reliability in competition.
GROUP_DELTAINTEGRALEEVO_DESC: A true rally legend, the <StyleBold>Lancia Delta Integrale Evoluzione</> needs no introduction. It was the undisputed dominator of Group A, thanks to its power (365 hp), handling (4WD), and robustness, combining extreme performance with reliability.

CARSETUP_PRESSURE_DESC:
Adjust <StyleBold>tyre pressures</> to maintain the optimal contact patch and working temperature of the tyres.

<StyleBold>Increasing</> tyre pressures increases the stiffness of the tyres sidewall, decreasing the amount of heat produced in the tyre preventing and/or reducing overheating. It does, however, also reduce the tyres contact patch with the road surface, which can decrease grip. 

<StyleBold>Reducing</> tyre pressure increases the tyres contact patch and improves grip, but it does also increase rolling resistance. Lower tyre pressures also allow the tyre to move around and flex more, raising tyre temperatures, but it can increase the risk of the tyre coming off the rim.

Try balancing tyre pressure to keep, for as long as possible, the tyres in their ideal temperature window for maximum grip and durability.

HISTORY_LATE80_DESC:
After the thrilling and tumultuous era of Group B cars, the late 1980s marked a shift toward a <StyleBold>safer and more regulated</> rally landscape. The FIA banned Group B at the end of 1986, reshaping the World Rally Championship (WRC) and ushered in the <StyleBold>Group A era</>, where manufacturers had to tame their machines to fit a new, more conservative formula.

The rally scene became characterized by cars that were more closely based on production models, with less outrageous power but a focus on reliability, technology refinement, and driver skill. The iconic brands that had fought in Group B like Lancia, Peugeot, and Audi, remained central, but they now competed within these stricter regulations. Lancia particularly excelled with the <StyleBold>Delta Integrale</>, a car that would earn legendary status for its dominance in rallying during this period. The other more relevant opponents was the <StyleBold>Audi 200 Quattro</>, which was somewhat a bridge from Group B’s quattro dominance with its all-wheel-drive prowess, and the <StyleBold>Ford Sierra RS Cosworth</>, showcasing the muscle of turbocharged rear-wheel and four-wheel-drive cars in the evolving field.

Among drivers, several names stood out for their skill and success, riding these machines to victory and fame. <StyleBold>Miki Biasion</>, driving for Lancia, won the World Rally Championship drivers’ title in 1988 and 1989, and was known for his smooth style and tactical approach. <StyleBold>Juha Kankkunen</> was another top competitor, a Finnish driver with multiple World Championships, who excelled at pushing the Lancia Delta to its limits. <StyleBold>Markku Alén</>, also with Lancia, was an experienced veteran bringing a relentless competitive edge. <StyleBold>Walter Röhrl</>, a German legend renowned for his precision and technical ability, competed effectively during this era with Audi. Other notable drivers included <StyleBold>Kenneth Eriksson</>, who drove the Volkswagen Golf, and <StyleBold>Stig Blomqvist</>, notable for his skill in Ford vehicles.

For enthusiasts and newcomers alike, the late 1980s represent a fascinating transition in rallying, a movement from raw, unbridled speed to a balance of engineering mastery and driver skill that laid the foundations for the more sophisticated, technology-driven competitions that define rally today. This era preserved the drama and excitement of rally racing while making it safer and more sustainable, ensuring the sport's continued growth and global appeal.

PARTNER_PIETROCIGNI_PALMARES:
As a co-driver, he has had great satisfaction in rallying, especially alongside Tommaso. Since they started competing together, they have achieved four podium finishes in 2023 with the Škoda Fabia R5 EVO, finishing third in the CIRT. In 2024, they earned four podiums and one victory — competing in three events with the Škoda Fabia R5 EVO and two with the Škoda Fabia RS, both prepared by Team Ereffe and equipped with Pirelli tyres — finishing second in the championship. Finally, in 2025, they collected five podiums, including two wins, still driving the Škoda Fabia RS prepared by Team Ereffe and equipped with Pirelli tyres, dominating the 2025 CIRT from the very start.

Although he has competed in relatively few events, with “only” 29 rallies to his name, he has been fortunate to meet great people and professionals along the way, such as Tommaso Ciuffi and his father Paolo, who believed in his potential and quickly brought him to the highest national level. He owes them a great deal and deeply thanks them for these experiences and for passing on such a broad wealth of knowledge in this sport.

Together with Tommaso, he has also taken part in various tyre development tests for Pirelli and tests for the development of racing components. Another major milestone has been becoming part of the Sparco world, using racing apparel and safety accessories on his Škoda.
PARTNER_YIPINGCHEN_ACTIVITIES:
As a rally co-driver, Yiping Chen participated in the World Rally Championship in 2010.

He also participated in the China Rally Championship from 2010 to 2021.

He took part in the Malaysia Rally Championship in 2013 and the FIA Asia-Pacific Rally Championship from 2010 to 2016 and in 2019.

As a team manager, he operated the Toyota Team for the China Touring Car Championship and the SUBARU Rally Team China for the China Rally Championship and the China RallyCross Championship.

Currently, Yiping Chen is still involved in the operation of GT races (Lotus) and Rally (Hyundai N) in China.

He is also promoting rally races between China and international events.

Yiping collaborated with Supernova in developing the pacenote system, providing valuable insights into the rally world and the co-driver’s role. He actively identified the best phrases and notes to accurately describe the various situations faced during a rally.
Additionally, he translated all the pacenotes into the Chinese language to offer players the most authentic linguistic adaptation possible, using, whenever feasible, the terms and expressions most commonly used by co-drivers who speak this language.
Finally, he contributed his voice and experience as a co-driver during an intense recording session lasting several days, delivering the pacenotes in the most realistic way, just as he would in real rally conditions.

PARTNER_VIGEA_RALLY:
As part of the collaboration with Supernova, VIGEA played a fundamental role in the creation of this next-generation racing video game by delivering high-precision 3D surveys and detailed topographic mapping. The main goal was to replicate real-world rally environments with exceptional accuracy and visual fidelity, enabling players to experience authentic and immersive driving scenarios.

VIGEA conducted extensive fieldwork in various locations focusing on iconic rally tracks known for their technical complexity and scenic landscapes.

The company deployed a comprehensive suite of geospatial technologies, including terrestrial laser scanners, mobile mapping systems mounted on both vehicles and wearable backpacks, drone-based photogrammetry, satellite data and GNSS equipment capable of centimeter-level precision.

These tools allowed VIGEA to collect massive volumes of georeferenced spatial data, capturing the full geometry of the environment, elevation and surface textures of the rally tracks and surrounding terrains.

From cliffs and slopes to vegetation and road surfaces, every element was recorded with meticulous detail.

The data was then processed to generate highly dense 3D point clouds, which served as the core dataset for the video game’s environment modeling team production.

These point clouds provided an accurate digital replica of the surveyed areas and were used to reconstruct the virtual racing environments with exceptional realism. The development team relied on this spatially accurate foundation to 3D model terrain deformations, road features, curves, gradients and environmental elements with precision rarely seen in racing games.

Thanks to VIGEA’s expertise, the game achieved a level of realism that significantly enhances the gameplay experience, combining scientific rigor with technological innovation. This project stands as a testament to VIGEA’s ability to bridge the gap between real-world landscapes and digital simulation, delivering value across both entertainment and geospatial sectors.
CH_I20RALLY2_NIGHT_TEST1_DESC: At night, the greatest challenge is visibility. The modern headlights of the i20 Rally2 provide excellent track illumination, but it is essential to maintain the necessary concentration to avoid mistakes that could damage the lighting system and compromise the stage.
CARSETUP_PVALVE_RATIO_DESC:
Basic or stock brake systems typically offer limited adjustability, but they can include an adjustable <StyleBold>Proportioning Valve</> to enhance brake balance. As the car decelerates, it requires increasing front brake bias for stability and control. 
The Proportioning Valve achieves this by <StyleBold>reducing the rear brake line pressure</> once a certain Preload pressure is reached. This reduction occurs according to a set Ratio, allowing fine-tuning of brake performance. 

Adjusting the ratio changes how much pressure is cut from the rear brakes: <StyleBold>higher ratios</> decrease the pressure reduction, making the rear brakes more aggressive, while <StyleBold>lower ratios</> increase pressure reduction for a more stable rear braking feel.
CARSETUP_PVALVE_PRELOAD_DESC:
Basic or stock brake systems typically offer limited adjustability, but they often include an adjustable <StyleBold>Proportioning Valve</> to enhance brake balance. As the car decelerates, it requires increasing front brake bias for stability and control. 
The Proportioning Valve achieves this by <StyleBold>reducing the rear brake line pressure</> once a certain Preload pressure is reached. This reduction occurs according to a set Ratio, allowing fine-tuning of brake performance. 

Adjusting the Preload pressure changes the point of the rear pressure cut. A <StyleBold>higher Preload</> delays the cut, making rear braking more aggressive, while a <StyleBold>lower Preload</> causes earlier cut, favoring front brake dominance.
PARTNER_NICOLAARENA_BIO:
Being born in 1968 (10 December) I’m currently 57. I’m Italian, originally from Genova but now I live in a small place called Santo Stefano Belbo, in the northwest of the country, an area which traditionally hosts a lot of rallies and where rallying is well radicated. Married, one daughter. I have a degree in physics. 
I have always been passionate in motorsport, but particularly in rallying, since I was a child, thanks to my parents that took me to spectate the main events around us, like Sanremo and Quattro Regioni. While everyone else was talking about football I was annoying my schoolmates talking about the last F1 Grand Prix or the World Rally Championship results! 
It was almost unavoidable for me to start codriving in rallies as soon as I had the legal age for it, and I didn’t stop since then. 
Being a codriver has gradually become a job and now I do it full time. Anyway I worked for 22 years as a weather forecaster (quite unusual job, but very useful for rallying when tyre choice becomes crucial… it was an advantage only a few times though…) until the moment when I couldn’t keep both jobs and I chose the most fun one!
My passion became my job, so I’m really lucky. But I do also have some hobbies: I love music (mostly rock music), travelling and reading (books, not just pacenotes!).
CARDESC_FIAT_124ABARTH:
Born during a golden era of motorsport, the <StyleBold>Fiat 124 Abarth Rally 16V</> was not just another vehicle; it was a symbol of Fiat's ambition to dominate the rally scene against fierce competitors like Lancia.

Originally equipped with a 1.8-liter twin-cam engine, the 1974 model boasted an impressive output of around <StyleBold>200 horsepower</> thanks to its innovative <StyleBold>16-valve</> head design. The engine's design included double vertical twin-choke Weber carburetors and a high-performance exhaust system, enhancing its power output and responsiveness on challenging rally stages. 

The car's lightweight construction, weighing in at just <StyleBold>900 kg</>, combined with its advanced suspension system, provided exceptional handling and stability. Unlike many rally cars of the time that relied on heavier components, the Fiat 124 Abarth utilized aluminum and fiberglass in its bodywork, eliminating unnecessary weight while maintaining structural integrity.

Visually, the Fiat 124 Abarth Rally was strikingly different from other cars of its era. It featured an aggressive design with no bumpers, plastic wheel arch trims, and a sleek hardtop that replaced the convertible roof. This not only contributed to its aerodynamic efficiency but also gave it an unmistakable racing aesthetic that appealed to fans and competitors alike.

The early 1970s marked a golden age for rallying, with manufacturers vying for dominance in an increasingly competitive environment. The Fiat 124 Abarth Rally was <StyleBold>first introduced in 1973</>, and quickly became part of the Group 4 category, which required cars to be based on production models but modified for racing.

In 1974, amidst an oil crisis that led to the cancellation of several races, Fiat still managed to showcase its prowess by securing multiple podium finishes in various competitions.

The Fiat 124 Abarth Rally it's a testament to an era where passion for speed met engineering excellence. Its distinct characteristics, competitive nature, and historical importance have established it as a lasting symbol in rally racing, captivating both enthusiasts and casual fans to this day.

PARTNER_DAVIDPRICE_BIO:
Born in 1964, Dave lives near Cheltenham, England. A retired aerospace engineer, he now devotes more time to rallying, cycling, and traveling with his wife across Europe in their motorhome where he is finally attempting to master French. An active cyclist with his local club, his enthusiasm once led to a serious setback when he fractured his pelvis on a ride, though he has since recovered fully.

Dave’s passion for rallying began in the early 1980s, watching the Lombard RAC Rally and witnessing first-hand the transition from rear-wheel-drive machines to the legendary Group B four-wheel-drive turbo cars. Among his formative memories was seeing Henri Toivonen claim victory in the 1985 RAC Rally at the wheel of the iconic Lancia Delta S4.

He first entered rallying in 1985 as a driver, finishing third overall in a regional championship the following year, despite an eventful debut where he slid into a tree and briefly knocked out his co-driver. Realizing his skills were stronger in the co-driver’s seat, he embraced navigation. In the era when UK events were “blind” and relied on map-reading rather than pace notes, his early mastery of maps set the foundation for a long and successful career.

He attended his first rally as a spectator at 2 years old and made his debut as a co-driver at 16. Today, he has turned this passion into his profession. CARDESC_ALPINE_A110:
Born in a time when rally racing was gaining momentum, the <StyleBold>1973 Alpine A110 1800</> was designed to be nimble, lightweight, and incredibly agile.

At the core of the A110 is its <StyleBold>1.8-liter four-cylinder engine</>, producing an impressive <StyleBold>180 horsepower</>. This power is channeled through a five-speed manual transmission, allowing the car to reach a top speed of approximately <StyleBold>210 km/h (130 mph)</> and accelerate from 0 to 100 km/h in just about <StyleBold>7 seconds</>. The rear-wheel-drive layout enhances its handling dynamics, making it excellent to drive on twisty roads.

Its <StyleBold>lightweight construction</> was achieved through the use of fiberglass body panels and a thin sheet metal frame, which not only reduced weight but also contributed to its distinctive aerodynamic profile. The car's dimensions, specifically its short wheelbase of <StyleBold>2 meters</>, further enhance its agility, allowing it to navigate tight corners with ease.

The suspension system is quite basic but still effective, featuring double wishbones at the front and swing axle at the rear. This setup allows for fine-tuning based on driving conditions, providing excellent road feedback and stability during high-speed maneuvers. Coupled with thin solid disc brakes on all four wheels, the A110 offers remarkable stopping power and contained unsprung masses, essential for rallying.

In 1973, the <StyleBold>World Rally Championship</> was officially inaugurated, and Alpine was determined to make its mark. The A110 quickly became a symbol of French engineering prowess, competing against giants like Lancia and Ford. That same year, it played a pivotal role in helping Alpine secure the inaugural WRC title for manufacturers, showcasing its dominance on various terrains.

Despite facing stiff competition from newer models like the mid-engine Lancia Stratos in subsequent years, the A110's legacy endures. It remains a beloved classic among collectors and vintage racing enthusiasts today. Its victories in major rallies during the early 1970s have etched it into motorsport history as one of the most successful rally cars ever produced.

PARTNER_TOMMASOCIUFFI_BIO:
Born on 24 November 1993 in Florence, Tommaso Ciuffi has been immersed in motorsport since childhood. His father Paolo was a successful driver in Tuscan rallies, achieving several overall wins and passing on a passion that became a natural legacy.

Growing up alongside his father at the rallies, Tommaso could not resist the call of the sport. His own career started only at 21, after completing his studies and working for a year as a waiter. It was Paolo’s rule: duty first, then pleasure. He made his debut in 2015 at the Liburna Ronde Terra with the MG Rover ex-Procar, followed by the Nido dell’Aquila with a Fiesta R2. At only his third rally he scored a first podium, second in class at the Rally della Val d’Orcia.

From that moment his career advanced steadily, marked by important results at national level and international experiences. Precise, methodical and determined, Tommaso brings into the cockpit the same will to excel that defines him outside the car.

Detail-oriented yet with a driving style that is personal, entertaining and irreverent, he represents the complete profile of a professional driver: talent, discipline and character. Today he is also active in the family business, D6 Drive Responsibly, a responsible and eco-driving school that provides training in safe, sustainable and electric driving for companies and private drivers, where Tommaso works as an instructor.
CARSETUP_ELECTRONICS&AEREO_DESC:
Brake control is essential to maintain the correct speed through corners: an efficient braking system is the key to achieving excellent performance.
It is crucial to pay attention to every component of the car’s braking system. You can select brake discs by considering not only their diameter but also their width and type of ventilation.
It is necessary to check which calipers are compatible with the chosen discs and finally select the proper compound for the brake pads.
Additionally, the brake master cylinder settings can be adjusted to quickly modify brake balance and braking power.
CARSETUP_BRAKES_DESC:
Brake control is essential to maintain the right speed in corners: an efficient braking system is the key to achieving excellent performance.
It is crucial to pay close attention to every component of the car's braking system. You can select the brake discs, considering not only their diameter but also their width and type of ventilation.
It is necessary to check which calipers are compatible with the chosen discs and finally choose the proper compound for the brake pads.
Additionally, the brake master cylinder settings can be adjusted to quickly modify the brake balance and braking power.
DAMAGE_BRAKES_DESC:
Brakes are fundamental in a rally car, allowing effective slowing down or stopping of the car. 
Like other components, they wear out with use. 
Replace the brake pads promptly to avoid damage to the discs, which otherwise overheat and wear out more quickly. Always monitor wear to ensure safety and optimal performance during the race.

PARTNER_CHRISINGRAM_BIO:
Chris Ingram is a professional rally driver from Manchester, United Kingdom, currently based in Monaco. Born in 1994, he has built his career through performance, resilience, and determination rather than privilege, becoming one of the most accomplished British rally drivers of his generation.

From the outset, Chris’s path through motorsport has been unconventional. While his passion for rallying was inherited from his father, a former national competitor, his progression has relied on results and personal drive rather than guaranteed opportunity. Early in his career, his talent earned recognition from Peugeot UK and Opel Motorsport, who each awarded him fully funded junior factory drives. Chris converted that backing into results and titles, establishing himself as one of Europe’s leading young rally prospects and laying the foundations for senior international success.

That mindset carried him to a defining milestone in 2019, when he became the first British winner of the FIA European Rally Championship in 52 years, after a thrilling finale to the championship at Rally Hungary. Uniquely, Chris's participation in the finale was secured thanks to the supporters of a crowdfunding campaign. Later that year, he stood on stage alongside <StyleBold>Lewis Hamilton</> at the FIA Awards in Paris, seemingly on the brink of a breakthrough to the sport’s highest level.

Instead, the global COVID-19 pandemic reshaped the landscape of motorsport. Opportunities vanished, funding dried up, and Chris spent nearly two years largely sidelined from top-level competition. Rather than walking away, he rebuilt from the ground up. Without the luxury of full-season budgets, extensive testing programmes, or guaranteed seats, he has returned step by step, re-establishing himself through performance, professionalism, and persistence.

Away from the car, Chris is a proud father, a lifelong Manchester City supporter, and invested in high-performance training, mindset work, and commercial opportunities in elite sport. His journey is defined by endurance as much as speed, a career shaped by adaptation, belief, and the ability to keep moving forward when the odds are stacked against him.

A unique journey, only part-way told, with the story still very much being written.
PARTNER_CHRISINGRAM_ACTIVITIES:
Chris Ingram’s rally career has been built step by step from grassroots junior rallying through to national, European, and world-level competition. Progressing without a fixed factory pathway, he advanced through results and hard work, earning each opportunity on merit before moving into junior factory programmes, FIA championships, and ultimately the highest tiers of international rallying.

His early international career was shaped by fully funded junior factory drives with Peugeot UK and Opel Motorsport, where he developed a reputation as a fast, adaptable, and consistent driver. This progression led him into senior FIA competition and ultimately the European Rally Championship.

A major step came in 2018 when Chris transitioned into four-wheel-drive machinery, immediately showing top-level pace. He joined the then-emerging Toksport WRT, where his performances contributed to the team’s rapid rise and growing reputation. Ingram secured a podium finish on his WRC2 debut at Rally Turkey driving a Skoda Fabia R5, underlining his ability to perform at World Championship level. The following season, in 2019, he delivered his breakthrough year by winning the FIA European Rally Championship, confirming his capacity to perform consistently across surfaces and under sustained pressure.

Following the disruption caused by COVID-19, Chris returned to competition in 2021 and 2022 through selected WRC2 events, using limited opportunities to rebuild momentum and accumulate crucial experience at the highest level. In 2023, he formed a new partnership with co-driver Alex Kihurani. On their first event together at Ypres Rally Belgium, they immediately fought for victory, battling Adrien Fourmaux and finishing a close second overall. They later competed in the French Rally Cup, where they went head-to-head with nine-time World Rally Champion Sébastien Loeb, trading fastest stage times throughout the event and securing a podium finish.

In 2024, Chris and Alex joined Castrol MEM and went on to win the British Rally Championship title, claiming four victories across the season while competing in both the Volkswagen Polo R5 and later the Toyota GR Yaris Rally2.

Chris is now focused on progressing toward a full FIA World Rally Championship campaign. Subject to funding, his objective is a full WRC2 season in 2026, with the longer-term aim of securing a manufacturer opportunity aligned with the new FIA technical regulations from 2027 onwards. His career to date has been funded entirely through external sponsorship and private investment, requiring him to operate not only as a driver, but also as a commercial operator.

PARTNER_CANDIDO_BIO:
Cándido Carrera Estévez was born on March 24, 1980 (45 years old) in Salvaterra de Miño (GALICIA/ESPAÑA﻿), a small town on the border with Portugal. He studied commercial administration and later vehicle electromechanics. His early jobs were as a truck mechanic, and later he worked in automotive component factories while also studying welding.

In 2011, he took a leave of absence from his company and has been professionally dedicated to co-driving since then. For the past 4 years, he has also worked in agriculture, where together with his wife they have a vineyard of Albariño wine and are partners in a winemaking cooperative.
Interestingly, neither his father nor his mother has a driver’s license. At home, there were only small motorcycles, although his older brother, who is a truck driver by profession, sparked his interest in cars, which they never had at home.

Besides rallying, Cándido regularly practices other sports such as cycling, tennis, kayaking, and hiking. Competitively, he participates in orienteering raids that combine various disciplines including trekking, cycling, kayaking, archery, rappelling, and more.
He is a member of the Vizhoja Cornelios club, with which they have been champions of the Galician and Spanish leagues in some editions, reaching participation in 3 world cup events in that discipline.
PARTNER_CANDIDO_ACTIVITIES:
Cándido Carrera’s beginnings in the world of four wheels involved building wooden cars with bearings (llamados carros de bolas﻿) together with his cousin, which they later used to compete in very popular downhill races in their local area.

In 1997, he started collaborating as a Marshall for reconnaissance and route commissioner in the Rallye Rias baixas﻿. By 2001, during the Rally do Lacón/Carballiño﻿, he began competing as a co-driver alongside a mechanic friend of his brother named Luis Lemos. Before debuting, he took a course with Diego Vallejo to understand the role of the co-driver. That same year, together with some friends from his village, he co-founded the Escudería Surco﻿, of which he remains a member today. This helped him progress in his career by deepening his understanding of rallying from an organizational perspective and strengthening his skills as a co-driver. He also worked actively with the Federación Gallega de Automovilismo﻿ as a Slalom observer and rallymix championship manager, while collaborating with other Escuderías at various events to gain more experience.

Sportingly, as a co-driver from his debut in 2001 until 2004, he competed in various regional championship rallies with different drivers from his area, many of whom were friends, racing mainly for fun while always trying to learn as much as possible. During this period, a co-driver from Vigo, José Ramon Seoane, supported him significantly, and they often met to practice notes whenever possible.

In 2005, he started competing in national single-make cups alongside driver Oscar Garre, with whom he achieved official driver status for Peugeot Sport España in 2008, although a couple of crashes led to the team separating them.

From 2008 to 2010, Cándido ran occasional races around Galicia. In 2010, he began competing with José Antonio Suarez, a partnership that lasted until 2018 with a brief hiatus in 2014 before returning in 2015.

From 2018 onward, he competed with Daniel Alonso, who had been their sponsor and mentor since 2011. Together, they participated in all kinds of races, including rally, historic rally, and raid events. In 2021, he debuted in raids at the Baja a Loule. Additionally, he took on various team roles with Daniel’s team, Past Racing﻿.

July 2021 marked the highest moment of his sporting career when Dani Sordo invited him to compete alongside him in the official Hyundai WRC team, a driver with whom Cándido remains connected today, sharing experiences in WRC, national competitions, and raids. That same year, while serving as coordinator for the second Dakar season with Eduard Pons’s team, he was contacted by Nasser Al-Attiyah to be his co-driver for Merc 2025.

Cándido collaborated with Supernova in developing the pacenote system, providing valuable insights into the rally world and the co-driver’s role. He actively identified the best phrases and notes to accurately describe the various situations faced during a rally.
Additionally, he translated all the pacenotes into the Spanish language to offer players the most authentic linguistic adaptation possible, using, whenever feasible, the terms and expressions most commonly used by co-drivers who speak this language.
Finally, he contributed his voice and experience as a co-driver during an intense recording session lasting several days, delivering the pacenotes in the most realistic way, just as he would in real rally conditions.

RULES_PENALTIES_DESC:
Everyone hates penalties, but they are essential to ensure that the competition rules are respected and that those who commit an irregularity do not gain an unfair advantage.

In some cases, penalties can help players immerse themselves more in the world of rally by recreating realistic penalties adapted to AC Rally.

The list of penalties that the player may incur is as follows (the severity of the penalty varies depending on the selected game options):

•	<StyleBold>False start:</> if the car moves before the countdown finishes, a time penalty (in seconds) is added to the race time.

•	<StyleBold>Blocking the starting position:</> remaining stationary at the start for too long may result in disqualification from the race.

•	<StyleBold>Blocking the road:</> stopping in the middle of the road for a prolonged period results in a time penalty added to the race time.

•	<StyleBold>Driving against traffic:</> driving against traffic for a significant stretch results in a time penalty or even disqualification, if the infraction is repeated multiple times.

•	<StyleBold>Knocking down anti-cut markers:</> knocking down the red stakes placed at the roadside to prevent cutting corners results in a time penalty added to the race time.

•	<StyleBold>Cutting a corner:</> leaving the track and then returning after gaining a time advantage compared to staying on the correct path results in a time penalty proportional to the advantage gained.

•	<StyleBold>Collision with spectators or officials:</> hitting any member of the crowd, safety personnel, race officials, or photographers with the car results in a time penalty added to the race time.

•	<StyleBold>Reaching track limits or forced re-entry:</> a forced re-entry onto the track always results in a time penalty calculated based on the distance the vehicle traveled off the road to return.

HISTORY_70_DESC:
From <StyleBold>1970 to 1979</>, rally racing experienced a remarkable evolution that ultimately gave birth to the <StyleBold>World Rally Championship</> (WRC) and shaped modern rallying as we know it today.

In the early part of the decade, rally events were organized under the <StyleBold>International Championship for Manufacturers</>, which ran from 1970 to 1972. This period gathered some of the most significant rallies but lacked a formal drivers' competition. It was a time when manufacturers were fiercely competing, setting the stage for something bigger.

Then, in 1973, the <StyleBold>FIA</> (Federation Internationale de l'Automobile) took a giant step forward by launching the World Rally Championship, uniting thirteen of the world’s most challenging and prestigious rallies into one global series. The inaugural season kicked off with the legendary Monte Carlo Rally. While initially only manufacturers were crowned champions, this new structure transformed rallying into a truly international sport with greater cohesion and visibility.

Renault made a strong statement right out of the gate, clinching the manufacturers' title with their agile Alpine A110, a car perfectly suited for the demanding rally stages. But the mid-1970s saw the arrival of even more revolutionary machines that captured the imagination of fans and competitors alike. The Lancia Stratos HF stood out as the very first car designed exclusively for rallying, boasting a powerful Ferrari V6 engine. Its dominance was undeniable, securing three consecutive manufacturers' titles. Meanwhile, the Ford Escort RS, driven by stars like Hannu Mikkola and Björn Waldegård, became a rally icon thanks to its versatility and sheer grit.

The competition increased more as Fiat entered the fray with its technically advanced 131 Abarth, adding another layer of rivalry to the mix. Each manufacturer brought unique strengths, Fiat excelled on tarmac, Ford on gravel,creating thrilling battles across diverse terrains.

Though rallying still awaited its <StyleBold>official drivers’ championship</>, the late 1970s featured the FIA Cup for Drivers in 1977 and 1978, spotlighting talents such as Sandro Munari and Markku Alén. Finally, in 1979, the first official World Rally Drivers’ Championship was awarded to Björn Waldegård, that helped Ford reclaiming the manufacturers’ crown with the Escort RS1800.

The 1970s were a vibrant, transformative decade, a melting pot of innovation, competition, and passion that laid the foundation for rallying’s golden age and a truly global motorsport phenomenon.

PARTNER_MACALUSO_BRAND:
Gino’s most mature tribute to the myth of the car was the recovery and restoration of some of the most significant rally cars in the history of the specialty and Gran Turismo, whose design made an indelible impression on the imagination of the world’s public in the second half of the twentieth century. 

Gino has always favored preserving the patina of time and the appearance of an object’s past whenever possible, especially with cars in which the signs of a glorious past are still legible, refusing radical reconstruction and the static display of machines designed for movement. 

The dent in the hood of a Mini Cooper S caused by the jumps at the 1000 Lakes’ Rally makes much more sense than its impeccable repainting. A car is not only more beautiful in itself than the Victory of Samothrace, it is also more beautiful because it is art in movement, to be touched, driven, sniffed, listened to and experienced to record authentic emotions.

The Gino Macaluso collection, consisting of motorsport and Gran Turismo cars, has no equal in the world because of the originality of its specimens and the important races they won, and it is today one of the few, or the only one, to have brought together all the Lancia Martinis that have made history on circuits and in rallies.

It has participated to international events including WRC Rally Japan, Goodwood Festival of Speed, Pebble Beach Concours d’Elegance, Sanremo Rally Storico, Bologna Auto e Moto d’Epoca, Automotoretrò, the Gino Macaluso Memorial, in occasion of the Cesana-Sestrières race and the Italy-France bilateral meeting at Palazzo Reale, Naples, in February 2020. 

The Fondazione has designed the exhibition concept “The Golden Age of Rally”, which through the cars of the collection presents the unique history of this discipline, from the 60s to the 90s. It has been displayed in international museums such as Museo dell’Automobile in Turin and Fuji Motorsport Museum in Japan. 

The cars have been exhibited in prestigious international museums such as Louwman Museum, Conservatory of the French Monoplace at MagnyCours, Museo Ferrari Maranello, Museo Enzo Ferrari, becoming a point of reference for scholars, collectors and enthusiasts.

PARTNER_FRANCOISDELACUOUR_BIO:
I am François Delecour, a professional rally driver from France, born on August 30, 1962, in Hazebrouck. Motorsport has defined my life and career for more than four decades. I am best known for finishing runner-up in the 1993 World Rally Championship, one of the most competitive seasons in rally history.
I began my career in the 1980s, progressing from regional rallies to the international stage through dedication, discipline, and passion. Over the years, I competed against some of the greatest drivers of my generation, achieving four WRC victories and numerous podium finishes. Driving for major manufacturers allowed me to gain invaluable experience across all surfaces gravel, asphalt, snow, and ice.
One particularly significant chapter of my career was my time as an official factory driver for Peugeot in 1997 and 1998. During that period, I drove the legendary Peugeot 306 Maxi at the highest level, a car that became iconic in asphalt rallying and I represented Peugeot as an official driver in the French Rally Championship. 
Beyond motorsport, I have always maintained a strong passion for sport and the outdoors. One of my main interests outside motorsport is cycling. Over the years, I have taken part in several demanding amateur cycling events and long-distance rides, particularly in mountainous regions where endurance and mental strength are essential.
I enjoy riding and training in areas known for their dramatic terrain, including volcanic roads and high-altitude climbs. The challenge of steep gradients and unpredictable weather conditions reminds me in many ways of rally driving it requires stamina, focus, and determination.
Even outside of a rally car, I continue to seek performance, endurance, and personal challenge — values that define both my sporting life and who I am.
PARTNER_NICOLAARENA_PALMARES:
I started codriving in 1988, thanks to a guy from Genova, Pino Spagnolo, that trusted me.
First years were mostly on regional events, where I won a Opel Corsa Cup in 1992 and some regional class championships (from 1992 to 1994) alongside Enrico Pagano. 
The big step was in 1996 when I began codriving Andrea Maselli: we headed outside Italy and won the Fiat Cinquecento Europa Cup. 
In 1997 with Maselli we were back in Italy where we won the Group N title in the 2 Liters Championship, at the same time I partially codrove Valter Ballestrero that won the Fiat Cinquecento Europa Cup. 
In 2006 I began competing in Middle-East championship, where I did compete regularly for more than ten years. This amazing experience gave me a FIA title in 2010 with the late Misfer Al-Marri, and also a Jordan Championship in 2007 with Amjad Farrah. 
In 2008 I also competed in bajas and with Majed Al-Ghamdi we finished second in the T2 FIA championship.
In 2015 Gianluca Linari and me won the Production Cup in the WRC, and also won the International Rally Cup in Italy with Corrado Fontana. 
2016 gave me a Group N codriver title in Middle-East, with Rashid Al-Naimi, 
In 2020 I won an Italian WRC Championship, again with Corrado Fontana. 
Finally in 2024 with "Zippo" we won the Category 3 in European Historic Rally Championship and in 2022 and 2024 with him we won the gold medal in the FIA Motorsport Games.

OPTION_PENALTY_DESC:

Penalties occur in the following cases:
•	Driving in the wrong direction

This indicates that the engine can no longer efficiently expel exhaust gases, thus reducing the car's overall performance during the race.
OPTION_IGNITION_DESC:

DAMAGE_WHEELGEOMETRY_DESC:
Impacts or harsh landings can deform the suspension geometry, causing misalignment.
This misalignment generates asymmetric forces that push the car sideways, compromising stability and handling.
Regular checks and adjustments of the suspension are essential to maintain optimal performance and control, especially in demanding rally conditions where precise vehicle dynamics are crucial for safety and speed.
