CARSETUP_BRAKE_BIAS_DESC:
In a car equipped with <StyleBold>two master cylinders</>, the brake pressure distribution can be adjusted by manipulating a lever that controls the <StyleBold>pressure bias ratio between the front and rear brakes</>. 

This system allows for fine-tuning the braking performance based on driving conditions and surface grip.

Shifting the Brake Bias forwards can make the car behave more predictably, biasing the car towards understeer during braking. Shifting the bias rewards will allow for more rotation and oversteer during braking, but can make the car more difficult to control. 
Find the right balance for your own driving preference and surface type you’re driving on.

It’s important to note that this pressure bias setting does not directly translate to the final brake torque at each wheel. Variations such as brake caliper efficiency, brake disc size, and tyre grip can all influence the actual torque applied. Therefore, always verify the final brake torque distribution on the wheels to ensure optimal balance and performance.
CARSETUP_CENTERATIOTOFRONT_DESC:
In a rally car, adjusting the <StyleBold>torque ratio sent to the front differential</> allows control over front torque distribution.

Setting this ratio higher than the rear shifts torque bias to the front, improving traction but also increasing the overall final drive ratio.
This change can reduce the top speed while enhancing acceleration.
To balance this, you can adjust the gearbox final ratio in the opposite direction to maintain desired overall gearing.

An asymmetric setup also preloads the center differential by introducing a small slip between front and rear outputs, enabling quicker response to axle slip and improving handling and stability on varied surfaces.
PARTNER_NICKELLIOTT_ACTIVITIES:
In addition to Escort success, Elliott has played a key role in the development and competitive rise of the Fiat 131 Abarth in British historic rallying. His involvement has helped establish the car as a genuine rival to the Escort, earning strong results and widespread admiration from fans and competitors alike.

Beyond results, Elliott is widely respected for his professionalism, experience, and technical understanding of rally cars. His ability to adapt across eras and machinery from historic to more modern categories has cemented his status as one of the most accomplished drivers in the British historic rally scene.

A defining feature of Elliott’s career has been his long-standing and highly successful partnership with co-driver Dave Price, a collaboration that has delivered sustained success at the highest level of historic rallying. Together, they have combined precision, pace, and reliability, often traded wins or pushing at the very front of the field.
CH_4WD_RAIN_TEST_DELTAINTEGRALE_DESC: In difficult conditions with low grip, such as on wet surfaces, the viscous differential of the Lancia Delta's all-wheel-drive system can cause the car to slide. On corner exit, applying the throttle too early can lead to understeer, while excessive throttle on corner entry can cause oversteer.
CARSETUP_ROD_LENGHT_DESC:
In many cars, the <StyleBold>ride height</> is adjusted using a push/pull-rod mechanism. This setup includes a rod connecting the coil over damper to the wheel assembly.

By changing the length of this rod, you can fine-tune the ride height without altering the damper’s working position. This means the damping characteristics remain consistent, eliminating the need for further adjustments after ride height changes.

Increase the Rod Length to raise the ride height of the car, preventing the car from bottoming out on rougher more bumpier surfaces, whilst decreasing the Rod Length will lower the ride height. 

This method provides precise control over vehicle stance and suspension geometry, essential for optimizing handling and performance on varied surfaces typical in rally racing.
CH_RWD_MIXED_TEST_131ABARTH_DESC: In mixed conditions, all-wheel drive delivers excellent performance and optimal grip in every situation. Selecting the right tire type remains essential, however, for maximizing the car's balance.
CH_4WD_MIXED_TEST_IMPREZAS3_DESC: In mixed conditions, all-wheel drive ensures excellent performance and grip in every situation. Selecting the right tire remains essential for optimizing the car's balance.
CH_FWD_MIXED_TEST_306MAXI_DESC: In mixed conditions, front-wheel-drive cars accentuate their typical understeer behavior. Selecting the right tire remains essential, however, to achieve the optimal overall vehicle balance.
CH_GENERIC_NIGHT_EVENT_DESC: In night stages, preserving the vehicle's lighting system is crucial. Rally cars are equipped with oversized headlights and powerful auxiliary lights, capable of providing deep and uniform illumination along every timed section. However, reduced lateral visibility can conceal treacherous obstacles at the track edges, and damage to the lights can irreparably compromise the stage performance.
PARTNER_FRANCOISDELACUOUR_ACTIVITIES:
In recent years, I have reunited with the 306 Maxi in historic rally competitions, continuing to demonstrate its competitiveness and legacy.
This season, I will compete in the FIA Historic World Championship (FIA EHRC) with the Peugeot 306 Maxi by IKE Racing. My objective is clear: to fight for overall victory and win the world title. Returning to world-level competition with a car that marked such an important chapter of my career is both symbolic and highly motivating.
With decades of experience and an unchanged passion for rallying, I remain fully committed physically, technically, and mentally to achieving this goal and continuing to represent the sport at the highest level.
Beyond competition, I remain deeply connected to motorsport through mentoring, ambassador roles, and historic rally events.
Even today, the adrenaline and focus required at the start line remain unchanged. Rallying is not just my profession it is my lifelong passion.
CH_306MAXI_SNOW_TEST1_DESC: In snowy conditions, the Peugeot 306 remains a manageable and agile car, also thanks to the contained torque of its naturally aspirated engine. However, the typical front-wheel-drive traits and weight balance tend to exacerbate rear-end traction loss during deceleration.
CARDESC_LANCIA_RALLY037EVO2:
In the <StyleBold>early 1980s</>, the world of rallying was undergoing a significant transformation with the introduction of Group B cars. Among these innovative vehicles, the Lancia Rally 037 Evo2 emerged as a testament to Lancia's determination and ingenuity. Born in 1984, this car represented the pinnacle of Lancia's efforts to dominate the rally scene, even as the industry was shifting towards four-wheel drive technology.

The commitment to <StyleBold>rear-wheel drive</> was one of the most distinctive features of the Lancia Rally 037 Evo2. In an era where four-wheel drive was becoming the norm, Lancia's decision to stick with rear-wheel drive made the 037 Evo2 the last of its kind to win a <StyleBold>World Rally Championship title</>. This choice underscored Lancia's confidence in the technology and its ability to deliver exceptional performance.

The 037 Evo2 also stood out for its use of a <StyleBold>supercharged engine</>, a departure from the turbocharging that many of its competitors adopted. This design choice eliminated turbo lag, providing instant throttle response and making the car a joy to drive on the twisty rally stages. The mid-mounted engine layout further enhanced the car's agility, allowing for better weight distribution and handling. Combined with its lightweight Kevlar body, the 037 Evo2 was both responsive and nimble.

The Evo2 version was equipped with a powerful <StyleBold>2.1-liter</>, four-cylinder engine that produced <StyleBold>325 horsepower</> at 8,000 rpm. This impressive power output enabled the car to accelerate from 0 to 100 km/h in just 3.9 seconds, making it a formidable competitor on the rally circuits.

The Lancia Rally 037 Evo2 was developed in response to the <StyleBold>Group B regulations</>, which required manufacturers to produce at least 200 road-going versions of their rally cars. Lancia initially met this requirement with the 037 model, but the Evo2 was part of a series of evolutionary steps aimed at maintaining competitiveness. Despite facing stiff competition from four-wheel drive cars like the Peugeot 205 T16, the 037 Evo2 secured notable victories, including <StyleBold>Markku Alén's</> win at the 1984 Tour de Corse.

Today, the Lancia Rally 037 Evo2 is remembered not only for its racing achievements but also for its innovative design and engineering. It pushed the boundaries of what was possible with rear-wheel drive technology, leaving a <StyleBold>lasting legacy</> that continues to inspire rally enthusiasts. As an iconic symbol of the Group B era, the 037 Evo2 represents a period in rally history marked by daring innovation and thrilling competition.

CARSETUP_TOE_DESC:
In the top-down/birds-eye view, car wheels are <StyleBold>Toe In</> if angled inward towards the centre of the car and <StyleBold>Toe Out</> if angled outward.

<StyleBold>Front Toe In</> boosts straight-line stability by keeping the car steady, while <StyleBold>Front Toe Out</> reduces Camber Thrust effects, sharpening turn-in and responsiveness of the car. 
 
<StyleBold>Rear Toe In</> enhances cornering stability by creating lateral force and improving grip, whereas <StyleBold>Rear Toe Out</> reduces stability, allowing more rotation leading to an increase in oversteer 

Rally setups often use slight Front Toe Out for better responsiveness and Rear Toe In for balanced cornering stability. Toe settings balance stability and agility based on driving needs.
CARSETUP_GEARBOX_DESC:

The overall speed or that of individual gears should be tailored to the specific demands of the track.
It is important to remember that additional adjustments to the differential ratios are available in the dedicated section.
CARSETUP_WHEELS_DESC:

These adjustments allow you to optimize tyre grip according to the type of surface you will be driving on.
CH_FABIARSR2_RAIN_TEST1_DESC: In wet conditions every surface becomes very slippery and, despite the Fabia RS’s all‑wheel drive, you need to pay maximum attention to braking points and to controlling the slide. In these conditions it is very easy to run off the road in a dangerous way.
CH_FULVIACOUPEHF_RAIN_TEST1_DESC: In wet special stages, tire grip is evidently compromised. On any surface, rain makes the road slippery, lengthening braking distances and highlighting understeer issues during acceleration, given the front-wheel drive of the Fulvia HF.
FORCEFEEDBACK_TRUEFORCEGAIN_DESC:
Increases the intensity of advanced force feedback effects sent to your wheel. Set to zero to disable these additional effects while keeping the default feedback active.

This feature requires a compatible wheel that supports advanced force feedback.
CARSETUP_ENGINE_COAST_MAP_DESC:
Increasing the <StyleBold>Engine Coast Map</> adjusts the engine’s behavior when off the throttle, boosting the coast torque. This higher coast torque <StyleBold>helps to slow down</> the driving wheels by increasing the amount of engine braking, which can improve control during off-throttle situations like corner entry or downhill sections.

While this increased engine braking can enhance traction by preventing excessive wheel spin, it can impact the cars ability to coast and modulate steady speeds through corners when off-throttle, and also raises the risk of locking the wheels under heavy braking or aggressive cornering.

CARDESC_MINI_COOPERS:
Launched in 1964, the <StyleBold>Mini Cooper S 1275</> revolutionized the automotive and rally worlds by combining practicality with thrilling performance. At a time when larger, more powerful vehicles dominated, the Mini Cooper S emerged as a strong contender in motorsport.

What made the Mini Cooper S 1275 stand out was its compact size and impressive engineering. Powered by a <StyleBold>1275 cc engine</> producing around 115 horsepower, it could accelerate from 0 to 100 km/h in under 11 seconds and reach nearly 160 km/h. Its lightweight construction and agile handling gave it a <StyleBold>go-kart-like feel</>, making it exceptionally nimble on winding roads and challenging terrains, key traits for rally success.

The Mini Cooper S became a <StyleBold>rally legend</>, securing three consecutive victories at the Monte Carlo Rally in 1964, 1965, and 1967. The 1964 win, driven by <StyleBold>Patrick "Paddy" Hopkirk</>, was particularly remarkable as it triumphed over much larger competitors, like the Ford Falcon V8. Hopkirk's victory demonstrated that skill could surpass sheer power, and the car's tartan red body with a white roof became an iconic symbol of British motorsport.

The success of the Mini Cooper S not only made it a rally champion but also a <StyleBold>cultural icon</> of the 1960s, representing fun and freedom. The results in motorsport helped boost its appeal to the public, making it a symbol of both performance and personality. This also influenced other manufacturers to invest in motorsport as a marketing tool, demonstrating that rally victories could significantly enhance a car's commercial appeal.

Additionally, he translated all the pacenotes into the French language to offer players the most authentic linguistic adaptation possible, using, whenever feasible, the terms and expressions most commonly used by co-drivers who speak this language.

PARTNER_MEGARIDE_RALLY:
MegaRide applies vehicle–tyre expertise to top-tier rally programs, supporting engineering decisions from pre-event preparation to post-stage analysis. MegaRide blends on- and off-road testing with physics-based methods to give teams a clear view of grip, wear and temperature evolution on mixed surfaces and over long stages. Field activities include targeted characterization of rally vehicles and tyres, objective handling maneuvers, and control-system checks, translating measurements into set-up choices that hold up across distance and terrain changes.

Data gathered in instrumented sessions is used to map road roughness, rolling radius and surface variability, then fed to predictive algorithms that anticipate performance trends as conditions shift. This enables tuning of suspension, tyre usage windows and energy management with a focus on durability and consistency, not just peak speed. The same procedures are exercised in human-in-the-loop environments, so what is learned in the field can be rehearsed virtually and re-applied before the next run.

MegaRide’s rally work operates at WRC-spec level within open testing weeks and dedicated sessions, reinforcing correlation between virtual roads and measured responses. When needed, the same approach supports embedded execution, linking trackside sensing to real-time estimation used by vehicle controls. The outcome is a repeatable workflow that helps define design choices, set-up windows and tyre-management strategies without disclosing any specific team or car.
PARTNER_MEGARIDE_BRAND:
MegaRide company is a SME and academic spin-off of the University of Naples Federico II, founded in 2016 within the Vehicle Dynamics research group. It serves the global automotive industry with a comprehensive suite for vehicle-dynamics simulation, enabling manufacturers to test and optimize vehicles in virtual environments. The company was formed within the university’s tech-transfer so research and engineering remain tightly connected.

MegaRide develops physics-based models and procedures that reproduce tire–road interaction in real time, turning laboratory knowledge into tools used on simulators, test benches and vehicles. From the outset, its work has sat at the intersection of racing and engineering prototyping, covering virtual development and simulator sessions, objective testing, and onboard estimation of grip and road conditions. 

Across world-championship paddocks, single-seater, prototype, two-wheel and electric series engineers use MegaRide softwares to quantify grip, thermal effects and wear so setup choices and control logics are grounded in physics rather than guesswork. In several series, methods originating from the MegaRide ecosystem are considered standard practice.

Beyond racing, MegaRide software supports vehicle manufacturers, tyre makers, Tier-1 suppliers and simulator providers. More than 70 contracts have been delivered to international players, extending applications to braking systems and other OEM domains, with the same objective: faster development cycles and traceable, physics-based decisions. The community’s response reflects this footprint, with recurring sector prizes for tyre modeling and simulation, academic and innovation awards for tech transfer, and selections as a case study or invited training at specialist events.

Today MegaRide operates as a tech-transfer micro-holding: alongside its core activities, it has started new ventures and completed a strategic acquisition, coordinating methods, IP and know-how across the group while maintaining a direct link with the university lab where its technologies originate.

DEVICE_PAD_STEER_TORQUE_GAIN_DESC:
Modify the steering input value by applying the forces transmitted from the wheels to the car's steering.
Increasing the value makes the input receive more force from the wheels; decreasing it attenuates the force.
CARSETUP_DISCS_DESC:
Modulating brake power becomes more difficult on low-grip surfaces, so choosing smaller brake discs can help by directly reducing the brake torque applied.

Brake discs are sorted by diameter and cooling efficiency, the larger the disc, the greater the potential brake torque and better cooling.

Smaller, non-vented discs tend to heat up more quickly than larger, highly vented ones, which is important to consider in your strategy.

Keep in mind that changing the discs will likely affect your brake bias as well.
PARTNER_NICOLAARENA_ACTIVITIES:
Motorsport has been with me for most of my life. I was a fan, I was a spectator, I have been marshaling a few times, I did work as a team coordinator, I did drive in a couple of events and most of the times I have been codriving. Rallies first of all but also bajas and regularity events. 
Rallying took me across the 5 continents, where I competed in 47 countries in a total of 612 events, still counting. 
Nearly half of my career was outside Italy: I did compete in WRC in various seasons (Junior WRC and Production Cup) or in scattered events, scoring points in a couple of occasions. I did follow regularly ERC (European Rally Championship), APRC (Asia-Pacific Rally Championship), MERC (Middle East Rally Championship) and EHRC (European Historic Rally Championship). 
I had over 90 drivers from 16 countries and I am codriving not only in Italian but also in English and in French. 
How did I get here? Passion, determination, hard work. It has been a fantastic journey and I’m still enjoying it a lot. I am still busy competing and being able to do it across the border enables me to combine travelling and rallying. 
I hope to be able to compete for many more years and to keep on enjoying what I am doing. I would like to reach the 100 WRC starts (I’m at 88 at the moment). I really enjoying doing longer events, which do not fit in the standard format of modern events, so I loved competing in the Safari Classic, in RAC Historic, in Tour Auto etc. Multi-days events and roadside service still have a great charme for me.
CH_LIVIGNO_FULL_F_DESC:
Nestled in the heart of the mountains of Northern Italy, the Livigno Circuit﻿ offers the opportunity to challenge both the driver's technical skills and the vehicle's mechanical performance on a complex surface like snow.

The circuit allows for long drifts, thanks to its wide track, providing a fair margin for error. However, the slippery surface is unforgiving and it can be easy to lose control of the vehicle.
PARTNER_NICKELLIOTT_BIO:
Nick Elliott is a highly respected British rally driver with a long and successful career across historic and modern rallying. Renowned for his smooth, committed driving style and deep mechanical sympathy, Elliott has built a reputation as one of the standout competitors on gravel and forest stages.

He rose to prominence through national rallying in the UK before becoming a front-running force in historic competition, particularly in the British Historic Rally Championship. Best known for his success in the iconic Ford Escort Mk2, Elliott has achieved numerous overall victories and has consistently been regarded as one of the crews to beat, especially on demanding gravel events.

A standout early highlight was his involvement in the Peugeot Talbot Sport GTi Challenge in the 1990s, a fiercely competitive, factory-backed series that placed him wheel-to-wheel with some of the best emerging talent in the UK, including a young Richard Burns. Matching times with such competition confirmed that Nick had the pace to compete at the highest levels.
PARTNER_NICKELLIOTT_PALMARES:
Nick has multiple overall wins in the British Historic Rally Championship achieving over 30 event victories, primarily in the iconic Ford Escort Mk2, and more recently in the Fiat 131 Abarth.

He has been a front-running historic rally driver for decades and consistently recognised as one of the crews to beat, particularly on gravel and forest events, where Nick’s pace and car control have made him a benchmark for others.

He achieved an overall rally win on his first event with long-time co-driver Dave, in the Dalby Forests, demonstrating immediate chemistry and competitive pace.

With decades of competition, hundreds of stage miles, and victories across the UK and Europe, Nick Elliott continues to be a prominent and influential figure in rallying, combining passion for the sport with a commitment to excellence behind the wheel.
CH_LIVIGNO_FULL_F_NIGHT_DESC: Nighttime visibility can be impaired by snow-covered surfaces reflecting light, making it difficult to accurately judge distances and potentially confusing the driver. For this reason, it is essential to stay fully focused, avoiding losing sight of the edges of the road and running into dangerous snowbanks.
CH_FABIARSR2_NIGHT_TEST1_DESC: Nighttime visibility is always reduced, but the modern headlights of the Škoda Fabia RS Rally2 mitigate the poor ambient lighting, providing acceptable conditions and excellent road surface visibility. Still, pay close attention to the road's profile and edges to avoid any hazards hidden by the low light conditions.
OPTION_VIDEO_HDR_NITS_DESC: Nits is a unit of brightness, technically candelas per square meter (cd/m²). It defines how bright the screen can get, which determines how well HDR content is displayed.
CH_4WD_GRAVEL_TEST_I20RALLY2_DESC: On gravel roads, all-wheel-drive cars like the i20 Rally 2 can use drifting to take corners at high speeds while keeping the vehicle stable. Slowing down and setting up corners require different techniques compared to asphalt, but the features of all-wheel drive provide optimal control at every phase of driving.
CH_IMPREZAS3_GRAVEL_TEST1_DESC: On gravel surfaces, the short wheelbase enables sharper direction changes and excellent roadholding, enhanced by all-wheel drive. The boxer engine delivers consistent power and torque even in the most challenging conditions of the special stages.
CH_RALLY037EVO2_GRAVEL_TEST1_DESC: On gravel, due to the high power of its rear engine, it is essential to anticipate the car's reactions and be extremely gentle with the throttle. The best approach is not to aim immediately for the maximum possible speed but to take advantage of the excellent chassis to find your own rhythm and connect the corners by exploiting the pendulum effect.
CH_FWD_GRAVEL_TEST_208RALLY4_DESC: On gravel, front-wheel-drive cars with medium power, such as the 208 Rally4, require careful control at corner entry to avoid oversteer and braking errors. By making the most of pendulum movements and weight transfers, it is possible to properly set the cornering line and maintain high speeds.
CH_306MAXI_GRAVEL_TEST1_DESC: On gravel, the Peugeot 306 II Maxi shows the typical front-wheel-drive behavior: marked understeer on corner entry and difficulties on exit. Proper use of the pendulum technique, combined with precise throttle control, still allows extracting satisfying performance for this category.
CH_I20RALLY2_GRAVEL_TEST1_DESC: On gravel, the i20 Rally2’s road-holding capabilities are put to the test. Compared to tarmac, the dirt surface tends to be more slippery, requiring a different approach to slowing down the car and setting the corners. At the same time, you can use drifting to your advantage to take turns while maintaining high speed.
CH_124ABARTH_GRAVEL_TEST1_DESC: On gravel, the oversteer caused by the rear-wheel drive of the 124 Abarth can pose a challenge, but the modest engine power still allows for controlled slides to better tackle the corners of the course. The rather slow steering requires careful handling to avoid or correct any mistakes.
CH_STRATOSHF_GRAVEL_TEST1_DESC: On gravel, the power delivered to the rear wheels ensures the Lancia Stratos HF maintains good traction and enables wide drifts. Careful and continuous control of the car is essential to avoid the typical oversteer characteristic of rear-wheel drive vehicles. The mid-mounted engine also demands anticipating the Stratos’ reactions to prevent driving errors.
CH_208RALLY4_GRAVEL_TEST1_DESC: On gravel, the understeer of the Peugeot 208 Rally4 is quite pronounced, so the most effective way to drive it is to take advantage of the chassis agility when entering the corner. This means initiating a pendulum-like motion to enter the corner sideways, keeping the steering as straight as possible after the apex, and modulating the throttle on exit.
CH_COOPERS_GRAVEL_TEST1_DESC: On gravel, to be fast with the Mini Cooper S you need to enter tight corners by quickly releasing the throttle to make the rear of the car slide. This allows you to get into the corner very quickly and then accelerate fast, taking advantage of the front-wheel drive to straighten the car.
CH_DELTAINTEGRALEEVO_RAIN_TEST1_DESC: On slippery wet tarmac, the viscous differential of the Lancia Delta Integrale, combined with low grip, tends to make the car slide. Applying the throttle too early on corner exit increases understeer, while too much throttle on corner entry can cause oversteer. Proper modulation of the throttle is key to achieving excellent stage performance.
CH_A110_SNOW_TEST1_DESC: On snow, the Alpine A110 behaves similarly to how it does on dirt, with heightened responsiveness and easy rear-wheel grip loss, making it challenging to control slides using the accelerator pedal.
CH_4WD_TARMAC_TEST_XSARAWRC_DESC: On tarmac roads, the all-wheel drive of the Citroën Xsara WRC provides high levels of grip, allowing precise control of the car through various stages of the corner and enabling full use of the engine's power. However, high speeds can cause braking difficulties and destabilize the car if concentration is not at its peak.
CH_RWD_TARMAC_TEST_131ABARTH_DESC: On tarmac, rear-wheel drive cars with high-powered engines, such as the Fiat 131 Abarth, can experience significant oversteer. Optimal use of the 131’s responsive steering allows the driver to maintain vehicle stability, preventing mistakes that could compromise the successful completion of the stage.
CH_GIULIAGTA1300_GRAVEL_TEST1_DESC: On the gravel section, the rear-wheel drive of the GTA 1300 Junior tends to cause greater sliding. The wide steering radius demands utmost attention in managing the countersteer and corrections: lack of precise control could lead to mistakes that would compromise the stage.
CH_GENERIC_RAIN_GRAVEL_EVENT_DESC: On wet roads, the gravel turns muddy and significantly slows the car both in acceleration and during slides. Using shorter gear ratios improves acceleration response and keeps the engine at higher revs, ensuring the torque remains sufficient. Although overall surface grip is reduced, special wet-weather tires are not necessary, as gravel tires provide adequate performance even in these conditions.
CH_A110_RAIN_TEST1_DESC: On wet surfaces, the Alpine A110’s characteristics, lightweight, low center of gravity, and rearward weight distribution, make it very responsive but also prone to front wheel locking and possible understeer when exiting corners.
CH_131ABARTH_RAIN_TEST1_DESC: On wet tarmac, the surface tends to be more slippery. It is important to avoid and control oversteer caused by rear-wheel drive and potential wheel lock-ups during braking, in order to make the most of the 131 Abarth's characteristics. During weight transfers entering a corner, delicate control of the controls is necessary to prevent excessive reactions from the vehicle.
GROUP_306MAXI_DESC: One of the few front-wheel-drive kit cars that, thanks to its low weight and exceptional power, managed to hold its own, at least on tarmac stages, against the top-tier World Rally Championship cars in the second half of the 1990s.

PARTNER_TOMMASOCIUFFI_ACTIVITIES:
Over the years Tommaso Ciuffi has gained experience in several championships, building a strong and complete career both on tarmac and gravel.

From the Italian Rally Championship, where he collected victories and podiums, to appearances in Junior WRC and the European Rally Championship, as well as single-make trophies such as the Peugeot 208 Competition, every step has been vital to his growth.
The variety of competitions, on both surfaces, has made him a versatile driver, able to adapt to different conditions and contexts. After his apprenticeship years, results soon arrived: class wins, strong overall performances and confirmation that he could compete with international rivals.
Direct competition with some of Europe’s top talents strengthened his determination and performance-driven mindset. Today his focus is mainly on the Italian Gravel Rally Championship, where in three years he has become one of the leading drivers.

At the wheel of a Škoda Fabia RS Rally2, Tommaso approaches every round with the aim of turning potential into results and establishing himself firmly in the title fight.

PARTNER_PIETROCIGNI_BIO:
Pietro Cigni is 24 years old and was born in Massa Marittima, but he has always lived in Castelnuovo di Val di Cecina﻿, a small village of 1,500 inhabitants nestled in the Tuscan hills.

He works at Enel and has had a great passion for Motorsport since he was a child. A passion that was passed down to him by his father, who was also a rally co-driver, although only at an amateur level.

Pietro has been involved in the world of rally since his childhood, first as a spectator and then, as soon as he turned 18, as a driver, participating in his first races with some friends.

He has always shared the passion for engines with his childhood friends; in fact, starting at 14 years old with their first mopeds, they began racing and modifying their vehicles. Often the modifications led to problems and broken engines, but they did not get discouraged: they would lock themselves in the garage and try to fix them.

Initially, Pietro practiced Enduro in the woods around his house, progressing from 50cc to 125cc at 16 years old, and then to a 300cc bike at 18 years old. He continued practicing both rally and Enduro, but when he started racing seriously with Tommaso Ciuffi, he gave up motorcycles to focus completely on rally.

PARTNER_RCBOOKS_RALLY:
RC Books aims to preserve a written record of a glorious sporting past, born and raised in Italy but that has thrilled millions of enthusiasts around the world.

All publications are available in bilingual format (Italian and English), to satisfy fans everywhere.

But it’s not just books!

During the extensive research conducted for each subject published, we have gladly supported activities beyond strict editorial work, which also contribute to spreading the technical, historical, and human heritage of the Racing Department.

Examples include the creation of “Multibody” models for vehicle dynamics analysis, often a brand-new approach for the vehicles studied, and the design of 3D models (with subsequent scale printing) of notable mechanical components such as the chassis. Lastly, support for creating faithful simulators for PC and consoles that reproduce with extreme accuracy the on-road behavior of cars that have become legends!

CH_RWD_SNOW_TEST_A110_DESC: RWD cars on snow allow for more controllable power slides using the accelerator pedal. The weight distribution and balanced setup enable more effective braking. The characteristics of the Alpine A110 1.8 require extra concentration and control to achieve good performance on slippery surfaces.
CH_FWD_RAIN_TEST_208RALLY4_DESC: Rain makes the surfaces even more slippery, accentuating oversteer problems when lifting off the throttle and understeer on corner exit. With the Peugeot 208 Rally4, it is essential to have smooth driving to avoid sudden weight transfers that could unbalance the car, leading to serious mistakes.
RULES_CARCATEGORYCLASS_DESC:
Rally cars, like in other types of motor racing, have historically been grouped into <StyleBold>Groups</> and <StyleBold>Classes</> that separate different cars based on the era they belong to or their performance levels, to ensure balanced races without excessive power disparities.

At the same time, by their nature, rallies often feature mixed overall classifications, with participants from different classes or even Groups competing together. In these cases, cars that are theoretically less competitive might achieve astonishing results thanks to skilled drivers or particular race circumstances. Nevertheless, the final victory always remains exclusive to the competitor’s class.

<StyleTitle>Groups:</>
Generally, Groups represent different eras of cars and aim to faithfully replicate the Groups that actually existed in the Rally World. Historic Groups like Group B, Group A, or the more recent Group R contain cars that belonged and still belong to these categories.

<StyleTitle>Classes:</>
Classes are subdivisions within Groups and categorize cars of the same Group based on their performance level to allow fair competition.
For example, Group R is divided into different R/Rally classes from 1 to 5 based on the technical characteristics and performance of the cars.

Groups and classes currently represented in AC Rally:
•	<StyleBold>Group 2/4:</> Cars derived from production models with limited modifications (Group 2) or extensive modifications (Group 4), historic high-performance rally cars.
•	<StyleBold>Group B (B2):</> Legendary and extremely powerful cars from the 1980s with great technical freedom and extreme performances, today considered collector’s vehicles.
•	<StyleBold>Group A (A8 Evo 2):</> Turbo 4WD cars derived from production models, powerful and highly competitive, used in rallies since 1987.
•	<StyleBold>Group WR (Evo 2):</> Evolved versions of World Rally Cars with technical improvements to maximize performance.
•	<StyleBold>Group R (Rally 4):</> 2WD turbo 1.2L cars, about 200 HP, entry-level sporty rally cars.
•	<StyleBold>Group R (Rally 2):</> Modern 1.6L turbo 4WD cars with around 280 HP, used in national and international championships.
DAY_CALENDAR_DESC:
Rally events typically take place over multiple days, with a maximum duration of four days. At the start of each day, there is a service park where teams can plan and prepare for the upcoming stages before reaching the next service area.

Each day also can be used to organize the chronological progression of stage start times.
PARTNER_DENNISZENZ_ACTIVITIES:
Rally was always Dennis's ultimate goal.
When he turned 16, he was allowed to become a rally co-driver in small national events and was immediately successful. This made him decide to stay in the co-driver seat, switching from his early idea of driving.

Starting with small Opel rally cars, he quickly progressed to driving various Mitsubishi Group N and A cars. In 2013, he completed a full season in the famous ADAC Opel Adam Cup.
At the end of 2015, he began a collaboration with former WRC driver Armin Schwarz, joining a junior program with the Ford Fiesta R5. The objective was to conduct proper testing and compete in selected international rallies the following year, preparing for the German Rally Championship fight in 2017. Unfortunately, the rally ended early due to two major crashes while he was in third place overall.

Between 2020 and 2023, he mainly focused on young driver development in the Baltics, participating in many races across those beautiful countries.

At the end of 2020, Red Bull selected Dennis for their Red Bull Off-Road Junior Program to race in the Dakar Rally and the Rally Raid World Championship in the T3 category.
In 2023, he became Rally Raid World Champion in the T3 category (equivalent to WRC2), and in 2024, he joined the top category with Toyota Gazoo Racing.

Dennis full focus right now is on Rally Raid and Dakar Rally with the clear goal of winning both. He made it to the top class of the sport, making his hobby into his profession and job. 

"I want to proof myself long-term in the sport and become the best." 
<StyleGray>cit. Dennis Zenz</>"

Dennis collaborated with Supernova in developing the pacenote system, providing valuable insights into the rally world and the co-driver’s role. He actively identified the best phrases and notes to accurately describe the various situations faced during a rally.
Additionally, he translated all the pacenotes into the German language to offer players the most authentic linguistic adaptation possible, using, whenever feasible, the terms and expressions most commonly used by co-drivers who speak this language.
Finally, he contributed his voice and experience as a co-driver during an intense recording session lasting several days, delivering the pacenotes in the most realistic way, just as he would in real rally conditions.
DAMAGE_SUSPENSIONS_DESC:
Rallying is a major stress on the car’s suspension, which keep the car poised above the ground and absorbs the forces from the terrain and cars dynamics.
Jumps and larger impacts can damage the shock absorbers, reducing their damping capacity. This deterioration compromises vehicle control, especially on uneven and difficult surfaces.
RULES_WHATSRALLY_DESC:
Rallying is a type of motorsport race that takes place mainly on roads closed to traffic and is characterized by <StyleBold>special stages</> on highly varied routes, which can include paved, gravel, or snowy roads. Unlike circuit races, where competitors complete multiple laps on a closed track, rallying occurs on public road sections spread across different areas of the territory, often featuring scenic landscapes.

A rally event is divided into several special stages, which are timed sections where the different teams try to complete the course in the shortest possible time, aiming for the right balance between speed and safety to avoid accidents and damage to the car. During the race, the driver is accompanied by a co-driver who reads the "pace notes", detailed descriptions of the route indicating curves, jumps, and hazards, allowing the driver to anticipate every difficulty at high speed.

The winner of the rally is the team with the <StyleBold>lowest overall time</>, obtained by adding up the times from all the special stages. The competition rewards <StyleBold>not only speed</> but also <StyleBold>precision</>, <StyleBold>endurance</>, and the ability to <StyleBold>adapt</> to often challenging conditions, making rallying one of the most spectacular and technical motorsports in the world.
HISTORY_ORIGIN_DESC:
Rallying is one of the oldest forms of motorsport, with its origins tracing back to the late 19th century. The very first known motor race was the 1894 Paris–Rouen Horseless Carriage Competition, organized by the Paris newspaper *Le Petit Journal*. This event featured cars racing between cities, starting individually against the clock rather than directly competing head-to-head. Participants navigated long distances on mainly gravel roads, dealing with various hazards such as dust, pedestrians, and farm animals. The event introduced key rallying features like time controls and road books, laying the foundation for future rally competitions.

Following this early competition, city-to-city road races became popular across Europe and the USA. In 1895, the Paris–Bordeaux–Paris race which covered over 1,200 kilometers, tested the endurance and reliability of early automobiles. However, as speeds increased, safety became a concern: after the 1903 Paris–Madrid race caused many crashes and fatalities, governments banned some races on public roads, shifting racing towards closed circuits.

Despite this, endurance road events continued and gained popularity, especially in the 1910s and 1920s. The Monte Carlo Rally, first held in 1911, became a landmark event, attracting competitors across Europe to test both their vehicles and driving skills in challenging winter conditions. The term “rally” itself was coined around 1907, from the French word *ralier*, meaning to unite or bring together, reflecting the sport’s unique blend of competition and collaboration between driver and co-driver.

The period from the 1950s to the 1960s is often considered a golden era of road rallying, with events like the Monte Carlo Rally, Safari Rally, and other long-distance road rallies gaining international prestige. These competitions combined high-speed driving with navigation and endurance, creating a thrilling motorsport that tested both human and machine.

PARTNER_SPEED_BRAND:
SPEED and FUSINA are making their special stage. As a young company, the development is running in two parallel directions.

<StyleBold>SPEED aims to become a reference for anyone wanting to develop fast running cars,</> just like they are doing with the 131 EVO II project, or within the partnership with LMT (Laboratori Meccanica Torino) and their incredible special vehicles: provide ultimate racing machines, which have something in common with the golden era of motorsports, and some benefits from the present. <StyleBold>FUSINA, their motorsport equipment and gear brand,</> is constantly expanding its catalogue and services, providing Italian quality and safety racing products where they are demanded is a mission, while doing that respectfully towards the past of the brand and still innovating, is the “how”. PARTNER_SPEED_HISTORY:
SPEED is a specialized engineering and design partner dedicated to motorsport, highly focused on special vehicles, ranging from modern and historic road and racecars, restomods and prototypes. Based near Turin, in one of the two hearts of Italy’s automotive industry, SPEED brings together advanced technical capabilities with decades of racing know-how to support teams, manufacturers, and private collectors at the highest level.

The core strength lies in precision engineering, by providing comprehensive <StyleBold>reverse engineering</> services supported by state-of-the-art <StyleBold>3D scanning technologies</>, enabling them to accurately capture, analyze, and reproduce complex components and assemblies. This expertise is crucial not only for development purposes, but also for restoration and optimization of rare and vintage vehicles, or for providing them with new spare parts for racing.

The SPEED team excels in <StyleBold>concept and functional design</>, as well as advanced simulations. Using <StyleBold>CFD (Computational Fluid Dynamics)</> for aerodynamics and <StyleBold>FEM (Finite Element Method)</> for structural analysis, SPEED optimizes performance, reliability, and safety under the most demanding racing conditions. From initial feasibility studies to complete engineering solutions, their workflow ensures that every detail is tested, validated, and race-ready.

SPEED is also recognized for his expertise in development of safety equipment for motorsport. <StyleBold>As a member of the FIA Industry Working Group</>, Speed is supporting Manufacturers and Teams through the design, development and certification processes, required to compete at international level. This combination of regulatory knowledge and engineering talent makes SPEED a trusted partner for both modern motorsport projects and special vehicles development, of which an example can be found at the now popular 131 EVO II rally car project, where SPEED joined forces with the rally driver Paolo Diana for the development of the entire vehicle.

SPEED is also known for bringing the FUSINA brand back to life, after its end in the 70s. FUSINA, the first italian car and driver equipment and gear oriented brand, is known for having provided steering wheels and seats for Lancia, Abarth, Alfa Romeo and Porsche models as an original equipment solution, alongside many other popular car manufacturers. FUSINA is now back with a 100% Made in Italy catalogue, ranging from steering wheels, to FIA and aftermarket racing seats, harness systems and more.
PARTNER_SPEED_RALLY:
SPEED is partnered with SUPERNOVA Game Studios to support vehicle modeling. Many of the cars featured in Assetto Corsa Rally are absolute relics of motorsport history, and most of these did not have full stack CAD models to begin with. Vehicles such as the Lancia Delta S4, or the Audi Quattro Group B, have been developed by passionate teams who were racing also in engineering, and that was not always compatible at all with complete CAD development of each detail of the car, like in the modern era. So, some of the solutions were “designed” directly at the rally.

SPEED, and its reverse engineering services, have been key to re-create meticulously all of these vehicles, providing 3D scans with sub-millimetric precision and reference data, to be then used by our artists for the final modeling and the in-engine import. Furthermore, SPEED’s experience in real life rallies became handy with networking, anecdotes and rally stories, which are making Assetto Corsa Rally the most friendly place for nostalgics of this discipline, in the modern era.

RULES_STARTINGORDER_DESC:
Since it is a timed race, rally competitors, unlike in circuit racing where all cars start simultaneously, start at <StyleBold>intervals of several minutes</> from each other. In fact, the objective is not to arrive ahead of your opponent, but to complete the special stage in less time than them.
For this reason, crews have a time gap from the crew ahead to minimize possible interferences that can occur in reality (such as extremely slow cars due to damage, dust raised which may reduce visibility, etc.).

Although we wanted to recreate these behaviors in minute detail, AC Rally allows each driver to tackle the stage in complete freedom, without other opponents physically present on the road.
That said, the <StyleBold>staggered start logic</> and its effects on the route and start times are faithfully reproduced.
Indeed, the starting order of each rally stage is calculated at the beginning of the stage and, depending on the options selected, determines the player’s starting position.

Each opponent or player will start several minutes apart, consequently <StyleBold>shifting the start time</> from the official beginning of the stage.
This can lead to significant variations in environmental visibility: events starting in the late afternoon may see some participants starting in the middle of the night.

Moreover, depending on the options chosen, a competitor starting in early positions might face completely <StyleBold>different weather conditions</> compared to a crew starting in the later positions: a sunny day can quickly turn into a sudden downpour.

Finally, the <StyleBold>road surface conditions</> change depending on the passage of the various cars (again based on selected options). For example, the grip level increases as cars pass over the road, so those starting early will encounter a dirtier surface with less grip, while those starting later will have a cleaner racing line with more grip but may face more debris off the ideal line.

The staggered starts, and consequently staggered finishes, mean that during the race, information about opponents’ performances and the <StyleBold>player’s position</> can be particularly dynamic and influenced by the player’s own starting position.
In fact, reliable information will only be available about opponents who have completed at least one split, and relative position can only be calculated with reference to opponents who reached the finish line before the player.
PARTNER_DAVIDPRICE_ACTIVITIES:
Since the mid-1980s, Dave has immersed himself in almost every aspect of rallying. He began with marshalling and event organization at his local motor club, gaining a deep respect for the volunteers who keep the sport alive. His early competitive experience came from night rallies and 12-car events before moving into stage rallying, co-driving for the first time in his own Mk1 Escort with Dave Kedward, who later became a renowned Group B car expert.

Drawing on his engineering background, Dave contributed to car builds, wiring looms, and electrical systems. This expertise led to a pivotal moment in the 1990s when, after completing a full rewire, he was invited to co-drive for Nick Elliott. Their partnership began with an overall win on their very first outing in the Dalby forests in a Mk2 Ford Escort and evolved into a long-standing collaboration.

Together, they entered the Peugeot Talbot Sport GTi Challenge, a fiercely competitive single-make series that regularly attracted more than 60 entries. This introduced Dave to international rallying, beginning with the Tour of Flanders in Belgium, and expanded his experience across a variety of machinery, from historic rally cars through Group N, A, B, and even genuine WRC cars, including the legendary Lancia 037.

After taking a break for family commitments, Dave reunited with Nick Elliott, and the pair went on to become front-running competitors in the British Historic Rally Championship. Their campaigns, often in the Group B-inspired Mk2 Escort, produced a reputation for being either unstoppable winners or all-or-nothing retirees. More recently, his involvement with Rallysport Development has seen him co-driving the stunning Fiat 131 Abarth, establishing it as a true rival to the Ford Escort and a fan favorite at historic rallies.

Dave collaborated with Supernova in developing the pacenote system, providing valuable insights into the rally world and the co-driver’s role. He actively identified the best phrases and notes to accurately describe the various situations faced during a rally.
Additionally, he translated all the pacenotes into the English language to offer players the most authentic linguistic adaptation possible, using, whenever feasible, the terms and expressions most commonly used by co-drivers who speak this language.
Finally, he contributed his voice and experience as a co-driver during an intense recording session lasting several days, delivering the pacenotes in the most realistic way, just as he would in real rally conditions.

CARSETUP_SERVO_DESC:
Some cars are equipped with a <StyleBold>brake servo</>, but using it is optional and doesn’t impact the brake bias or significantly increase maximum brake torque.

The main advantage of a brake servo lies in the pedal response: it makes <StyleBold>braking more digressive</>. With minimal foot force, you can achieve more brake pressure, which can improve driver comfort and reduce fatigue during long stages.

If you prefer a more linear, proportional brake pedal feel, you might choose to <StyleBold>disable it</> for a more direct connection to the brakes.

CARSETUP_DUCTS_DESC:
Some rally cars feature <StyleBold>adjustable brake ducts</> that can be partially opened or closed to optimize brake cooling.
You can control airflow by <StyleBold>closing (decreasing)</> or <StyleBold>opening (increasing)</> the ducts. The goal is to maintain the brakes within their ideal operating temperature range, preventing overheating and increased brake fade.

Proper adjustment helps keep the brake components <StyleBold>"green,"</> indicating efficient performance, while avoiding the <StyleBold>"red"</> zone, which signals excessive heat leading to reduced braking effectiveness.
CARSETUP_SUSPENSION_ATTACCHING_DESC:
Specific car’s suspension systems feature multiple <StyleBold>mounting points</>. Different configurations offer different Roll Center height and Anti-Feature combinations. You can check the results of each setting in the graph.

Typically, the higher the roll center height, the higher the camber recovery and the higher the jacking forces. While a high camber recovery is beneficial to tyre contact patch, a too high Roll Center can make the inside wheel lift from the ground during cornering, increasing the risk of a rollover. 

The higher the Anti-Features, the more the load transfer is supported by the suspension instead of the spring, minimizing squat and dive making the car more responsive, but also less compliant.
CH_SISTERON_FULL_R_DESC:
Starting from Saint-Geniez, this special stage descends towards Sisteron over 13 very fast kilometers. A mix of technical corners and complex sections, with plenty of dangers lurking around every bend.
Characterized by a very fast first part with wide curves and a narrow track, the road changes in the second part, becoming more technical and twisty but with a wider track. The dangers along the sides are constant and require high concentration.
CH_SISTERON_FULL_R_SNOW_DESC:
Starting from Saint-Geniez, this special stage descends towards Sisteron over 13 very fast kilometers. A mix of technical corners and complex sections, with plenty of dangers lurking around every bend.
On these roads, as altitude increases, it's easy to encounter snow and ice: caution is essential in such cases. With snow, grip is reduced to a minimum, especially without proper winter or studded tires. Pushing hard with dry tires and then slowing down in snowy sections can be a winning strategy, but also extremely risky.
CH_SISTERON_FULL_R_NIGHT_DESC:
Starting from Saint-Geniez, this special stage descends towards Sisteron over 13 very fast kilometers. A mix of technical corners and complex sections, with plenty of dangers lurking around every bend.
Tackling this special stage at night can be extremely challenging: despite the powerful night lights fitted on the cars, the constant direction changes obscure the driver's view, a factor amplified by the poor nighttime visibility.
CH_SISTERON_FULL_R_SS_DESC:
Starting from Saint-Geniez, this special stage descends towards Sisteron over 13 very fast kilometers. A mix of technical corners and complex sections, with plenty of dangers lurking around every bend.
This stage demands concentration and speed to challenge your rivals. However, remember that speed isn’t everything in rallying: reaching the finish with your car intact and performing well can secure the victory.
CH_SISTERON_FULL_R_RAIN_DESC:
Starting from Saint-Geniez, this special stage descends towards Sisteron over 13 very fast kilometers. A mix of technical corners and complex sections, with plenty of dangers lurking around every bend.
Wet asphalt becomes particularly slippery at high speeds; pay special attention to harsh braking, which can extend stopping distances. A small misjudgment can compromise the entire stage.

HISTORY_60_DESC:
The 1960s were a pivotal decade for rallying, marking its transformation into a globally recognized motorsport, defined by endurance, skill, and innovation. This era is characterized by long-distance, grueling events that severely tested both drivers and their machines.

Iconic rallies such as the Monte Carlo Rally, Acropolis Rally, and the East African Safari Rally gained immense prestige during the 1960s. These events challenged competitors with a variety of harsh terrains and demanding conditions, from snowy mountain passes to rough, arid landscapes, making them true tests of endurance and precision driving.

The decade also saw the rise of legendary rally cars like the Ford Cortina, Mini Cooper, Porsche 911, and Lancia Fulvia. These vehicles were noted for their lightweight construction, powerful engines, and exceptional handling, which made them well-suited to the intense and varied rally stages of the period.

In terms of human achievement, pioneering drivers emerged who earned lasting fame through their skill and bravery. Drivers such as Rauno Aaltonen, Erik Carlsson, and Timo Mäkinen became icons by mastering the challenging routes and harsh conditions that defined 1960s rally competitions. Their ability to navigate with precision under extreme pressure helped elevate rallying’s profile worldwide.

The 1960s were also important for organizational growth. State and national rally championships were established in countries like Australia, marking a shift towards more structured competition formats alongside traditional endurance events. The decade witnessed the creation of new rallies that further diversified the sport, such as the Southern Cross Rally, starting in 1966.

Overall, the 1960s laid crucial groundwork for rallying’s evolution, combining endurance racing with navigation skills and evolving automotive technology. This blend helped establish rallying as a major motorsport discipline, appealing to both participants and fans globally by the end of the decade.
GROUP_RALLY037EVO2_DESC: The <StyleBold>037 Evo</> was the last rear-wheel-drive car to challenge and win against the legendary giants of Group B. The 325 hp supercharged engine, a feature that distinguished it from its rivals, provided exceptional acceleration, ideal for rally racing.
HISTORY_90_DESC:
The <StyleBold>1990s</> in rally history marked a dynamic and highly competitive era that both consolidated the transition from the raw power of the 1980s Group B and heralded the rise of <StyleBold>Japanese manufacturers</>, creating a captivating spectacle for rally enthusiasts and casual followers alike. The decade was dominated initially by the continued supremacy of Lancia, whose <StyleBold>Delta Integrale</> remained an iconic force, securing six consecutive manufacturers' titles from 1987 through 1992. This was a time when rally cars were strictly homologated under Group A regulations, which enforced production-based builds and limited power compared to the wild Group B machines, yet technological developments kept the competition fierce and the pace blistering.

Among the standout drivers, <StyleBold>Juha Kankkunen</> and <StyleBold>Miki Biasion</> of Lancia upheld their status as rally legends, each claiming multiple world championships, with Kankkunen winning his fourth title in 1993 after moving to Toyota. This period also saw the emergence of <StyleBold>Toyota’s Celica GT-Four</>, which challenged Lancia’s dominance and gave rise to intense rivalries between manufacturers and drivers. <StyleBold>Carlos Sainz</>, the charismatic Spaniard driving the Toyota Celica, became a two-time world champion in 1990 and 1992, known for his calculated yet aggressive style that captivated fans worldwide.

By the mid-1990s, the sport witnessed a major shift as Japanese manufacturers like <StyleBold>Subaru</> and <StyleBold>Mitsubishi</> rose prominently. The <StyleBold>Subaru Impreza S3</>, piloted by Scotland’s <StyleBold>Colin McRae</>, brought a new wave of excitement. McRae’s flamboyant and fearless driving style earned him the 1995 World Rally Championship, making him the first British driver to win the title, solidifying Subaru's position as a rally powerhouse. Mitsubishi, with its Lancer Evolution series driven by Tommi Mäkinen, dominated the latter half of the decade. Mäkinen impressively won four consecutive driver's titles from 1996 to 1999, helping Mitsubishi also clinch the manufacturers’ crown in 1998.

This decade also featured memorable rivalries, not just between teams but among star drivers, fueling passionate contests at events across varied terrains. The <StyleBold>Ford Escort RS Cosworth</> also became a rally icon during the 1990s, notable for its aerodynamic innovations and solid presence in competition.

The 1990s, were a period of evolving technology, intense competition, and rising global interest. They bridged the gap between the fearless era of Group B and the modern, highly technical World Rally Championship era, providing a rich narrative of drivers and machines that shaped rallying into a global motorsport phenomenon enjoyed by enthusiasts and spectators worldwide.
CARDESC_LANCIA_DELTAINTEGRALEEVO:
The <StyleBold>1992 Lancia Delta HF Integrale Evoluzione</>, often affectionately referred to as the "Evo" or "Il Deltone", stands as a monumental figure in the world of rally cars, embodying a blend of engineering prowess, racing heritage, and sheer driving excitement. This car is not just a vehicle; it’s a symbol of Lancia's dominance in the World Rally Championship during the late 1980s and early 1990s.

At its core, it features a <StyleBold>2.0-liter turbocharged inline-four engine</> that produces an impressive <StyleBold>365 horsepower</> and <StyleBold>535 Nm of torque</>, enabling it to accelerate from 0 to 100 km/h in just six seconds and reach a top speed of 215 km/h (134 mph). The power is transmitted through a five-speed manual gearbox and an all-wheel-drive system, providing outstanding grip and stability on all types of surfaces, from gravel to tarmac.

The Evo stands out with its <StyleBold>stiffened body</>, wider wheel arches, and upgraded suspension, designed to tackle rally stages. The car's design also included larger brakes for improved stopping power and aerodynamics that helped it slice through the air with ease.

By the early 1990s, Lancia had already secured <StyleBold>six consecutive manufacturer titles</> in the world championship, thanks to earlier iterations of the Delta series. The introduction of the Evo in 1992, in the hand of legendary drivers like <StyleBold>Juha Kankkunen</> and <StyleBold>Miki Biasion</>, was a strategic move to fend off fierce competition from Japanese manufacturers like Toyota, who were making significant strides in the sport.

The Evo was not merely an upgrade; it represented Lancia's commitment to maintaining its competitive edge, showcasing Lancia's relentless pursuit of perfection in motorsport engineering. Despite its success, winning eight out of fourteen events in 1992, the Delta Evo ultimately won with Lancia the Manufacturer’s title but lost the Driver’s championship to Toyota’s Carlos Sainz.

The Lancia Delta HF Integrale Evoluzione is celebrated not just for its performance but also for its <StyleBold>legacy</>. It is often regarded as one of the most successful rally cars ever built, with a record that includes numerous victories and accolades throughout its racing career. With its roots deeply embedded in rally history and its striking design that pays homage to its racing lineage, the Evo remains an iconic figure that continues to inspire admiration among car lovers around the world.

CARDESC_SKODA_FABIARSRALLY2:
The <StyleBold>2022 Škoda Fabia RS Rally2</> is a technically advanced rally car developed from the fourth-generation Škoda Fabia production model launched in 2021. It belongs to the Rally2 category defined by FIA regulations, serving as the successor to the extremely successful Fabia Rally2 evo, which dominated the rally scene globally with over 1,500 wins and multiple championships from 2015 to 2022.

Underneath its sleek body, the Fabia RS Rally2 features a newly developed <StyleBold>1.6-liter turbocharged four-cylinder</> engine, derived from the EA888 engine series used in Škoda’s road cars but extensively reworked for racing. This engine delivers around <StyleBold>214 kW (289 hp)</> and <StyleBold>430 Nm</> of torque, which is available over a broader range of engine speeds compared to its predecessor. The power is transferred through a sequential five-speed gearbox to all four wheels, with mechanical self-locking differentials on both the front and rear axles, permitting precise traction control on varying rally surfaces like gravel, tarmac, and even snow.

Aerodynamics have been significantly improved over the previous model. The car benefits from the new production Fabia’s longer wheelbase and wider body, enhancing weight distribution and overall balance. Key aerodynamic features include air curtains integrated into the front bumper, a redesigned splitter, and a new rear wing that nearly doubles the downforce compared to its predecessor. These refinements increase stability and cornering speeds, which are critical in rally driving where rapid direction changes on loose surfaces are common. The car’s aerodynamic efficiency also helps minimize drag, contributing to its on-stage performance.

The chassis and suspension arrangement build on the tried-and-tested McPherson setup but are specially adapted for endurance under the intense stresses of rally competition. The suspension features longer-travel shock absorbers and reinforced components to manage impacts from rough terrain. Braking is handled by high-performance brakes with improved cooling and durability features to withstand repeated heavy use.

In terms of safety and driver feedback, the Fabia RS Rally2 incorporates a reinforced roll cage, advanced fire suppression systems, and racing harnesses compliant with the highest FIA standards. The car also includes an integrated telemetry system allowing teams to monitor performance in real-time and fine-tune setup and driving strategy.

The rally car is designed to run on <StyleBold>100% sustainable fuels</>, consistent with the FIA’s push towards ecological responsibility in motorsport. These fuels are made from renewable raw materials and synthetic components, reflecting Škoda Motorsport’s commitment to future-forward technologies.

Born from a desire to continue Škoda's dominance in Rally2 competition, the Fabia RS Rally2 builds on the experience gained from its highly successful predecessor while integrating technological advances from the latest Fabia road car. This combination of proven rally engineering and modern production car technology results in a balanced, reliable, and competitive rally weapon capable of tackling diverse rally challenges worldwide.

OPTION_ABS_DESC:
The <StyleBold>ABS (Anti-lock Braking System)</> is an active safety system that prevents the wheels from locking during sudden braking, thus avoiding skidding and loss of grip.

Select if ABS is disabled for all cars, it can still be re-enabled during the race, provided the game mode allows it, either through direct inputs or in-game controls.
CARSETUP_ABS_MAP_DESC:
The <StyleBold>ABS (Anti-lock Braking System)</> is an active safety system that prevents the wheels from locking during sudden braking, thus avoiding skidding and loss of grip.

When the ABS detects locking, it acts cyclically (hundreds of times per second) temporarily reducing the brake pressure on the wheel about to lock. Once the wheel starts to rotate again, the brake pressure is restored.

When the ABS is <StyleBold>deactivated (OFF)</> the control of the brake pressure is completely in the hands of the driver. As the <StyleBold>ABS values ​​increase</>, the system becomes more sensitive to the pressure, anticipating the wheel lock and optimizing the response.

The braking distance with the ABS active may be slightly longer than with a driver-controlled braking without locking the wheels. However, in the event of a wheel lock, stopping times are significantly longer without ABS.
On slippery surfaces, such as dirt and snow, the ABS may be too intrusive due to the ease with which the wheels lock.
CARDESC_ALFAROMEO_GIULIAGTA1300:
The <StyleBold>Alfa Romeo GTA 1300 Junior</>, produced between 1968 and 1975, is a rally car that embodies the spirit of Italian motorsport with its blend of style, performance, and engineering excellence. This compact powerhouse was not just a car; it was a symbol of Alfa Romeo's racing heritage and a favorite among enthusiasts and drivers alike.

Originally engineered for <StyleBold>circuit racing</>, the GTA 1300 was often used in rally events across Italy and France such as the "Monti Savonesi 1973" driven by Giuseppe Bay and Maurizio Rimondi in the "San Martino di Castrozza 1976"

Weighing in at around <StyleBold>760 kg</>, the car featured a <StyleBold>1.3-liter inline-four engine</> that initially generated about 95 hp but was later tuned to produce up to <StyleBold>163 hp</>. This engine, combined with a <StyleBold>5-speed manual transmission</>, allowed the car to achieve impressive speeds of up to <StyleBold>185 km/h (115 mph)</>. The use of aluminum panels over a steel monocoque body not only contributed to its low weight but also gave it a distinctive look that turned heads on and off the rally stage.

The GTA 1300 Junior was equipped with <StyleBold>disc brakes</> all around and an independent front suspension system, which provided excellent handling and stability on various terrains. Its design included a sporty two-door coupe layout that emphasized aerodynamics, making it agile and responsive, qualities essential for navigating the twists and turns of rally courses.

The late 1960s and early 1970s marked a transformative period in motorsport, with rally racing gaining immense popularity across Europe. Manufacturers were pushing boundaries to create cars that could not only compete but also captivate audiences. Alfa Romeo, known for its racing pedigree, sought to develop a vehicle that combined performance with accessibility for amateur racers.

The GTA 1300 Junior, with its lightweight design, powerful engine, and agile handling, was perfectly suited for <StyleBold>hill climb events</>, where it remained a fierce competitor for years. These types of races demand rapid acceleration and precise cornering, and the GTA 1300 Junior excelled in both, thanks to its performance-focused engineering.

Its legacy continues today among classic car collectors and rally enthusiasts. Its historical significance in motorsport is celebrated at vintage rallies and events worldwide, where it remains a testament to Alfa Romeo's commitment to engineering excellence.

<StyleTitle>Trivia</>
•	The GTA 1300 Junior was part of a broader family of GTA models, which included variants like the more powerful <StyleBold>GTA 2000</>, showcasing Alfa Romeo's versatility in performance tuning. 
•	In its GTA 1600 version, the car made history in the early Italian rally events, driven by the rally pioneer <StyleBold>Arnaldo Cavallari</>.
•	Approximately <StyleBold>450 units</> of the GTA 1300 Junior were produced, making it relatively rare today and highly sought after by collectors.
•	The car’s design was influenced by the iconic <StyleBold>Giulia series</>, which laid the groundwork for many successful Alfa Romeo models.

<StyleGraySmall>* updated late 2024</>
CARSETUP_ANTI_LAG_MAP_DESC:
The <StyleBold>Anti-Lag Map</> is designed to minimize turbo lag by maintaining the turbine’s speed through intensified exhaust gas pressure. It achieves this by injecting additional fuel and adjusting the ignition timing to create stronger combustion events in the exhaust system, keeping the turbo spooled even when the throttle is released. This continuous turbine rotation ensures quicker boost response and improved acceleration out of corners, a crucial advantage in rally racing.

However, increasing the Anti-Lag Map settings significantly raises thermal and mechanical stress on the turbocharger components, potentially reducing their lifespan. So it must be managed carefully to <StyleBold>balance performance and durability</> across multiple longer length stages.
OPTION_TRANSMISSION_DESC:
The <StyleBold>Automatic Transmission</> option handles gear changes autonomously, without any intervention from the driver. The system engages the gear at the correct point on the torque curve, minimizing the drop in power output to a minimum. It is particularly advantageous for less experienced drivers, allowing them to concentrate more on controlling the vehicle, while still ensuring excellent performance in all conditions.

In contrast, the <StyleBold>manual transmission</> allows the driver to have full control over the timing of the gear change, which must be activated manually. An expert and conscious use of the manual transmission allows the gear change to be made at the most optimal moment, ensuring superior performance and minimizing the risk of unwanted changes that could occur with the automatic system.
CARSETUP_BOOST_PRESSURE_DESC:
The <StyleBold>Boost Pressure</> setting on the car loader controls how much extra air is forced into the engine, directly influencing power output. <StyleBold>Increasing</> the boost pressure will provide a significant power gain, enhancing acceleration and overall performance, especially in demanding racing conditions.

However, higher boost also results in a <StyleBold>more aggressive power delivery</>, which can make the car harder to control and puts more stress on the engine, accelerating wear and <StyleBold>reducing reliability.</>
CARSETUP_BUMP_HEAVE_TRANSITION_DESC:
The <StyleBold>Bump Heave Transition</> in a rally car’s suspension is adjusted by the Fast Heave Bump preload, controlled via a simple screw. 
This adjustment either anticipates or delays the full opening of the piston holes, affecting the damper's response rate. 

Increasing the value delays the opening, keeping the suspension more damped during rapid vibrations, preventing excess ossiclation.

Decreasing the Heave Bump Transition value allows the opening to free up sooner, leading to a softer damper response, which will allow for faster compression.

This fine tuning balances ride control and road grip.
CARSETUP_BUMP_THRESHOLD_SPEED_DESC:
The <StyleBold>Bump Threshold Speed</> in a car's suspension is adjusted using the Fast Bump preload via a simple screw. This adjustment controls when the piston holes fully open, transitioning the damper to its softer setting.

Increasing the Bump Transition delays the opening, making the suspension maintain higher damping during rapid vibrations, improving stability but potentially increasing tyre contact losses.

Decreasing the Bump Transition value allows the opening to free up sooner, causing the softer damping phase to activate sooner, reducing the force applied during normal body movements.
While this can enhance comfort, it may also lead to unwanted vehicle oscillations, affecting overall handling and control.
INPUT_TYPE_CARSYSTEMS_DESC: The <StyleBold>Car systems</> are a list of basic but not essential functions of the car. Some of these can be controlled automatically by activating specific Driving Helps.
CARDESC_CITROEN_XSARAWRC:
The <StyleBold>Citroën Xsara WRC</> made its debut in the World Rally Championship in 2001 and quickly became a symbol of success and innovation in motorsport. Designed by Citroën Racing, this car was not just a modified version of the Xsara road car; it was a purpose-built machine that showcased cutting-edge technology and engineering excellence.

The  2.0-liter turbocharged inline-four engine of the Xsara WRC, produced around <StyleBold>310 horsepower</> and an impressive <StyleBold>570 Nm of torque</>. The power was controlled by an advanced six-speed sequential gearbox and a permanent four-wheel-drive system, providing outstanding traction across diverse terrains. The car weighed in at just <StyleBold>1,230 kg</>, meeting WRC regulations while delivering thrilling performance on the rally stages.

One of the most notable aspects of the Xsara WRC was its aerodynamics. The design included a low-drag rear wing and body modifications that enhanced downforce without sacrificing speed. These features were developed using wind tunnel testing, which helped optimize performance on both tarmac and gravel surfaces.

The car's dimensions, measuring <StyleBold>4,167 mm in length</> and <StyleBold>1,770 mm in width</>, contributed to its stability and agility, making it a formidable competitor.

The Xsara WRC emerged during a transformative period in rallying. In the late 1990s, Citroën had already established itself with the successful Xsara Kit Car, which dominated the Kit Car category. However, as regulations evolved, Citroën shifted focus to developing a full-fledged World Rally Car. The transition was marked by strategic planning and extensive testing, culminating in the Xsara's competitive debut.

Under the skilled hands of drivers like <StyleBold>Sébastien Loeb</>, who would go on to become one of the most successful rally drivers in history, the Xsara WRC claimed numerous victories. It secured three consecutive Constructors' Championships from 2003 to 2005 and helped Loeb clinch three Drivers' Championships during that same period.

The car's combination of reliability, speed, and innovative design made it a fan favorite and solidified Citroën's reputation in the world of motorsport.
