DEVICE_WHEEL_BRAKES_DEADZONE_DESC:
The <StyleBold>Deadzone</> reduces the amount of input that comes into play at the start of the brake pressure and at the end of it.

The <StyleBold>lower end</>, manages the first part of the input value, limiting involuntary brake pressure, or delaying the moment in which braking begins.

The <StyleBold>higher end</>, instead, cuts the final part of the input value, anticipating the moment in which braking reaches 100%.
DEVICE_WHEEL_CLUTCH_DEADZONE_DESC:
The <StyleBold>Deadzone</> reduces the amount of input that comes into play at the start of the clutch pressure and at the end of it.

The <StyleBold>lower end</>, manages the first part of the input value, limiting involuntary clutch pressure, or delaying the moment in which the clutch pressure begins.

The <StyleBold>higher end</>, instead, cuts the final part of the input value, anticipating the moment in which the clutch reaches 100%.
DEVICE_WHEEL_HANDBRAKE_DEADZONE_DESC:
The <StyleBold>Deadzone</> reduces the amount of input that comes into play at the start of the handbreke pressing and at the end of it.

The <StyleBold>lower end</>, manages the first part of the input value, limiting involuntary Handbrake pressing, or delaying the moment in which the handbrake pressing begins.

The <StyleBold>higher end</>, instead, cuts the final part of the input value, anticipating the moment in which the Handbrake reaches 100%.
DEVICE_PAD_STEER_DEADZONECENTER_DESC:
The <StyleBold>Deadzone</> reduces the amount of input that comes into play at the start of the steering pressure.

The <StyleBold>center deadzone</>, manages the first part of the input value in both steer directions, limiting involuntary Steering, or delaying the moment in which steering begins.
DEVICE_WHEEL_THROTTLE_DEADZONE_DESC:
The <StyleBold>Deadzone</> reduces the amount of input that comes into play at the start of the throttle pressure and at the end of it.

The <StyleBold>lower end</>, manages the first part of the input value, limiting involuntary throttle pressure, or delaying the moment in which accelerating begins.

The <StyleBold>higher end</>, instead, cuts the final part of the input value, anticipating the moment in which accelerating reaches 100%.
CARSETUP_ESP_DESC:
The <StyleBold>Electronic Stability Program (ESP)</> is a car component designed to enhance vehicle stability during dynamic driving conditions. By continuously monitoring the car’s movement and driver inputs, the ESP’s electronic control unit (ECU) actively manages brake pressure and engine power to prevent skidding or loss of control.

When activated, ESP helps maintain optimal traction and balance, especially on slippery or uneven surfaces, by <StyleBold>automatically correcting oversteer or understeer</>. While this system greatly improves safety and handling, having ESP ON means it will intervene to keep the car stable, <StyleBold>reducing</> the driver’s ability to <StyleBold>intentionally destabilize the vehicle</> for advanced maneuvering.
INPUT_TYPE_ELECTRONICS_DESC: The <StyleBold>Electronics</> input list contain all function of the car related to Driving Helps and other digital and mechanical system that helps the driver control the car.
CARSETUP_ENGINE_MAP_DESC:
The <StyleBold>Engine Map</> controls how torque is delivered to the wheels. Different maps adjust engine performance to suit varying driving conditions, optimizing power output and responsiveness.

<StyleBold>Lower maps</> prioritize maximum torque from lower rpms for aggressive acceleration on smooth surfaces, while <StyleBold>higher maps</> offer smoother, more controlled power delivery with high rpms powerband for looser surfaces.

By switching between these maps, drivers can adapt to terrain changes, enhancing traction, stability, and overall vehicle control.
GROUP_131ABARTH_DESC: The <StyleBold>Fiat 131 Abarth</>, a compact rear-wheel-drive ’70s car with iconic Alitalia livery and 245 hp, became a rally legend, dominating competitions until the Group B era began.
GROUP_GIULIAGTA1300_DESC: The <StyleBold>GTA 1300</>, an iconic car of the 1960s and 1970s, was capable of winning on the track, hill climbs, and rally. With 163 hp and rear-wheel drive, it offered advanced performance for its time.
OPTION_HADBRAKEHELP_DESC:
The <StyleBold>Handbrake Start Assist</> eliminates the need to keep the handbrake on during the starting procedure to prevent the car from going forward.

With the assist <StyleBold>activated</>, the starting procedure will be started by pressing the accelerator, and the car will remain stationary thanks to the automatically activated handbrake, until the countdown expires. At the start, the brake will be progressively deactivated by the system and the car will be able to start.

With the assist <StyleBold>deactivated</>, however, the driver must start the starting procedure by pulling the handbrake and keep it on until the countdown expires to avoid early starts.

The manual control of the handbrake guarantees better response times for more experienced drivers, requiring greater control over both acceleration and brake release. The assist, on the other hand, allows for less control by the player, but offers adequate and consistent response times.
CARSETUP_HEAVE_REBOUNDSTOP_DESC:
The <StyleBold>Heave Reboundstop</>, used in conjunction with the Heave Spring, plays a crucial role in managing the suspension system of a rally car.

Increasing the value will soften the extension of the Heave Spring, by having the reboundstop engage earlier and making its extension more gradual. Decreasing the value will allow the suspension to extend and drop more quickly, with the reboundstop engaging later and more sharply in its length of travel. 

By carefully tuning the Heave Reboundstop, you can prevent excessive spring oscillations that might cause damage to suspension components during aggressive driving.

CARDESC_LANCIA_FULVIAHF:
The <StyleBold>Lancia Fulvia Coupé Rallye 1.6 HF</>, particularly the 1970 "Fanalone" version, represents a significant technical achievement in the world of rallying. It emerged during a peculiar time when rally racing was evolving from a largely amateur endurance challenge into a highly specialized and competitive sport. This transition period saw manufacturers pushing the boundaries of engineering to create machines that balanced power, agility, and reliability.

What made the Fulvia 1.6 HF distinctive was its narrow-angle V4 engine, a rather uncommon configuration at the time. The engine displaced <StyleBold>1,584cc</> and featured a tight 11.2-degree angle between its cylinder banks, resulting in a remarkably compact design. Mounted at a 45-degree tilt, the engine was fed by twin large carburettors, allowing the road cars to produce up to <StyleBold>115 horsepower</>, while rally-prepared versions could reach between <StyleBold>130 and 152 horsepower</> depending on their specific setup. Power was transferred to the wheels via a close-ratio five-speed gearbox, a feature that helped drivers make the most of the car’s potent engine across diverse rally stages. This gearbox was notable for its range of selectable gear ratios and final drives, emphasizing Lancia’s commitment to adaptable, motorsport-focused solutions.

Building on its technical prowess, the Fulvia embraced lightweight materials and construction techniques. Early rally models incorporated aluminum body panels and plexiglass windows to reduce weight, while Group 4 competition cars pushed this further with stripped interiors, minimalist bucket seats, and enlarged fuel tanks capable of holding up to 90 liters for endurance racing. In full rally trim, the car’s weight could drop to a mere 920 kilograms, enhancing its agility on twisty, demanding courses.

Suspension-wise, the Fulvia combined a sophisticated double wishbone front setup with a transverse leaf spring and a solid live rear axle. This arrangement, along with four-wheel disc brakes, a rarity for its era, gave the car excellent handling and stopping power. The wide alloy wheels and extended wheel arches hinted at its competitive capabilities.

The Fulvia 1.6 HF was developed at a time when the World Rally Championship was just beginning, and rallies were shifting character from long-distance endurance events to precise special stage contests. Lancia’s expertise allowed them to produce a front-wheel-drive car that could hold its own against rear-wheel-drive rivals. Its nimble chassis, combined with the clever engineering of its unique engine and transmission, earned the Fulvia notable successes, including a famous victory at the <StyleBold>1972 Monte Carlo Rally</>.

Ultimately, the engineering sophistication of the Fulvia 1.6 HF laid an important foundation for Lancia’s later rally successes, including the legendary Stratos and Delta models. Its balance of technical innovation, manageable size, and tunability made it a favorite among professional rally drivers and enthusiasts, earning it a respected place in rally history. Far from being just a power machine, the Fulvia relied on intelligent design and driver skill, traits that continue to endear it to classic rally fans around the world.

CARDESC_LANCIA_STRATOSHF:
The <StyleBold>Lancia Stratos HF</> was a car so <StyleBold>revolutionary</> it changed the face of rallying forever. The '70 rally legend not only dominated its era but also became an iconic symbol of speed and style. Developed by Lancia in collaboration with <StyleBold>Bertone</>, under the creative direction of <StyleBold>Marcello Gandini</>, this rally car was specifically engineered to excel in competition.

The Stratos featured a distinctive <StyleBold>wedge-shaped bodywork</> that not only provided an aerodynamic advantage but also facilitated quick access to both the engine and spare wheel through dual clamshell hoods. This design element significantly reduced pit stop times during rallies. With a weight range between <StyleBold>900 and 950 kilograms</>, it was remarkably lightweight compared to its contemporaries. The car was powered by a <StyleBold>Ferrari Dino V6 engine</>, which produced up to <StyleBold>320 horsepower</> in competition specification. Its compact dimensions, just over two meters in wheelbase, allowed for exceptional agility on tight rally courses.

In the early 1970s, rallying underwent rapid evolution as manufacturers began focusing on <StyleBold>purpose-built vehicles</> rather than adapting existing models for competition. Under Cesare Fiorio's leadership alongside Mike Parkes and Sandro Munari, Lancia embarked on an ambitious project aimed at creating a dedicated rally car. This effort culminated in three consecutive World Rally Championships from 1974 to 1976 under drivers like Sandro Munari and Björn Waldegård. The Stratos also achieved multiple victories at prestigious events such as the Monte Carlo Rally.

Despite internal shifts within Fiat favoring other models later on (e.g., Fiat 131 Abarth), private teams continued finding success with the Stratos into the early <StyleBold>'80s</> due to its robust design and performance capabilities.

From a broader perspective, Marcello Gandini's work on this project contributed significantly to what became known as <StyleBold>wedge design</>, influencing future sports cars globally.

Today, when discussing iconic rally cars that have left lasting impacts on automotive history books (and enthusiasts' hearts), Lancia Stratos HF remains notable for combining innovative engineering with competitive prowess effectively. Whether you're an avid fan or just discovering this piece of automotive history now, there’s no denying that this <StyleBold>Italian marvel</> remains an exciting example of technical innovation.

•	The Lancia Stratos was inspired by Marcello Gandini's earlier concept, the <StyleBold>Stratos Zero</>, which debuted at the 1970 Turin Auto Show. This futuristic design laid the groundwork for the production model
•	Only about <StyleBold>492 road-going</> versions were produced between 1973 and 1978 to meet homologation requirements for racing

GROUP_STRATOSHF_DESC: The <StyleBold>Lancia Stratos HF</>, with its 250 hp Ferrari engine, rear-wheel drive, and cutting-edge design, dominated rallying in the 1970s. Powerful yet challenging to drive, it required exceptional skill, cementing its status as a motorsport legend.
CARSETUP_LAUNCH_CONTROL_MAP_DESC:
The <StyleBold>Launch Control Map</> allows you to adjust the engine’s starting RPM during launch.

<StyleBold>Increasing</> the setting raises the initial RPM, providing more power off the line, which is ideal for high-traction surfaces like <StyleBold>dry tarmac</>.

<StyleBold>Lower</> launch RPM settings reduce wheel spin and offer better control on slippery, low-grip surfaces such as <StyleBold>gravel or wet dirt.</> Too low however can cause the car to bog down and have a slower initial launch.

Find the right balance for the surface and conditions you’re launching on.
CARSETUP_LSD_PRELOAD_DESC:
The <StyleBold>Limited Slip Differential (LSD) preload</> is the initial torque resistance that must be overcome for any speed difference to occur between the two driven wheels on the same axle.

Until this torque threshold is exceeded, both wheels rotate at the same speed, similar to a locked axle. At low lateral accelerations, this preload causes slower corner entry, reduced steering response, and some understeer. However, under high lateral load transfer, it improves traction and stability. 

Preload is especially important on loose surfaces, providing needed traction before the differential fully locks. Front differentials typically require less preload to preserve steering feel.
CARSETUP_SPRING_STIFFNESS_DESC:
The <StyleBold>Main Spring</> determines the natural frequency of a car's suspension system, impacting how the car responds to driver input and absorbtion of bumps from the terrain. It also affects wheel droop, reducing rebound if too stiff, causing frequent loss of wheel contact and spring oscillations that may damage the suspension.

This is where Helper Springs and Rebound Stops become crucial, preventing damage by managing suspension travel.

Generally, a higher rear spring frequency is preferred to help the rear wheels better synchronize with the front wheels over bumps, improving stability.

Increasing front spring stiffness tends to increase understeer, while softer front springs promote oversteer. The opposite happens for the rear, where increasing rear springs tends to increase oversteer, while softer rear springs brings the rears balance back towards understeer. Tune the two to find yours and the car’s ideal handling balance.
CARSETUP_MASTER_CYLINDER_DESC:
The <StyleBold>Master Cylinder</> converts the driver’s foot force into hydraulic pressure for the braking system.

In rally cars, it can come as a single unit with two internal cylinders for the front and rear axles. This design limits direct adjustment of brake bias, but bias can be indirectly influenced by altering the diameters of these cylinders.

Alternatively, some setups use two separate Master Cylinders, one for each axle. This allows for direct brake bias control through a lever mechanism, which adjusts how much the brake pedal pushes on each cylinder, giving the driver fine-tuned <StyleBold>braking balance between</> front and rear wheels.

Increasing the Master Cylinders value will reduce the line pressure, decreasing braking power, making it harder to lock by requiring heavier braking inputs. This is ideal for more loose or low grip surface. Decreasing the Master Cylinder will increase the line pressure, increasing braking power to the point that the brakes lock, which is better suited for higher grip tarmac stages.
CARDESC_PEUGEOT_208RALLY4:
The <StyleBold>Peugeot 208 Rally4</> was designed to meet the Rally4 category regulations and serves as the successor to the highly successful Peugeot 208 R2. The development process began in mid-2018, with extensive testing across various terrains to ensure it could handle extreme conditions effectively. The goal was clear: create a fast, reliable, and fun-to-drive rally car that would appeal to a wide range of competitors.

At the heart of the Peugeot 208 Rally4 is a turbocharged <StyleBold>1.2-liter three-cylinder engine</>, producing a robust 208 horsepower at <StyleBold>5,450 rpm</> and a maximum torque of <StyleBold>290 Nm at 3,000 rpm</>. This engine is derived from the road-going version of the Peugeot 208 but has been meticulously tuned for competition use, featuring a larger turbocharger and an advanced <StyleBold>Magneti Marelli</> engine management system. It features a <StyleBold>5-speed sequential</> gearbox from <StyleBold>SADEV</>, which is manually controlled.

With a minimum weight of just <StyleBold>1,080 kg (approximately 2,381 lbs)</>, the Rally4 is designed for agility on various surfaces, whether gravel or tarmac. The chassis is reinforced with a welded multipoint roll cage to enhance safety without compromising performance.

The car features <StyleBold>McPherson-type</> suspension with Öhlins three-way adjustable shock absorbers at the front and torsion beam at the rear, allowing fine-tuning for different rally conditions. One of the standout aspects of the Peugeot 208 Rally4 is its drivability. Designed with both performance and accessibility in mind, it allows drivers to unlock competitive setups with minimal effort. This ease of use has made it popular among teams looking for reliability alongside speed.

Its ability to perform well on all surfaces has led to numerous class victories and accolades, reinforcing its status as a formidable contender in the rally scene, making it not only a competitive machine but also an accessible option for aspiring rally drivers.

CARDESC_PEUGEOT_306IIMAXI:
The <StyleBold>Peugeot 306 II Maxi Kit Car</>, homologated in 1997, is a remarkable example of late-90s rally engineering, designed predominantly for tarmac racing within the FIA’s 2-Litre World Rally Cup. Its development grew from the earlier 306 S16, but with significant technical upgrades tailored for rally competition, particularly in national and international tarmac events.

At its core, this car is powered by a naturally aspirated <StyleBold>2.0-liter inline-four engine</>, the PSA XU10 J4RS, which was highly refined to produce around 280 to 300 horsepower at a screaming <StyleBold>11,000 rpm</>. The engine features a squared bore and stroke configuration (86.0 mm x 86.0 mm), a notably high compression ratio of 12.5:1, and utilizes double overhead camshafts with 16 valves for efficient breathing and high-rev performance. This allowed the engine to deliver strong torque peaking at about <StyleBold>265 Nm</> around <StyleBold>8,900 rpm</>, well-suited for the sharp acceleration and quick throttle response required in rally stages.

Its lightweight construction contributed heavily to its agility. With a dry weight around <StyleBold>960 kg</> initially (increasing slightly to about 1,000 kg in later years), the ratio of weight to power was remarkably low, approximately <StyleBold>3.4 kg per horsepower</>, enabling blistering pace and nimble handling. The body was a steel monocoque with integrated roll-cage safety and featured broad extended wheel arches along with carbon fiber panels and a rear wing designed to enhance aerodynamic stability on high-speed bends. The car's dimensions were compact but purposeful: just under 4 meters in length, about 1.83 meters wide, and a low height around 1.33 meters, optimizing below-center-of-gravity mass and lowering drag.

On the suspension front, the 306 Maxi employed MacPherson strut suspension at the front with lower wishbones, coil springs, and telescopic shocks, paired with trailing arm and torsion bar suspension at the rear, including passive rear wheel steering characteristics. This setup was critical for precise handling and stability during the high-speed cornering characteristic of tarmac rally stages. The braking system was advanced for its time, featuring ventilated discs at the front (with options for multi-piston calipers) and solid or ventilated discs at the rear, all supported by a dual-circuit system with servo assistance for confidence-inspiring stopping power.

Transmission was a front-wheel-drive layout paired with a 6-speed ZF sequential gearbox designed for rapid shifts and durability under racing conditions. A limited-slip front differential helped optimize traction by distributing torque efficiently between the front wheels, vital for maintaining control on twisty, high-grip surfaces.

The Peugeot 306 Maxi emerged in an era when French manufacturers were pushing the envelope in the 2-Litre Kit Car category, which emphasized naturally aspirated engines in front-wheel-drive chassis. This class focused on lightweight, agile vehicles optimized for asphalt rather than the gravel where World Rally Cars dominated. The 306 Maxi was notably competitive because of its blend of power, lightness, and fine-tuned chassis dynamics, making it faster on tarmac than many costlier four-wheel-drive WRC rivals. Its success contributed to the eventual ban of Kit Cars from top-tier international rally competitions, as their performance upset the established hierarchy.

CARSETUP_LSD_RAMP_DESC:
The <StyleBold>Ramp Angle</> of a <StyleBold>Limited Slip Differential (LSD)</> controls how much input torque clamps the two output shafts together. The Power side angle (left value) affects clamping under acceleration, while the Coast side angle (right value) affects it under deceleration.

<StyleBold>Lower angles</> increase clamping force and traction but reduce speed difference and steering agility.
<StyleBold>Higher angles</> improve steering but allow more slippage or less stability. The Locking Effect (LE) shows the percentage of torque clamping the shafts, higher LE means stronger lock. Front LSDs typically have higher angles for better steering.

Remember that brakes don’t influence Coast side locking since LSD responds to engine torque.
CARSETUP_REB_HEAVE_TRANSITION_DESC:
The <StyleBold>Rebound Heave Transition</> is adjusted by the Fast Heave Rebound preload via a simple screw. This adjustment controls the timing of when the piston holes fully open, setting the damper to its soft rate.

Increasing the value delays the opening, keeping the wheel more damped during fast vibrations, improving stability but potentially increasing contact loss between the tyre and the road surface.

Decreasing the value anticipates the opening, reducing damping force earlier, which can lead to less effective body control and unwanted vehicle oscillations.
CARSETUP_REBOUND_TRANSITION_DESC:
The <StyleBold>Rebound Transition</> in a car suspension is adjusted using the Fast Rebound preload, controlled by a simple screw.

This mechanism either anticipates or delays the full opening of the piston holes, which sets the damper to its soft rebound rate.

Increasing the Rebound Transition value will delay the opening, maintaining higher damping during fast vibrations, improving stability but potentially increasing tyre contact losses.

Lowering the Rebound Transition value will anticipate the opening, reducing damping force earlier during rebound, which can lead to less control over body movements through unwanted oscillations, but is better suited to rougher and bumpier surfaces.
CARDESC_SUBARU_IMPREZAS3555:
The <StyleBold>Subaru Impreza S3</> of 1993 marked Subaru’s serious entry into the World Rally Championship (WRC) with a car designed specifically for Group A regulations. It replaced the larger Legacy RS and aimed to bring improved agility and competitive edge through technical refinements rather than radical reinvention.

At its core, the Impreza S3 was based on the earlier Subaru Impreza road car introduced in 1992, but was extensively developed by <StyleBold>Subaru Technica International</> (STi) and Prodrive, Subaru’s motorsport partner. Key mechanical upgrades included a revised 2.0-liter aluminum <StyleBold>boxer 4-cylinder engine</> equipped with a new turbocharger, improved intercooler, and enhanced cylinder heads. These modifications boosted output to approximately <StyleBold>300 horsepower at 5,500 rpm</> and torque of roughly <StyleBold>480 Nm at 4,000 rpm</>.

One distinctive engineering feature was the use of active differentials, starting with an active center differential and later adding a cockpit-adjustable hydraulic front differential. These systems allowed dynamic torque distribution among the wheels, improving traction and handling on the varied surfaces of rally stages. The chassis retained the Legacy’s well-balanced architecture but was reduced in size: the Impreza was 160 mm shorter in length with a 60 mm shorter wheelbase, improving its responsiveness and maneuverability.

The suspension utilized a strut setup tailored for rally conditions, and the entire vehicle was designed for a favorable front-to-rear weight distribution. The focus on weight balance and a low center of gravity, helped by the horizontally opposed boxer engine, enabled drivers to manage corners at higher speeds with better stability. Weighing around <StyleBold>1,208 kg</> (2,663 lbs), the car was relatively light, contributing to its competitive performance.

The Impreza S3 first competed late in the 1993 WRC season, making its debut at Finland’s tough 1000 Lakes Rally with Ari Vatanen finishing second, a promising start that underlined its potential. Subsequent model years saw incremental improvements including a switch to Pirelli tyres and further development of the active differential system. The 1994 car introduced a fully active <StyleBold>center differential</> controlled electronically from the cockpit, a significant technical advancement at the time.

The Subaru Impreza S3 came into its own in the mid-1990s with renowned drivers like <StyleBold>Colin McRae</> and <StyleBold>Carlos Sainz</> behind the wheel. McRae clinched the Drivers’ World Rally Championship in 1995 with this car, becoming the youngest champion ever at that time. The model also helped Subaru secure multiple manufacturers’ titles through 1996 and 1997.

Born from Subaru’s desire to improve upon the Legacy’s platform with a more agile and technically refined machine, the Impreza became a foundational car that established Subaru as a major force in WRC history without resorting to hype, its technical merits and racing pedigree remain the facts that define its legacy.

OPTION_TRACTIONCONTROL_DESC:
The <StyleBold>TCS (Traction Control System)</> is a traction control system that prevents the drive wheels from slipping during acceleration by reducing engine power or intervening on the brakes when it detects that one wheel is spinning faster than the others.

Select if TCS is disabled for all cars, it can still be re-enabled during the race, provided the game mode allows it, either through direct inputs or in-game controls.
CARSETUP_TCS_MAP_DESC:
The <StyleBold>TCS (Traction Control System)</> is a traction control system that prevents the drive wheels from slipping during acceleration by reducing engine power or intervening on the brakes when it detects that one wheel is spinning faster than the others.

The system optimizes the performance and stability of the vehicle, especially during acceleration in difficult conditions such as rain, snow or slippery surfaces. Furthermore, by reducing wheel slippage during extreme acceleration, it improves traction and ensures more efficient power transfer.

With the <StyleBold>TCS deactivated (OFF)</> the driver has full control over acceleration. Greater experience is required in dosing the pressure, preventing loss of grip and thus obtaining superior performance.

By <StyleBold>increasing the intensity</> of the system, the TCS becomes more sensitive to wheel slippage, intervening to reduce it and ensuring adequate performance even for those with less experience, reducing the need to carefully control the accelerator.
CARSETUP_THROTTLE_MAP_DESC:
The <StyleBold>Throttle Map</> controls how the engine responds to accelerator input, adjusting throttle sensitivity to suit different driving conditions.

Varying throttle maps allow the driver to select the ideal response for traction and control, whether on loose gravel, tarmac, or slippery surfaces.

A <StyleBold>more sensitive map</> delivers quicker engine response for aggressive driving, while a <StyleBold>gentler map</> provides smoother, more manageable power delivery to prevent wheel spin.

This adaptability helps optimize performance and stability, giving the driver better control and confidence across diverse rally stages with changing terrain and grip levels.
CARSETUP_TORSEN_TBR_DESC:
The <StyleBold>TorSen differential</> in a rally car doesn’t lock the two output shafts (axles or wheels) together on throttle or coasting unless there’s a difference in torque at the wheels. When torque difference occurs, it transfers some power from the spinning axle to the one with better traction, improving grip compared to a standard open differential.

This ability depends on the <StyleBold>Torque Bias Ratio (TBR)</>, which defines the torque multiplication between wheels. If one wheel has zero torque, no transfer occurs, and the vehicle can get stuck.

Increasing TBR will add more locking effect at the wheels, improving traction on more loose surfaces when on throttle and adding stability off throttle. Too much locking effect though, can create more understeer in situations where there are higher grip levels.

Unlike LSDs, TorSen offers smooth operation without friction plates, reducing wear.
PACENOTES_CONJUNCTIONS_DESC:
The <StyleBold>conjunctions</> between notes are elements that provide important information to the driver about a <StyleBold>sequence of corners</> and how they are positioned relative to each other on the stage. Thanks to them, the driver will be able to better interpret the rhythm of the stage, the difficulty presented by the different sequences of corners, and the peculiarities of the track.

The conjunctions can be <StyleBold>"AND"</>, generally represented by the symbol +, or <StyleBold>"INTO"</> for which an arrow symbol is used. These symbols are not used in the visual notes of AC Rally.

<StyleTitle>AND Conjunction</>

The <StyleBold>AND</> is used in the following cases:
· The previous corner is of <StyleBold>equal or greater difficulty</> than the next one (a 4 precedes a 6). The conjunction can therefore be interpreted as an opportunity to push and attack the second corner at a higher speed.
· There is a certain <StyleBold>distance</> between the first and second corners; the second is not immediately after the first, so the driver can interpret the conjunction as a short “pause” between the two corners. The distance is still less than 20 meters.

<StyleGray>Example:</> 4 Right <StyleBold>AND</> 6 Left 80

In this case, the first corner, a 4 Right, is two difficulty grades easier than the following 6 Left. Also, there will be some distance between the two corners, allowing the driver time to set up each corner individually.

<StyleTitle>INTO Conjunction</>

The <StyleBold>INTO</> is used in the following cases:
· The first corner is of <StyleBold>lower difficulty</> than the next (a 5 precedes a hairpin). In this case, the driver must pay more attention to the next corner and approach the sequence by progressively reducing speed.
· The two corners are <StyleBold>immediately</> one after the other. After the first corner, there is no “pause” before facing the next corner; therefore, the driver can set up the sequence aware of this difficulty.

<StyleGray>Example:</> 5 Left <StyleBold>INTO</> Hairpin Right 50

In this case, the two corners follow immediately one another, and a fast 5 Left is followed by a complex hairpin in the opposite direction. The driver must approach the 5 knowing that on exiting the corner they must already be ready for the hairpin.

<StyleTitle>Conjunctions and Details</>

In some cases, the AND and INTO junctions can be used to connect a corner to a descriptive element of the track, highlighting difficulties such as jumps, ditches, fords, etc.

<StyleGray>Example:</> 6 Right <StyleBold>AND</> Jump <StyleBold>INTO</> 3 Left

In this case, after a fast corner there will be a short pause before a jump, which will then quickly be followed by a complex left corner.
CARSETUP_HANDBRAKE_FORCE_DESC:
The <StyleBold>handbrake system</> can be finely tuned by adjusting or replacing components such as the handbrake calipers, brake pads, or the master cylinder pressure. With Handbrake Force, you are adjusting the whole system to increase or reduce its effect.

Increasing the Handbrake Force requires less pull on the handbrake to lock the wheels, even on smoother and grippier surfaces, making it easier to rotate the car with less modulation required.

Decreasing the Handbrake Force will require more pull on the handbrake to lock the wheels, reducing the cars desire to rotate as quickly or sharply when trying to engage or modulate the handbrake. 

Tune based on the your preference and the amount of available grip.
CARSETUP_HEAVESPRING_STIFFNES_DESC:
The <StyleBold>heave spring</> is a third spring that connects the left and right suspensions, working alongside the main springs.

Its unique linkage design allows it to only respond to bumps impacting the car on both sides simultaneously, by stiffening the suspension vertically when both wheels move together, such as during jumps or dips in the road. It does not engage during roll motions, so it doesn’t affect lateral dynamics.

This selective stiffness helps prevent bottoming out and excessive diving in more aero dependant vehicles, improving stability and control without compromising handling during cornering or uneven terrain.

Increasing the Heave Spring makes it stiffer, reducing the chance of bottoming out and improving the aerodyanmic grip for cars that utilize it. Decreasing the Heave Spring will soften it, improving mechanical grip and the cars ability to absorb jumps and dips in the road surface.
CARSETUP_HELPER_SPRING_DESC:
The <StyleBold>helper spring</> in a car suspension is typically used alongside long-travel dampers that have short, stiff main springs. Its primary role is to prevent oscillations of the main spring during rebound, which can potentially damage the suspension components.

When designed to be stiff and long enough to avoid full compression under static load, the helper spring also enables a dual-rate spring effect. This means the suspension benefits from a softer initial travel to absorb small surface bumps and a firmer resistance for bigger impacts, such as jumps, improving overall durability and ride quality during rough rally stages.
CARSETUP_REBOUNDSTOP_DESC:
The <StyleBold>reboundstop</> is designed to prevent excessive spring oscillations that can cause damage during rough terrain driving.

Increasing the value will soften the extension of the suspension, by having the reboundstop engage earlier. Decreasing the value will allow the suspension to extend and drop more quickly, with the reboundstop engaging later and sharper in its length of travel. 

By working alongside the Helper, you can fine-tune the reboundstop settings to ensure optimal suspension performance and durability.
CARSETUP_ADJUSTER_RING_DESC:
The <StyleBold>ride height</> is adjusted using an adjuster ring that shifts the spring perch up or down, raising or lowering the car. Changing the spring seat alters the chassis height and static corner weights, but it also affects the damper’s working point.

Increasing the Adjuster Ring value will raise the ride height of the car up, helping to prevent the car from bottoming out but can make the car feel softer and less responsive in turns. Decreasing the value will drop the ride height, making the cars handling feel more responsive to driver inputs, but increasing the chance of bottoming out on rougher terrain. 

After changing ride height you must check damper travel and spring compression to ensure there’s still sufficient bump and rebound range and no bottoming or topping out.
Re-verify bump stops, ride frequency and alignment settings, and make further adjustments to spring preload or damping as needed so the suspension operates safely and effectively across rally terrain.
RULES_SERVICEPARK_DESC:
The <StyleBold>service park</> is a fundamental element in rally competitions. It is the place where teams and crews can work on their cars to prepare them as best as possible for the upcoming special stages.

In real life, the time available at the service park is limited, and service parks are interspersed between multiple special stages. In AC Rally, however, there are no strict limits on the number of service parks that can be scheduled during a rally, and their duration is limited only by the time needed to repair the car's damage.

<StyleTitle>Event information:</>
At the service park, the crew has all the time needed to consult the event schedule and all the information regarding the special stages ahead. This allows them to carefully plan every aspect of the car setup, repairs to be made, and tyre management.

<StyleTitle>Car Setup:</>
Only at the service park is it possible to modify the car’s setup, by changing components or adjusting parameters, to best prepare the vehicle for the characteristics of the upcoming special stages. For example, if a stage takes place on asphalt, the car will be set up with lower ride height and all necessary adjustments for that surface.

<StyleTitle>Tyre Management:</>
Tyres are a crucial component in rally: choosing the right type and compound for each special stage can make the difference between winning and retiring. Punctures and tyre damage are common, so it is essential to plan which tyres to mount at the start of each stage and which to carry as spares. This allows for quick repairs between stages or even roadside tyre changes during a stage. Often, losing a few minutes to change a damaged tyre is more advantageous than completing the entire stage with a compromised tyre.

<StyleTitle>Car Repairs:</>
Finishing a special stage without any damage often matters more than the final position in the standings. Damage caused by collisions, accidents, or normal wear and tear is common in rallying. Learning to manage and minimize it leads to more reliable and consistent results.
At the service park, mechanics can perform all necessary repairs before heading out for the next sequence of special stages. The available repair time depends on game settings, but it is often challenging to fix multiple damaged parts simultaneously.
If the allowed repair time is exceeded, the crew will incur a time penalty added to their overall event time.

It is therefore essential to prevent damage as much as possible by driving carefully, balancing the desire for speed with the need to keep the car in top condition. Rallying is first and foremost an endurance competition—often, the winner is the one who reaches the finish, rather than the fastest driver who suffers errors and damage.
CARSETUP_STEARINGRATIO_DESC:
The <StyleBold>steering ratio</> determines how much the cars front wheels turn relative to the drivers steering wheel’s rotation. 

A <StyleBold>higher setting</> lowers the steering ratio, meaning fewer degrees of steering wheel input is needed to turn the wheels fully.

This makes steering maneuvers faster and more responsive, allowing the car driver to react quickly to driver input which is useful for tight twisty sections of road. It does however, make it more difficult to be accurate with steering inputs in faster and more openly flowing sections. 

<StyleBold>Decreasing the steering ratio</> makes the car less sensitive to small inputs by increasing the steering effort to turn the wheel. This however is not ideal for tighter and twistier sections of road that require rapid changes of direction.  

Balancing the steering ratio is crucial for optimizing control and handling in rally driving.
CARSETUP_STEARINGSERVO_DESC:
The <StyleBold>steering servo</> assists the driver by providing consistent steering effort up to its maximum torque capacity. It helps maintain control by reducing the physical effort required to turn the wheels, ensuring precise and responsive handling. However, some drivers may choose to uninstall or disable the servo to increase direct feedback from the road, enhancing the driver's feel and control during demanding rally conditions. 

This compromises assistance but improves tactile connection between the steering wheel and the terrain, which can be beneficial for experienced drivers seeking maximum road sensation.
CH_A110_NIGHT_TEST1_DESC: The Alpine A110’s lights, mounted low and very close to the road, do not provide very long-range visibility but still allow driving in low-visibility conditions. The A110 demands extra focus in these situations and careful attention to avoid frontal collisions to protect the lighting system.
TRACK_LOCATION_ALSACE_DESC: The Alsace Rally features exclusive asphalt stages, picturesque vineyard landscapes, and unpredictable grip levels, demanding precise driving skills and quick adaptations to challenging weather conditions.
CH_XSARAWRC_TARMAC_TEST1_DESC: The Citroën Xsara WRC has consistently achieved excellent results on tarmac stages. Its handling is outstanding, and the all-wheel drive system allows full exploitation of the engine’s power. The perfect balance between speed and control ensures both excellent performance and safety.
CH_124ABARTH_TARMAC_TEST1_DESC: The Fiat 124 Abarth, thanks to its very low profile and ground-hugging setup, is highly responsive and easy to handle on tarmac special stages, also due to its relatively modest engine power. The rear-wheel drive can cause oversteer, but this can be controlled with proper use of counter-steering.
CARDESC_FIAT_131ABARTH:
The Fiat 131 Abarth Group 4 rally car is a legendary machine that transformed from a humble family sedan into a fierce competitor on the rally stages of the 1970s. Built between 1976 and 1978, with the aim of replacing the Fiat 124 Abarth Rally after the "Fiat Abarth X1/9 Rally" project was stopped, only 400 units were produced to meet FIA homologation requirements, making it a rare gem in automotive history. 

At its heart lies a robust <StyleBold>2.0-liter inline-four engine</>, which in its racing form could produce between <StyleBold>225 to 245 horsepower</>. This power was channelled through a <StyleBold>five-speed manual transmission</> and a ZF limited-slip differential, allowing the car to tackle challenging terrains with agility and speed. The vehicle's lightweight design, aided by <StyleBold>resin body panels and aluminium doors</>, contributed to its impressive performance for the age, with a top speed exceeding <StyleBold>190 km/h (118 mph)</> and acceleration from 0 to 60 mph in just <StyleBold>6.6 seconds</>. 

The Fiat 131 Abarth's design was the brainchild of the renowned Bertone Style Centre, which added wider wheel arches and spoilers for enhanced aerodynamics and grip. Its distinctive yellow and blue livery became iconic, especially during its success in competitions, where it secured multiple championship titles against formidable rivals like the Ford Escort RS1800. 

The car's combination of power, style, and engineering excellence made it a favourite among drivers such as <StyleBold>Walter Röhrl</> and <StyleBold>Markku Alén</>, who showcased its capabilities on various international stages

Driving the Fiat 131 Abarth is an exhilarating experience; the growl of the engine resonates through the chassis, providing an adrenaline rush that captures the essence of rallying. With its blend of performance and heritage, the Fiat 131 Abarth Group 4 remains a celebrated symbol of motorsport history, cherished by enthusiasts around the globe.

PARTNER_MACALUSO_HISTORY:
The Fondazione Gino Macaluso per l’Auto storica has been founded in Turin in October 2018 in memory of Gino Macaluso, by the will of his wife and family. 

Luigi Macaluso was born in Turin on 1948. At the end of the 1960’s, in his early twenties, he joined the world of racing competitions, starting his career at Pinerolo Corse, a small team founded by Gianfranco Silecchia. More and more crews converged at Pinerolo Corse, including the one formed by young Cristiano Rattazzi and Luca Cordero di Montezemolo; Gino made his racing debut alongside Luciano Trombotto.

His skill led him to join the official Fiat Abarth team after a short time: as co-driver, he won the European Rally Championship and Mitropa Cup already in 1972, paired with Emanuele Pinto in a Fiat 124 Spider. For the first time in its history, the name of Fiat was written in the roll of honor of an international championship, comparable to the World Championship which had not yet been established at the time.

The success was repeated in 1974, with the victory in the Italian Rally Championship, together with Maurizio Verini in a Fiat 124 Abarth.

Gino began to be assigned, at that point in his career, to increasingly important roles; in the same year he was entrusted with the program for the X1/9 Abarth, which was to take up the legacy of the 124 Abarth Spider: a prototype specially made for rallies and to give the newborn Lancia Stratos a hard time.

However, Fiat decided not to continue development of the X1/9 Prototipo due to its marketing strategies. Gino's last adventure as a navigator was the Giro d'Italia alongside Clay Regazzoni with the X1/9, which will soon be destined for retirement.

In 1975, he started to work in watchmaking when he was hired by an Italian distributor of prestigious Swiss brands. In 1982, he started his entrepreneurial career by founding MGA, which will later become Tradema. The company distributed in Italy Swiss and American brands: Blancpain, Breitling and Hamilton. Just seven years later, in 1989, he became a shareholder of the historical Girard-Perregaux manufacture in Chaux-de-Fonds, Switzerland, and in 1992 he became its President. 

Despite his hard work and achievements in watchmaking, Gino did not forget his first love: the world of cars and racing competitions. In 1987, he joined Club Italia, an association of Italian car manufacturing lovers. A few years later, at the beginning of the 1990’s, he became President and remained in office for almost two decades.

In his efforts to promote the cultural, social, aesthetic and historical values of automobiles, he decided to restore rally cars from the golden years of rallying. It’s the beginning of what is one of the most relevant collections in this field.
PARTNER_MACALUSO_RALLY:
The Fondazione Gino Macaluso per l’Auto storica has been founded in Turin in October 2018 in memory of Gino Macaluso, by the will of his wife and family. The purpose of the Foundation is to enhance the car as a cult object that has combined technological innovation with humanistic culture and artisan tradition with the beauty of avant-garde design, and which has influenced habits and society of the last century.

Gino Macaluso considered the car “the most intense expression of the Twentieth-Century creativity”.

The Fondazione Gino Macaluso per l’Auto storica intends to promote those extraordinary and glorious expressions all around the world, spreading the culture of vintage cars and in particular sport cars, as well as paying tribute to the pilots and the people who have given their contribute to motorsport, talking not only to enthusiasts but also to a wider and heterogeneous audience.

The Fondazione Gino Macaluso per l’Auto storica intends to disseminate the culture of vintage cars and sporting competitions to an increasingly wider audience, making Gino’s dream real. Through his famous collection, it organizes, promotes and participates in events, competitions, rallies, exhibitions, fairs, seminars, conferences, workshops related to historic car, motoring and its protagonists. It also collaborates with leading universities and higher education institutes to pass on the know-how relating to the history, maintenance and restoration of historic cars.
CH_FULVIACOUPEHF_GRAVEL_TEST1_DESC: The Fulvia's balance issues and understeer under braking remain significant even on gravel: the surface characteristics can mitigate some behaviors, but at the same time, they can introduce additional challenges for the driver.
CH_GIULIAGTA1300_TARMAC_TEST1_DESC: The GTA 1300's excellent weight distribution and easy handling ensure excellent performance on tarmac special stages. Rear-wheel drive can cause natural oversteer; with its wide turning circle, quick corrections are required to avoid problems.
HISTORY_80GROUPB: The Golden Era Of Group B
TRACK_LOCATION_GREECE_DESC: The Greece Rally, known for its diverse and challenging terrains, with rocky paths, dirt roads, and river crossings. Held in hot summer conditions, it’s a unique rally that requires strategic driving skills.
WEATHER_STARTGRIP_DESC:
The Grip level describes how much traction the track surface offers to tyres, influencing vehicle handling and performance.
The surface evolution caused by weather changes, temperature and car passing, will change the grip level over time.

<StyleBold>Dirty:</> The track grip is Very low and very slippery, the worst possible condition.
<StyleBold>Slow:</> The track grip is low and slippery.
<StyleBold>Green:</> The ideal trajectory is clear and the grip is not much, but improving.
<StyleBold>Fast:</>  The track is faster near its best and improving.
<StyleBold>Optimal:</> Maximum grip available for the track.
CH_I20RALLY2_TARMAC_TEST1_DESC: The Hyundai i20 Rally2 offers excellent grip on tarmac. Its handling, combined with high performance, allows it to tackle special stages at extremely high average speeds. This is definitely an advantage in terms of stage times but can become a challenge if the necessary concentration is not maintained to avoid mistakes.
GROUP_I20RALLY2_DESC: The Hyundai i20 Rally2, one of the most popular cars in its category, is a turbocharged 4WD with excellent performance and great ease of use. It is ideal both for novice drivers and for veterans seeking a reliable car.
GROUP_IMPREZAS3_DESC: The Impreza S3, introduced in 1993, replaced the Legacy in Subaru's Group A rally program. With its iconic blue-and-yellow livery, revolutionized the World Rally Championship and was thrust into the spotlight by legendary driver Colin McRae.
CH_FULVIACOUPEHF_NIGHT_TEST1_DESC: The Lancia Fulvia Coupé Rallye 1.6 HF was also known by the nickname "Fanalona" for its distinctive enlarged front headlight cluster, capable of providing exceptional illumination during night stages. Despite this, poor visibility along the sides of the road can hide dangerous obstacles at the track edges, and damaging the lights can completely compromise the special stage.
CH_COOPERS_TARMAC_TEST1_DESC: The Mini Cooper S is a very agile car, and its front-wheel drive makes it easy to handle on paved surfaces. Despite being front-wheel drive, understeer is kept to a minimum thanks to the moderate engine power, which still allows for good performance, helped by the vehicle’s light weight.
TRACK_LOCATION_MONTECARLO_DESC: The Monte Carlo Rally is famous for unpredictable weather, featuring snow, ice, and dry asphalt. It tests drivers' skills and adaptability, making it one of the most challenging rallies in the world.
GROUP_208RALLY4_DESC: The Peugeot 208 Rally4 is a modern front-wheel-drive car that is extremely agile and responsive. It can be very fast but requires very smooth driving to manage the quick rotation of the rear axle and avoid spinning out.
CH_208RALLY4_TARMAC_TEST1_DESC: The Peugeot 208 Rally4 is a very fast car on asphalt, but you need to be very careful on high-speed corners. Its extremely agile chassis and very quick steering make it quite nervous during deceleration, and if you don't drive smoothly, it's easy to spin. Under acceleration, power is managed through the limited-slip differential, and understeer is minimal.
CH_FWD_TARMAC_TEST_208RALLY4_DESC: The Peugeot 208 Rally4 is extremely fast on asphalt but also very responsive and nervous. High-speed corners are particularly challenging, requiring attention during braking and corner entry. Precisely modulating the accelerator allows maintaining good grip on the front wheels.
CH_208RALLY4_RAIN_TEST1_DESC: The Peugeot 208 Rally4, being a front-wheel-drive car, can suffer from understeer, especially on wet tarmac where the surface is particularly slippery. It is essential to make the most of weight transfers to achieve better cornering entry.
CH_306MAXI_TARMAC_TEST1_DESC: The Peugeot 306 Maxi is an extremely effective car on asphalt, thanks to its low weight and naturally aspirated engine that revs up to nearly 11,000 rpm. At these RPMs, it delivers high power and manageable torque, perfectly suited to front-wheel drive. This makes the Maxi easy to control and highly agile in any situation.
HISTORY_70: The Seventies And The World Titles
TRACK_LOCATION_WALES_DESC: The Wales Rally features challenging gravel stages through rolling hills and dense forests, demanding precise driving skills amidst unpredictable weather conditions.
CH_I20RALLY2_SNOW_TEST1_DESC: The absence of the central differential in the I20 Rally 2 allows for excellent traction and control on snow. Its drifting  maneuverability enables drivers to take the track’s curves very quickly while maintaining a high average speed throughout the entire circuit.
PARTNER_RCBOOKS_HISTORY:
The acronym RC can be read in two ways: as the initials of the founders' surnames, Roberti and Cordasco, or as the initials of Reparto Corse, the core around which the topics of the proposed publications revolve.
RC Books was founded in 2015, following the successful experience with the book Lancia Delta S4 published by Luca Gastaldi. Subsequently, Vittorio Roberti, who for years was a designer and technical manager of the Abarth Reparto Corse, and Alessandro Cordasco, an engineer and passionate technical illustrator, continued their joint path with new editorial projects always focused on Lancia racing.
The strength of their publications is probably the most hidden and fascinating part of Reparto Corse: the technical development of the cars, from the blank sheet to the latest evolutions. Thanks to a very dense network of contacts, which grows with each book, ideas as well as notes and sketches left for years in the shadow of a drawer or an archive folder have been brought to light.

So far, the following titles have been published:
•	Lancia Sport Gr.6 (LC/1): everything about this "little boat," which narrowly finished second in the World Endurance Drivers' Championship. From the first wind tunnel shots to the drawings from the Dallara archive, its entire genesis and technical features have been reconstructed.

•	Lancia Delta S4 in detail: the technical aspects like never seen before. Chassis, suspension, engine, transmission, various systems, and cockpit analyzed in minute detail through dozens of technical illustrations and unpublished photographs.

•	Lancia Stratos Gr.5: the version that raced in non-rally competitions. Little known but equally fascinating is its story: from the initial prototypes to Gr.5 races up to the latest evolutions, including the turbocharger.

•	Lancia Rally 037: over 500 pages for the last 2WD car that won a world title against 4WDs. Step by step, everything on its design and development, with dozens of photographs and unpublished technical documents.

•	Lancia Delta S4 Backstage: to celebrate the 40th anniversary of its WRC debut. But not only that: this publication also offers more than 200 illustrations including unpublished liveries, service vehicles, team structures (Martini Racing, Esso Grifone, and Jolly Club Totip), and team apparel.
CH_DELTAINTEGRALEEVO_NIGHT_TEST1_DESC: The additional lighting system of the Lancia Delta Integrale Evoluzione is quite modern and provides adequate illumination during night special stages. However, it is important to watch out for any damage to the front of the car, as this could affect the lights’ performance and lead to reduced visibility while driving.
CARSETUP_DAMPERS_DESC:
The adjustment of the dampers allows control over the car's behavior during transients, meaning the moments when load transfers occur.
By exploiting all the adjustment options available on the shock absorbers, it is possible to find the best setup suited to your driving style and the specific stage conditions.
It is important to remember that shock absorbers should not be used for mechanical balancing; that role is fulfilled by the suspension springs and anti-roll bars.
Instead, dampers must be tuned to match the damping to the suspension stiffness.
CH_FABIARSR2_SNOW_TEST1_DESC: The all-wheel drive and excellent performance of the Škoda Fabia RS Rally2 deliver outstanding capabilities on every surface. On snow, the car's power ensures excellent traction at all times, while its characteristics provide good oversteer control. This allows for consistently high average speeds without compromising special stage times.
CH_FABIARSR2_GRAVEL_TEST1_DESC: The all-wheel drive and excellent performance of the Škoda Fabia RS Rally2 deliver outstanding results on any surface. On gravel, it ensures superb control of slides, thanks to traction always ready on all wheels. The car's superior capabilities allow drivers to focus fully on the track's challenges to tackle them effectively.
CH_FABIARSR2_TARMAC_TEST1_DESC: The all-wheel drive and excellent performance of the Škoda Fabia RS Rally2 deliver superior capabilities on every surface. On asphalt, it enables precise handling and extreme speeds, combined with outstanding braking performance. Nonetheless, maximum concentration must be maintained to avoid overconfidence that can lead to disastrous results.
CH_DELTAINTEGRALEEVO_TARMAC_TEST1_DESC: The all-wheel drive of the Lancia Delta makes it extremely versatile and relatively easy to control on tarmac. The well-designed central differential ensures predictable handling in corners, allowing the driver to take them in a controlled slide while maintaining both stability and vehicle control.
DAMAGE_BODYWORKS_DESC:
The bodywork of a rally car is not just for aesthetics or protection: it also dictates the airflow over the car.
Any damage compromises aerodynamics, increasing drag, reducing downforce, and worsening stability, especially in yaw, negatively affecting the vehicle’s overall performance.
CH_208RALLY4_SNOW_TEST1_DESC: The chassis and setup of the Peugeot 208 Rally 4 make it very agile on snow. Thanks to the front-wheel drive and the weight balance shifted towards the front, the front axle gains better grip. This enhances traction but can also lead to dangerous loss of rear grip during throttle release.
DAMAGE_DIFFERENTIAL_DESC:
The clutch-type limited-slip differential (LSD) uses clutches that wear out during normal use.
As wear increases, the locking capacity decreases, causing an imbalance in the vehicle’s dynamics and reduced traction on slippery surfaces, compromising stability and control during driving.

The complete 18 km stage, first part uphill to Col de Turini, then downhill to La Bollène.
Its characteristics make it particularly challenging to tackle: very fast curves alternate with tight, twisting hairpins, flanked by stone and rock walls on both sides of the road. It demands maximum concentration and flawless technique to complete without errors.
CH_BOLLENE_FULL_R_SNOW_DESC:
The complete 18 km stage, first part uphill to Col de Turini, then downhill to La Bollène.
On these roads, as altitude increases, it's easy to encounter snow and ice: caution is essential in such cases. With snow, grip is reduced to a minimum, especially without proper winter or studded tires. Pushing hard with dry tires and then slowing down in snowy sections can be a winning strategy, but also extremely risky.
CH_BOLLENE_FULL_R_NIGHT_DESC:
The complete 18 km stage, first part uphill to Col de Turini, then downhill to La Bollène.
Tackling this special stage at night can be extremely challenging: despite the powerful night lights fitted on the cars, the constant direction changes obscure the driver's view, a factor amplified by the poor nighttime visibility.
CH_BOLLENE_FULL_R_SS_DESC:
The complete 18 km stage, first part uphill to Col de Turini, then downhill to La Bollène.
This stage demands concentration and speed to challenge your rivals. However, remember that speed isn’t everything in rallying: reaching the finish with your car intact and performing well can secure the victory.
CH_BOLLENE_FULL_R_RAIN_DESC:
The complete 18 km stage, first part uphill to Col de Turini, then downhill to La Bollène.

HISTORY_CURRENT_DESC:
The current era of rallying is one of dynamic evolution, blending tradition with fresh challenges and bold regulatory changes that promise to reshape the sport’s landscape. During the 2025 season, the World Rally Championship (WRC) has expanded to an intense fourteen-round calendar spanning four continents, including a groundbreaking addition, the <StyleBold>Rally Saudi Arabia</>, as the new season finale. This signals the sport’s growing global footprint and ambition, introducing fans to exotic terrains and new rally cultures.

The cars dominating the stages are largely Rally1-spec machines, but 2025 marks a significant regulatory pivot: the sport has abandoned the hybrid-electric powertrains introduced in 2022 in favor of solely internal combustion engines. This surprising move aims to <StyleBold>reduce costs and enhance competitiveness</>, rekindling the raw mechanical intensity rally enthusiasts cherish. Manufacturers must now finesse powerful yet simpler Rally1 cars under these fresh technical standards, heightening engineering creativity and driver skill significance.

Toyota Gazoo Racing remains the powerhouse team, fiercely contesting the manufacturers crown with a dominant presence. The <StyleBold>Toyota GR Yaris Rally1</> is arguably the era’s most famous and formidable car. Among drivers, <StyleBold>Ott Tänak</> stands as a central figure, leading the 2025 drivers championship closely followed by Elfyn Evans and the legendary Sébastien Ogier, whose Monte Carlo win boosted his tally to ten victories in that emblematic rally alone. 

Looking ahead, regulation trends suggest a continued emphasis on cost containment, sustainability, and global expansion. With new venues and fewer technical complexities, WRC aims to be more inclusive, thrilling, and economically viable. The removal of hybrid elements hints that future technological innovations might balance performance excitement with environmental responsibility in more subtle ways.
DAMAGE_GAUGES_DESC:
The dashboard gauges in a rally car do not directly affect performance but are an essential support for the driver.
They provide crucial information about the vehicle's condition, such as mechanical faults and useful data, including speed, engine rpm, fuel level, etc, allowing constant monitoring to improve safety and vehicle management during the race.
HISTORY_2000_DESC:
The decade from <StyleBold>2000 to 2009</> was a riveting period marked by intense rivalry, technical evolution, and the emergence of some of the sport’s most legendary figures. This era unfolded during the <StyleBold>World Rally Car</> regulations era, where cars like the <StyleBold>Peugeot 206 WRC</>, <StyleBold>Subaru Impreza WRC</>, <StyleBold>Ford Focus WRC</>, and <StyleBold>Citroën Xsara WRC</> set the stage for fierce competition. 

At the dawn of the 2000s, Finnish driver <StyleBold>Marcus Grönholm</> emerged as a dominant force behind the wheel of Peugeot’s 206 WRC, claiming his first World Championship in 2000 and helping Peugeot to multiple manufacturers titles. His aggressive yet calculated style defined much of the early decade’s spirit. Meanwhile, British driver <StyleBold>Richard Burns</> achieved a landmark victory for Subaru in 2001, showcasing the Impreza’s strength and his own racing tenacity in a heated battle with Grönholm and other title contenders.

<StyleBold>Colin McRae</>, already a rally icon from the 1990s, continued to captivate fans with his raw speed and fearlessness, particularly with M-Sport’s Ford Focus. The team enjoyed significant success at the Acropolis Rally, known for its rugged terrain, where McRae’s mechanical sympathy and grit led to multiple wins in the early 2000s, often clashing in thrilling duels with <StyleBold>Carlos Sainz</>.

Emerging towards the middle and latter part of the decade was <StyleBold>Sébastien Loeb</>, who revolutionized rally driving with astonishing consistency and mastery over the <StyleBold>Citroën Xsara WRC</> and later the <StyleBold>C4 WRC</>. Loeb’s dominance, winning multiple Driver's Championships from 2004 onward, set new standards of excellence and introduced a new era of French rally supremacy. His rivalry with drivers like Mikko Hirvonen and Petter Solberg added depth and tension to the championship battles.

This decade was not just about the cars and drivers but also about the evolution of rally as a global sport. Subaru and Mitsubishi’s fierce competition persisted, even as manufacturers like Ford, Citroën, and Peugeot battled for supremacy.
CARSETUP_DIFFERENCIALS_DESC:
The differential settings are among the most important and at the same time most complex aspects in tuning a rally car, as they significantly affect the vehicle's behavior.
Therefore, it is advisable to make gradual adjustments in order to fully understand the impact of each setting on driving.
Always adapt the settings according to the type of terrain you are facing.
PACENOTES_DISTANCES_DESC:
The distance between one corner and the next, or more generally the straight sections of the course, is communicated by the co-driver to allow the driver to anticipate and better interpret the rhythm of the special stage.

For example, when the co-driver indicates: <StyleBold>“4 Left, 50”</>, it means that after the left corner of degree 4 there is a short straight of about 50 meters, at the end of which the next corner will be called.

Similarly, with the note <StyleBold>“4 Left, 200”</>, the driver knows they can exploit a long straight of about 200 meters, free of particular hazards or rhythm changes, following the left corner.

Generally, distances shorter than 40 meters are not communicated, as they are too short to significantly influence driving style and can be implicitly indicated through the conjunctions between notes.

To ensure clarity, even distances under 100 meters are expressed as even numbers (40, 60, 80, etc.), while distances above this threshold are preferably odd numbers (130, 150, etc.), minimizing the risk of misunderstandings, especially in multilingual communications.

Correct management of distances is fundamental to modulate speed between corners, facilitating moments of recovery and preparation. However, even the longest straights can hide hazards, such as changes in grip, surface imperfections, or undulations in the track, which at high speeds can compromise vehicle stability and safety.

DAMAGE_CLUTCH_DESC:
The engine clutch, essential for transferring power from the engine to the wheels, is naturally subject to wear due to continuous use.
If too worn, it may lose effectiveness, preventing full power transfer and reducing the car's performance during rally driving, compromising acceleration and control.
DAMAGE_ENGINE_DESC:
The engine is obviously a fundamental part of the car. Any damage to it can cause drastic reductions in vehicle performance and compromise power delivery.

If the car's engine is located at the front, pay attention to any frontal collisions. Additionally, the loss of the hood can lead to further damage.
If, however, it is in a central or rear position, damage to the rear of the car can pose risks to the engine, such as the loss of the tailgate, which can increase the likelihood of damage.

HISTORY_EARLY2020_DESC:
The first part of the 2020 decade in rally racing marked a significant and transformative era, widely known as the <StyleBold>Hybrid era</>, introducing revolutionary technology to the World Rally Championship (WRC). It began with the debut of hybrid-powered <StyleBold>Rally1</> cars in the <StyleBold>2022 season</>, representing the sport’s bold leap toward sustainability without compromising high performance. The hybrid system combined a traditional 1.6-liter turbo engine with a 100 kW electric motor, backed by a 3.9 kWh battery, providing an electrifying boost of around 134 horsepower and pushing these machines to become <StyleBold>the fastest rally cars ever seen</>.

Among the stars of this era was the <StyleBold>Toyota GR Yaris Rally1</>, the flagship hybrid rally machine which carried on Toyota’s storied legacy in the sport. After making a strong comeback in 2017 with the non-hybrid Yaris WRC, Toyota dominated part of this hybrid era with multiple championships largely driven by iconic drivers such as <StyleBold>Sébastien Ogier</>, a legend who secured his eighth world championship during these years. Ogier’s fierce rivalry with Hyundai’s top drivers, including Ott Tänak and Thierry Neuville, energized fans and underscored the intense competition between Toyota and Hyundai, two manufacturers that defined this period with technological innovation and relentless pursuit of speed.

The lead driver's seat for Toyota, owned by Ogier, was taken by young <StyleBold>Kalle Rovanperä</> when the French legend decided to retire and focus only on part-time rallying during the year. Kalle quickly became the youngest driver to win a World Rally Championship event, winning the 2021 Rally Estonia. In 2022, he became the <StyleBold>youngest world champion ever</>, winning the 2022 Rally New Zealand the day after his 22nd birthday. The following year, he dominated the championship once again and secured his second consecutive title.

<StyleBold>Hyundai</> also stamped their mark, notably clinching the manufacturers' championship in 2020 with their i20 N rally car before transitioning into the hybrid era. Their hybrid Rally1 suffered early setbacks with reliability issues, yet they persisted and finally won the driver championship with <StyleBold>Thierry Neuville</> in 2024.

Despite the initial technological challenges and the high costs associated with hybrids, the era showcased the cutting edge of rally engineering. However, by 2025, the FIA decided to scrap the hybrid system due to its complexity and shifting priorities, planning to return to purely internal combustion engine cars while allowing some Rally1 hybrids to coexist briefly until 2026.

This hybrid era, though brief, remains a landmark in rally history, a thrilling chapter where the blend of raw power, electrification, and legendary rivalries created unforgettable moments.
CH_BOLLENE_PART1_R_DESC:
The first part of the stage consists of about 6 km of fast and twisting curves that climb up to the iconic Col de Turini.
The road is narrow and demands maximum concentration to avoid mistakes that can lead to catastrophic off-road excursions.
CH_SISTERON_PART1_F_DESC: The first part of the stage starts from the outskirts of Sisteron, climbing up mountain road sections leading towards Saint-Geniez. This section features a fairly wide carriageway but tight and technical corners. Setting the trajectory in the corners is straightforward, but maximum attention must be paid to speed and braking points.
CH_BOLLENE_PART1_F_DESC: The first part of the stage tackles the climb up to the iconic pass. Starting from La Bollène, it winds up for about 11 km with nearly 1000 m of elevation gain. Very narrow roads, brick walls on one side and a rocky walls on the other. One hairpin after another, this stage pushes the driver's concentration and precision to the absolute limit: the slightest mistake can completely ruin the result.
CH_HAFREN_NORTH_PART1_F_DESC:
The first short section of this stage begins near the mouth of the Severn River and follows part of its course, venturing into the Hafren Forest. With a length of 6.1 km, it is full of hazards, fast curves, uneven terrain, and intersections that can challenge the driver.

Great care must be taken at the edge of the road, which conceals dangers and traps: even a single wheel off the road can lead to mistakes and complications.
CH_MUNSTER_PART1_F_DESC:
The first short section takes place in the northern part of the stage, starting from the outskirts of the city of Münster. This 7 km special stage winds through the woods and is characterized by hairpin bends and very technical corners, almost entirely uphill.

Speeds are high, while the narrow road leaves no room for error.
CH_HAFREN_NORTH_PART1_R_DESC:
The first short stage of this stage starts from the area near the Afon Biga river and leads into the Hafren Forest. Characterized by very fast sections and wide curves, its 5.4 km are tackled at extremely high speeds.

These conditions can make life difficult for the driver, especially if stability is lost due to the uneven surface of the terrain.
CH_MUNSTER_PART1_R_DESC:
The first short variant covers the upper section of the stage. It is 5.6 km long and extremely fast, starting with an uphill section followed by a very quick stretch, then cresting and descending into the surrounding woods.

Fast corners and undulating straights keep the speeds above average, demanding intense concentration.
CH_ELATIA_PART1_F_DESC: The first variant of Elatia, almost entirely uphill, features wide roads and fast hairpins. Here you can fully exploit the car's power: controlling slides is essential to carry speed through the broad, high-speed turns. There are no specific hazards on the road itself, but rocks and bushes at the edges can become dangerous if not approached with proper caution.
CH_LOUTRAKI_PART1_F_DESC: The first variant of the special stage starts on the outskirts of Loutraki and climbs into the hills along generally wide roads that are nevertheless full of bumps and exposed rock. The route features many roadside ditches and the carriageway is strewn with loose stones that can jeopardize grip. The road layout allows for numerous trajectory cuts, but those shortcuts carry the significant risk of hitting dangerous bumps and rock spires that can ruin a run.
