DAMAGE_TURBO_DESC:
The forced induction system, whether a mechanical compressor or a turbocharger, delivers air into the engine to increase its power. 
Damaging it reduces the forced induction to the engine, causing a consequent loss of power.

The turbo is generally located close to the engine, and depending on its position, damage in the same area or excessive boost pressure can compromise it.
CH_COOPERS_SNOW_TEST1_DESC: The front-wheel drive and low power make the Mini Cooper S extremely agile on snow. At the same time, its short wheelbase makes it very responsive and demands high concentration while driving to avoid mistakes.
CH_FWD_TARMAC_TEST_MINICOOPERS_DESC: The front-wheel-drive characteristics of the Mini Cooper S allow it to tackle a special stage on tarmac with full control. Understeer is limited by the moderate engine power, and the track conditions provide sufficient grip to achieve optimal performance.
CH_SAVERNE_FULL_F_DESC:
The full 9.1 km special stage starts on the narrow internal roads of the Saverne Forest, then continues onto the wider roads of the region, reaching the Steigenbach area.

Fast corners, sudden hairpins, and intersections define this stage, making it both challenging and technical.
CH_SAVERNE_FULL_F_NIGHT_DESC:
The full 9.1 km special stage starts on the narrow internal roads of the Saverne Forest, then continues onto the wider roads of the region, reaching the Steigenbach area.

Tackling this stage at night is definitely an added challenge: reduced visibility demands greater focus, and the silhouettes of the trees can often confuse even the most experienced drivers.
CH_SAVERNE_FULL_F_SS_DESC:
The full 9.1 km special stage starts on the narrow internal roads of the Saverne Forest, then continues onto the wider roads of the region, reaching the Steigenbach area.

This stage demands concentration and speed to challenge your rivals. However, remember that speed isn’t everything in rallying: reaching the finish with your car intact and performing well can secure the victory.
CH_SAVERNE_FULL_F_RAIN_DESC:
The full 9.1 km special stage starts on the narrow internal roads of the Saverne Forest, then continues onto the wider roads of the region, reaching the Steigenbach area.

When it rains, the French tarmac becomes especially slippery, and the fast, technical corners of this stage can prove extremely challenging. Be careful with sudden braking, as it may easily cause you to go off the road.
CH_ELATIA_FULL_R_DESC: The full special stage from Zeli to Elatia. The first section is more technical, featuring narrow, twisty roads and a very short stretch of dusty tarmac. In the second section the route drops quickly toward the finish, with very fast, sweeping corners and open hairpins to be negotiated with controlled drifting.
CH_MUNSTER_FULL_R_DESC:
The full special stage, 10.3 km long, starts at the top of the mountain and descends down to the town of Luttenbach, on the outskirts of Münster. The route mainly runs through the surrounding forests, featuring a mix of fast sections and extremely technical corners.

It combines the two shorter versions and is a very fast special stage, requiring high concentration due to narrow roads and numerous hazards at the sides, such as cliffs, trees, and uneven terrain.
CH_MUNSTER_FULL_R_NIGHT_DESC:
The full special stage, 10.3 km long, starts at the top of the mountain and descends down to the town of Luttenbach, on the outskirts of Münster. The route mainly runs through the surrounding forests, featuring a mix of fast sections and extremely technical corners.

Tackling this stage at night is definitely an added challenge: reduced visibility demands greater focus, and the silhouettes of the trees can often confuse even the most experienced drivers.
CH_MUNSTER_FULL_R_SS_DESC:
The full special stage, 10.3 km long, starts at the top of the mountain and descends down to the town of Luttenbach, on the outskirts of Münster. The route mainly runs through the surrounding forests, featuring a mix of fast sections and extremely technical corners.

This stage demands concentration and speed to challenge your rivals. However, remember that speed isn’t everything in rallying: reaching the finish with your car intact and performing well can secure the victory.
CH_MUNSTER_FULL_R_RAIN_DESC:
The full special stage, 10.3 km long, starts at the top of the mountain and descends down to the town of Luttenbach, on the outskirts of Münster. The route mainly runs through the surrounding forests, featuring a mix of fast sections and extremely technical corners.

When it rains, the French tarmac becomes especially slippery, and the fast, technical corners of this stage can prove extremely challenging. Be careful with sudden braking, as it may easily cause you to go off the road.
CH_ELATIA_FULL_F_DESC: The full special stage, from Elatia to Zeli, runs along very wide roads that allow fast slides and let drivers fully exploit the engine’s power. The first section is almost entirely uphill, featuring high-speed curves and a few wide hairpins. The second section is more winding, with constant ups and downs, yet it remains fast and wide. The final part is the most technical: for a short stretch the stage runs on tarmac, the road suddenly narrows and becomes especially challenging, with continuous direction changes.
CH_4WD_TARMAC_TEST_I20RALLY2_DESC: The grip of an all-wheel-drive car on asphalt is excellent. The Hyundai i20 Rally2 is no exception: its agility, combined with high performance, allows it to tackle corners with precision and control, maintaining a high average speed throughout the stage.
CH_XSARAWRC_SNOW_TEST1_DESC: The high torque performance of the Xsara WRC, combined with the low grip of the surface, allows driving with higher gears, ensuring a good pace during the test and torque power always available to the driver. These features are especially useful on slippery surfaces like snow.
CH_BOLLENE_FULL_F_NIGHT_DESC:
The legendary Col de Turini stage, 18 km of hairpin turns and narrow roads with an elevation change of nearly 1000 m.
Tackling this special stage at night can be extremely challenging: despite the powerful night lights fitted on the cars, the constant direction changes obscure the driver's view, a factor amplified by the poor nighttime visibility.
CH_BOLLENE_FULL_F_SS_DESC:
The legendary Col de Turini stage, 18 km of hairpins and narrow roads with an elevation change of nearly 1000 m. 
This stage demands concentration and speed to challenge your rivals. However, remember that speed isn’t everything in rallying: reaching the finish with your car intact and performing well can secure the victory.
CH_BOLLENE_FULL_F_DESC: The legendary Col de Turini stage, 18 km of hairpins and narrow roads with an elevation change of nearly 1000 m. The stage runs from La Bollène-Vésubie to Peïra Cava, with a constant climb in the first part, then a fast descent after tackling the two hairpins of the famous pass. Driving precision and technique in handling the dangerous curves of this stage are essential to reach the finish.
CH_BOLLENE_FULL_F_SNOW_DESC:
The legendary Col de Turini stage: 18 km of hairpin turns and narrow roads with nearly 1000 m of elevation change.
On these roads, as altitude increases, it's easy to encounter snow and ice: caution is essential in such cases. With snow, grip is reduced to a minimum, especially without proper winter or studded tires. Pushing hard with dry tires and then slowing down in snowy sections can be a winning strategy, but also extremely risky.
CH_BOLLENE_FULL_F_RAIN_DESC:
The legendary Col de Turini stage: 18 km of hairpin turns and narrow roads with nearly 1000 m of elevation change.
Wet asphalt becomes particularly slippery at high speeds; pay special attention to harsh braking, which can extend stopping distances. A small misjudgment can compromise the entire stage.
CH_STRATOSHF_NIGHT_TEST1_DESC: The lighting system of the Stratos HF is designed to ensure good visibility during night stages, but the lights mounted on the hood are particularly vulnerable and prone to damage. This can cause a drastic reduction in visibility, significantly increasing the risk of driving errors.
DAMAGE_LIGHTS_DESC:
The lights of a rally car, whether front, rear, or additional, are essential for driving. They don’t directly impact the cars performance, but they allow the driver to tackle curves and bends in low-visibility conditions, illuminating the path and ensuring safety during night stages and low visibility.
Without them, driving would be extremely dangerous.

CH_208RALLY4_NIGHT_TEST1_DESC: The modern lighting system of the 208 Rally4 ensures adequate visibility during night special stages. The moderate engine power in the Rally4 classes limits the speed, providing the driver with longer reaction times.
PACENOTES_DIRECTIONS_DESC:
The notes indicate the <StyleBold>direction</> (left or right) of the curve and a <StyleBold>difficulty level</> from 1 to 6. A lower number (e.g., 1) represents a tight, difficult curve to be taken at low speed, while a higher number (e.g., 6) indicates a shallow and relatively easy curve to be taken at high speed.

Some directional notes do not include a difficulty rating but instead describe the type of curve, adding details necessary to best approach it. Examples include <StyleBold>Hairpins</> or very fast <StyleBold>Flat</> curves.

Here is a description of the curve notes, ordered by increasing difficulty (from easiest to hardest):

•	<StyleBold>Kink Left/Right:</> a slight bend on a straight section of road, to be taken at full speed.

•	<StyleBold>Flat Left/Right:</> a gentle curve to be taken at very high speed.

•	<StyleBold>6 Left/Right:</> a very simple curve usually not requiring braking but may need some speed reduction.

•	<StyleBold>5 Left/Right:</> a medium/easy curve that may require braking and attention in specific cases.

•	<StyleBold>4 Left/Right:</> a curve of medium difficulty that requires speed moderation and the use of brakes.

•	<StyleBold>3 Left/Right:</> a medium/high difficulty curve needing precise speed control at entry and proper braking.

•	<StyleBold>2 Left/Right:</> a difficult curve requiring careful use of brakes and, in some cases, the handbrake.

•	<StyleBold>Square Left/Right:</> a curve similar to difficulty 2 but with a 90° angle, often at junctions or intersections.

•	<StyleBold>Sudden Left/Right:</> an abrupt curve changing direction opposite to the previous one or hidden from the driver's view.

•	<StyleBold>1 Left/Right:</> a very difficult curve to be taken at low speed, often requiring the handbrake.

•	<StyleBold>Hairpin Left/Right:</> a 180-degree turn to be approached carefully at low speed, using the brake or handbrake.

•	<StyleBold>Tight Hairpin Left/Right:</> a very tight 180-degree turn, often at junctions or intersections.

•	<StyleBold>Chicane Left/Right:</> a sequence of two or more closely spaced curves alternating in opposite directions (e.g., right, left, right).

CH_IMPREZAS3_TARMAC_TEST1_DESC: The outstanding all-wheel drive of the Subaru Impreza S3 delivers superb road holding on asphalt, allowing full exploitation of the generous power from its turbo boxer engine. The short wheelbase enhances its agility, making it quick and precise when setting up corners.
CH_LIVIGNO_FULL_F_SNOW_DESC: The packed snow, typical of this circuit, can become even more slippery with the arrival of fresh snow. Additionally, falling snow during the challenge can further reduce visibility on the circuit, increasing the risk of mistakes.
DAMAGE_RADIATOR_DESC:
The radiator is one of the necessary parts for maintaining the proper temperature of the engine. 
Damaging this component makes cooling less efficient, which can lead to overheating and possible engine damage. 

The radiator is generally mounted at the front of the car to take advantage of greater airflow. 
This position makes it more exposed to frontal impacts that can easily damage it and cause water leaks. 
In rare cases, the radiator can be installed on the sides or at the rear of the car.
CH_GIULIAGTA1300_SNOW_TEST1_DESC: The rear axle of the Alfa Romeo GTA 1300 Junior offers excellent control compared to other rear-wheel-drive cars. However, due to the high steering ratio, greater precision is required when handling the steering wheel to keep the car stable and avoid dangerous loss of grip.
CH_A110_TARMAC_TEST1_DESC: The rear overhanging engine layout and low center of gravity, combined with the Alpine’s lightness, make it very challenging to drive. It’s easy to lose rear grip when entering a corner, but it can also induce understeer on corner exit.
CH_131ABARTH_SNOW_TEST1_DESC: The rear-wheel drive and strong power of the 131 Abarth allow long drifts, while the balanced weight distribution provides better control of the car. Steering can be managed through throttle modulation, as with all RWD vehicles, which is made easier by the slippery surface.
CH_RWD_TARMAC_TEST_037EVO2_DESC: The rear-wheel drive of the Lancia 037, combined with its high-performance engine, ensures excellent control both in drifting and traction. Oversteer can be an issue due to the power delivered to the rear wheels; countersteering and throttle control are key to managing it effectively.
CH_A110_GRAVEL_TEST1_DESC: The rearward-shifted center of gravity, combined with the low grip of gravel surfaces, makes the Alpine very responsive, so it's easy to lose traction at the rear. Compared to other rear-wheel-drive cars, managing the drift angle through throttle control is more challenging.

CH_STRATOSHF_RAIN_TEST1_DESC: The responsiveness of the Startos HF becomes extremely pronounced on slippery surfaces such as wet gravel. To achieve optimal performance and avoid mistakes, the driver must carefully modulate the throttle and anticipate the car’s movements and weight transfer.
CH_SISTERON_PART2_F_DESC: The second part of the stage features very fast straight sections with wide curves that allow for high speeds. The road narrows, demanding precise and error-free driving; the hazards along the roadside require maximum concentration.
CH_BOLLENE_PART2_F_DESC: The second part of the stage is completely different from the first: you descend starting from the Col de Turini, on fast roads featuring treacherous curves. The 6.3 km of the stage must be tackled at very high speed, requiring maximum attention to hazards on both sides of the road and careful judgment of the curves and braking points.
CH_BOLLENE_PART2_R_DESC: The second part of the stage starts from the legendary Col de Turini and descends to La Bollène over 11 km of tight, twisting hairpins. Along the roadside there are long stretches of stone walls that, on the one hand, prevent cars from going off the road, but still remain a constant danger in every corner, leaving virtually no margin for error.
CH_HAFREN_NORTH_PART2_R_DESC:
The second short stage of 6.1 km starts from the Hafren forest and reaches the Pumlumon Cwmbiga area. The high speeds typical of this rally alternate with technical corners and intersections.

The uneven surface adds an extra challenge that can compromise the car’s stability.
CH_MUNSTER_PART2_F_DESC:
The second short variant tackles the upper part of the stage, almost entirely outside the woods. It is an extremely fast section of 5,3 km, mostly uphill, leading to a crest that precedes a final technical sector characterized by very high speeds.

The fast corners can be more challenging than they appear, and a small misjudgment can prove catastrophic.
CH_MUNSTER_PART2_R_DESC:
The second short variant takes place in the northern section of the stage, starting from the grazing meadows and finishing on the outskirts of the city of Münster. This 6.8 km special stage winds through forests and is characterized by hairpins and very technical corners, almost entirely downhill.

Speeds are high, and the downhill corners can be slippery, posing potential challenges for the drivers.
CH_LOUTRAKI_PART2_F_DESC: The second variant is very fast and slightly wider, allowing more room for slides and, overall, a higher average speed. Trees and rocks at the sides of the road pose a hazard if sufficient attention is not paid, while the roadway, although broad, is covered with debris and small stones that can compromise the vehicle's grip.
CH_LOUTRAKI_PART2_R_DESC: The second variant unfolds on very wide but dirty roads; there are many cutting opportunities, yet debris, bumps and rocks can easily compromise grip, making cuts rewarding but risky. The average speed is very high and the sweeping corners allow for long drifts. Although fast, the route remains twisty, creating the right balance of speed and skill required.
CH_ELATIA_PART2_F_DESC: The second variant, which reaches the outskirts of Zeli, features a more winding road with continuous changes in elevation. For a short section the surface changes from the typical Greek gravel to very dirty tarmac. In the final part the carriageway narrows and the route becomes particularly technical, demanding maximum attention to avoid dangerous off-road incidents.
DAMAGE_GEARBOX_DESC:
The sequential mechanical transmission, subjected to high stress during the race, wears out quickly and its condition must be monitored frequently to avoid breakages. 

On the other hand, the manual dog-ring transmission, although more durable, can be compromised by driver errors caused by the frantic use during the race.
CH_SAVERNE_PART1_F_DESC:
The short version of this special stage runs through the Saverne forest towards Steigenbach, along medium-width roads that encourage high speeds.

It is essential to pay close attention to hidden hairpin turns and the numerous intersections that characterize this stage.
CH_SAVERNE_PART1_R_DESC:
The shorter version of this special stage starts from the Segenbach area and goes into the Saverne Forest. Speeds are very high thanks to the medium-width road and wide-radius curves.

However, some dangerous intersections and sudden hairpin bends can prove challenging.
CH_GENERIC_SNOW_GRAVEL_EVENT_DESC: The snow-covered gravel surface is more slippery, though it does not require drastic changes to the typical driving style used on this terrain. It is essential to pay close attention during braking and deceleration to avoid losing control of the car. Gravel tires are also suitable for these conditions, providing adequate grip and biting into the surface even in extreme situations.
CH_LOUTRAKI_FULL_F_DESC: The special stage is 10.2 km long and starts on the outskirts of Loutraki. The roads are wide and provide plenty of room for maneuvering, but the road edges are very dirty, with bumps and debris. This encourages cutting corners and long slides, yet it also hides potential hazards to the car’s integrity and to traction.
CH_LOUTRAKI_FULL_R_DESC: The special stage long 10.2 km opens with a twisty, technical section featuring many junctions that can confuse drivers about the correct line. Listening to the co‑driver is essential. The road is wide but littered with debris and rocks; the ditches at the sides make intentional cuts very risky, but if executed correctly they can be hugely advantageous.
CH_ELATIA_PART1_R_DESC: The special stage starts on the outskirts of Zeli and features a complex layout: the opening section is narrow and technical, while the second part opens into faster, wider stretches. A short portion of the road is paved but dusty; the surface change does not demand major driving adjustments, yet caution is still necessary. The high steering ratio makes controlling the car challenging, demanding utmost concentration and quick reactions behind the wheel, along with precise throttle modulation to manage the drift angle.

Although less responsive compared to more modern cars, the Delta still delivers excellent control during slides.

CH_COOPERS_RAIN_TEST1_DESC: The wet ground becomes much more slippery, but thanks to the agility and front-wheel drive of the Mini, it is possible to handle the car easily even in difficult conditions. CH_I20RALLY2_RAIN_TEST1_DESC: The wet tarmac is very slippery and, despite the i20’s all-wheel drive, great care must be taken when braking and in fast corners. It is very easy to make mistakes, overshoot the corner entry, or lack enough grip to keep the car stable through the turn.
DAMAGE_WINDSHIELD_DESC:
The windshield of a rally car protects the crew from external elements like wind, dust, and debris, ensuring safety and comfort during the race. Its main function is to maintain clear visibility of the road, essential for high-speed driving.
A damaged windshield seriously compromises visibility, increasing the risk of accidents.
RULES_OVERVIEW_DESC:
The world of rally is governed by numerous <StyleBold>regulations</> that ensure the proper conduct of races, maintaining a balanced level of competition, and guarantee the safety of the crews and all participants.

<StyleBold>AC Rally</> is a true rally simulator designed to offer the most realistic video game representation possible of what happens in real competitions. However, not all real rules are perfectly applicable to a video game, and in some cases, it has been necessary to adapt them to ensure both realism and the right amount of fun for all players, from the most experienced drivers to beginners.

The goal of the <StyleBold>AC Rally Regulations</> is to provide the tools to better appreciate the world of rally in its most faithful representation and, as in reality, maintain an adequate level of competition, discouraging unsportsmanlike behavior that could spoil the gaming experience for every participant, and allow every virtual driver to feel like a real rally driver.
GROUP_FABIARSR2_DESC: The Škoda Fabia RS Rally2 is one of the most widely used cars in recent years in regional and national championships. Its balanced performance and excellent handling make it one of the best in its class.
RULES_RALLY101_DESC:
There are fundamental techniques and concepts every rally driver should know. These will be very helpful in your learning journey within the world of AC Rally.

<StyleTitle>Understeer:</>
Understeer occurs when, during a turn, the car tends to go straight instead of following the steering angle because of loss of grip on the front wheels. In rallying, this can cause loss of control, increasing the distance traveled through the corner and slowing the driver down. Understeer is particularly dangerous as it limits precision and the ability to turn quickly, requiring rapid correction to avoid running off the road or crashing. The most common technique to manage understeer is to reduce the throttle, allowing the front wheels to regain grip.

<StyleTitle>Oversteer:</>
Oversteer happens when the rear wheels lose grip during a turn, causing the rear of the car to slide outward and resulting in a sudden rotation around the vertical axis, risking a spin. Common causes include sudden acceleration, sharp steering inputs, or abrupt throttle release. To correct oversteer, one uses countersteering—turning the wheel opposite to the curve direction—and carefully modulates the throttle while avoiding harsh braking.

<StyleTitle>Weight Transfer and Tyre Grip:</>
Weight transfer and tyre grip are fundamental for a rally car’s performance and control. During driving, the car’s weight shifts differently between the front and rear wheels depending on acceleration, braking, and cornering. This load transfer directly affects the tires’ adhesion to the ground. Proper balance allows the tyres to maintain maximum contact with the surface, increasing grip and improving stability. Well-calibrated tyres, adapted to the terrain conditions (tarmac, gravel, dirt), can make the most of this weight transfer, which is essential for tackling rally stages at high speed.

<StyleTitle>Pendulum:</>
The pendulum technique is used to tackle corners on low-grip surfaces. It consists of initially steering away from the curve direction to trigger a weight transfer that unsettles the car and allows a controlled rotation of the rear in the desired cornering direction. This maneuver helps initiate a controlled slide, reduces understeer, and enables higher cornering speeds. It involves quickly steering against the curve, then steering into the corner while controlling the wheel and throttle.

<StyleTitle>Throttle Control:</>
Throttle control is essential to manage traction and stability on different surfaces and corners. Modulating engine power maintains maximum grip, preventing understeer or oversteer. In corners, the throttle balances weight transfer and influences car behavior, enabling controlled drifts or optimal traction. Gas should be applied progressively, avoiding abrupt changes that destabilize the vehicle.

<StyleTitle>Braking:</>
Brake control involves modulated use of the brake pedal to transfer weight onto the front wheels, improving their grip on corner entry. This helps manage oversteer, increases stability, and allows precise handling of tight corners. Typically, the driver brakes firmly before the corner, modulating pressure while steering and releasing the brake at the apex to maintain optimal control.

<StyleTitle>Handbrake:</>
In rally, a hydraulic handbrake is often used, unlike traditional ones, which locks the rear wheels quickly and strongly by compressing a fluid. This allows the driver to brake sharply and induce controlled slides, facilitating drifts and rapid direction changes on challenging surfaces. On corner entry, the driver pulls the handbrake lever sharply to temporarily lock the rear wheels, causing the car to slide into the desired trajectory, then releases it and resumes steady acceleration.

<StyleTitle>Front-Wheel Drive (FWD):</>
Front-wheel drive, common in medium-power cars, transfers the engine's force to the front wheels, which also handle the steering. These cars generally tend to understeer, especially when exiting a corner. To try to reduce understeer, the rear suspension is stiffened considerably, making the car nervous under braking, and limited-slip differentials are installed to help transfer power to the ground. During acceleration, it is common to feel the steering wheel pull towards the inside of the corner, a sensation very different from that of a typical road car. These cars are small, light, nervous, very fun, and suitable for beginners. Fine control of the throttle and steering wheel is crucial to be fast.

<StyleTitle>Rear-Wheel Drive (RWD):</>
Rear-wheel drive transfers power to the rear wheels, leaving the front wheels with the sole task of steering. In rally driving, it offers greater agility and sensitivity, making the driving experience more engaging and pure but also more demanding, as oversteer in corners is frequent. It is necessary to precisely modulate the brake and throttle: once the car is positioned in the corner, the accelerator must be carefully adjusted to maintain control. In general, applying throttle increases the angle of drift, while easing off the throttle reduces the angle of drift. This setup emphasizes balance and responsiveness but requires practice to avoid losing control.

<StyleTitle>All-Wheel Drive (4WD):</>
All-wheel drive (AWD) distributes the driving torque to all wheels, improving traction on slippery and uneven terrain. This increases cornering speed and road holding, making the cars more stable and competitive. Controlling a 4WD car requires mastering the power management distributed to all wheels in order to maximize grip on variable surfaces. The driver must carefully modulate the accelerator, brake, and steering to maintain the ideal balance between oversteer and understeer. Techniques such as weight transfer, gentle throttle control, and, if necessary, the use of the handbrake to induce oversteer are fundamental to maintaining control and optimizing the trajectory in tight corners and on slippery surfaces. Compared to a rear-wheel-drive car, a smaller counter-steering angle is required to effectively manage power-induced drifting.

<StyleTitle>Driving on Asphalt:</>
Even in rally racing, driving on asphalt requires utmost precision to fully exploit the car’s grip and achieve the cleanest and smoothest possible lines. Concepts such as outside-inside-outside, apex point, and ideal racing line also apply in rally, but the narrower road width limits their effectiveness, demanding even greater attention from the driver to avoid errors. Sliding can be extremely useful on asphalt as well, especially when tackling sudden tight turns like hairpins or 90 degrees turns.

<StyleTitle>Driving on slippery surfaces (Gravel and Snow):</>
Gravel and snow are typical surfaces in rally competitions and require driving techniques different from those used on asphalt. To achieve good results on slippery surfaces, it is necessary to approach corners by transferring the car’s weight onto the front wheels to increase grip. It is also essential to control the drift angle by modulating the throttle and steering to avoid oversteering, which can cause a spin, or understeering, which will push the car toward the outside of the corner.

OPTION_STARTSEQUENCE_DESC:
There are two types of <StyleBold>Starting Procedures</> to choose from at the start of a special stage and any event.

The <StyleBold>Quick Start</> is a simplified and shorter starting procedure. It takes place close to the starting line and with just a few seconds left in the countdown.

On the contrary, the <StyleBold>Complete Start</> is a longer procedure, but it allows the driver to have more freedom and time available. Starting from the time control station, you must approach the starting line and stop the car where indicated by the stewards, preparing for the start of the stage.

HISTORY_2010_DESC:
This era was largely shaped by the extraordinary careers of <StyleBold>Sébastien Loeb</> and <StyleBold>Sébastien Ogier</>, two French champions who collectively reigned over the World Rally Championship (WRC) for the better part of the decade.

At the decade’s start, Sébastien Loeb, driving the <StyleBold>Citroën C4</>, continued to build on his record-breaking legacy, already holding the most event wins in WRC history. Loeb’s smooth style and strategic brilliance made him nearly unbeatable, earning multiple championships and securing his place as the sport’s greatest icon. As Loeb’s dominance began to taper off by the mid-2010s, a new star rose: Sébastien Ogier. 

Ogier, initially part of the <StyleBold>Volkswagen</> team driving the <StyleBold>Polo R WRC</>, emerged as the leading driver, clinching multiple consecutive world titles with Volkswagen, then <StyleBold>M-Sport Ford</>, and later <StyleBold>Toyota</>. His rivalry with <StyleBold>Thierry Neuville</> from <StyleBold>Hyundai</> brought fierce competition, pushing the sport’s intensity to new heights.

This decade also saw a shifting landscape among manufacturers. <StyleBold>Volkswagen’s Polo R WRC</> emerged as a legendary car of the era, renowned for its speed, reliability and innovation, dominating the early to mid-2010s. <StyleBold>Toyota</>’s return to WRC in 2017 with the <StyleBold>Yaris WRC</> revitalized the competition and their team, led by former champion <StyleBold>Tommi Mäkinen</> as principal, quickly rising to prominence. <StyleBold>Hyundai</> also became a key challenger, especially with Neuville’s spirited driving, sparking memorable battles in rallies around the world.

The rivalry climaxed towards the late 2010s when <StyleBold>Ott Tänak</> from Toyota broke the long-standing French dominance by winning the <StyleBold>2019 driver’s title</>, a seismic shift in rally history. Tänak’s aggressive driving style and the reliability of the Toyota Yaris helped him secure this breakthrough, signaling a more open and unpredictable era ahead.
CARSETUP_DIFFERENTIAL_LOCK_DESC:
This switch allows mechanical or electrical <StyleBold>locking of the differential</>, effectively turning it into a spool. With a spool, both wheels on the axle rotate at the same speed, eliminating any speed difference.

This delivers traction and stability benefits when on-throttle, especially useful when a damaged or slipping wheel would otherwise drain engine torque. However, locking the differential causes significant understeer off-throttle and reduces steering responsiveness, making it harder to turn.

Because of these handling compromises, it should only be engaged in extreme conditions where maintaining traction is critical, such as severe wheel slip in rough rally terrain.
CH_LOUTRAKI_PART1_R_DESC: This variant starts uphill with a particularly technical section, then descends toward Loutraki. The roadway, especially along the edges, is very dirty: loose stones and bumps can compromise grip and, if tackled carelessly, lead to an unintended retirement.
CH_FWD_GRAVEL_TEST_MINICOOPERS_DESC: To best tackle a special stage on gravel with a low-powered front-wheel-drive car like the Mini Cooper S, it is essential to fully utilize the pendulum technique and weight transfers. These techniques help in easing the corner entry and allow the Mini’s characteristics to provide stability on exit.

PARTNER_PIETROCIGNI_ACTIVITIES:
Upon turning 18, he obtained his racing license and began his competitive career alongside driver Giacomo Saitta in a Citroën Saxo VTS N2, competing in the N2 category. His first competitive experience took place at the 2020 Rally Val Tiberina on gravel, a race marked by challenging conditions that put small-displacement cars to the test. Despite the difficulties, he finished first in his category. During the same year, he also took part in two tarmac rallies held in the Maremma hills, known for their technical routes.

In 2021, he continued competing with Saitta, entering the Raceday Rally Terra championship. The season was plagued by numerous mechanical issues and off-road incidents, which prevented them from finishing several stages.

In 2022, an important professional step occurred: he joined the reconnaissance team for the Italian Rally Championship, collaborating with Paolo Ciuffi, who was responsible for driver Tommaso Ciuffi. At the same time, he continued racing alongside Saitta.

Starting in 2023, he took on the role of co-driver for Tommaso Ciuffi in a Škoda Fabia R5 EVO, competing in the Italian Gravel Rally Championship (CIRT), where they finished third overall. In 2024, he confirmed his participation in the CIRT once again, achieving strong results, although an off-road incident in the final race cost them the overall victory, ending the season in second place.

He is currently competing once more in the Italian Gravel Rally Championship, where he has been leading the standings since the beginning of the season, with the final phase now approaching.

Pietro collaborated with Supernova in developing the pacenote system, providing valuable insights into the rally world and the co-driver’s role. He actively identified the best phrases and notes to accurately describe the various situations faced during a rally.
Additionally, he translated all the pacenotes into the Italian language to offer players the most authentic linguistic adaptation possible, using, whenever feasible, the terms and expressions most commonly used by co-drivers who speak this language.
Finally, he contributed his voice and experience as a co-driver during an intense recording session lasting several days, delivering the pacenotes in the most realistic way, just as he would in real rally conditions.

PARTNER_VIGEA_BRAND:
VIGEA – Virtual Geographic Agency is a highly specialized company operating in the sector of 3D modeling, topographic surveying and digital reconstruction of landscapes and heritage sites.

Built on the integration of scientific expertise and cutting-edge technologies, VIGEA stands out for its ability to operate with precision and innovation across complex and multidisciplinary fields, including environmental research projects for archaeology, geology and territorial analysis.

With a multidisciplinary team composed by geologists, archaeologists, technicians and developers, VIGEA applies high-resolution data acquisition methods using tools such as terrestrial laser scanners, mobile mapping systems, drone-based aerial photogrammetry, high-precision GNSS instruments and Earth observation satellite data. These technologies allow for the generation of dense point clouds, 3D models and virtual environments that are both scientifically accurate and visually compelling.

VIGEA has extensive experience in large-scene international research projects, including collaborations with the European Space Agency (ESA) on landscape exploration and monitoring, and with National Geographic on documentary projects aimed at promoting natural and cultural heritage. The company has also taken part in several scientific expeditions and research programs in remote and extreme environments, contributing geospatial data and 3D reconstructions for documentation, analysis and storytelling.

In addition to its scientific and technical work, VIGEA creates immersive and interactive digital content for museum exhibitions, documentaries, video games and virtual/augmented reality experiences. These productions, grounded in real-world data and scientific accuracy, offer educational and engaging experiences for a broad audience merging the informative power of data with the emotional impact of visual storytelling.

Innovation, technical precision and scientific integrity are the cornerstones of VIGEA’s approach. The company acts as a bridge between the physical world and its digital representation, using technology to enhance understanding, communication and appreciation of our environment and shared cultural legacy.
PARTNER_VIGEA_HISTORY:
VIGEA – Virtual Geographic Agency is an Italian company specialized in 3D scanning for the digital reconstruction, analysis and visualization of landscapes, cultural heritage and built environments using cutting-edge geospatial technologies. 

Founded in 2017 by geologists and topographic surveyors with previous experience in the 3D digitization of civil and geographical environments, over the years the company has specialized in mapping and digitization of difficult to access areas such as deserts, glaciers or caves and 3D scanning of racing circuits.

VIGEA’s mission is to transform complex spatial and scientific data into intuitive, visually compelling experiences that support knowledge sharing, preservation and decision-making. The company operates across the world in a wide range of sectors such as geology, archaeology, architecture, cultural heritage and environmental studies, offering advanced services including 3D surveys, photogrammetry, laser scanning, mobile mapping, virtual and augmented reality. Its core areas of expertise include drone and laser scanning surveys (UAS) to acquire high-precision geographical data such as 3D models, orthophotos and detailed cartography, and 3D modeling to create photorealistic reconstructions of architectural assets and archaeological sites to make them accessible through virtual and augmented reality.

Through a multidisciplinary approach, VIGEA partners with universities, museums, research institutes, private companies and public institutions to transform complex data into accessible and immersive visual experiences for communication and analysis, supporting scientific research activities, heritage preservation and the development of immersive environments for video games. Wheter capturing ancient archaeological sites, simulating geological phenomena or building immersive digital environments for gaming or museum exhibitions, VIGEA combines technical precision with storytelling and creativity bridging the gap between the physical world and its virtual representation.

WEATHER_PERSISTENCY_DESC:
Weather Persistence control determines how long a weather condition lasts over time.

Increasing the persistence results in slower transitions between different weather states, with single weathers condition lasting longer.
Decreasing it causes faster and more erratic weather changes.
CH_GIULIAGTA1300_RAIN_TEST1_DESC: Wet dirt tends to become more slippery, and the oversteer issues of the GTA 1300 Junior caused by its rear-wheel drive can be worsened. It is necessary to shift more weight to the front to properly set up the corner and avoid mistakes.
CH_RALLY037EVO2_RAIN_TEST1_DESC: Wet tarmac can become very slippery, and the rear-wheel drive of the Lancia Rally 037 Evolution 2, combined with the mid-mounted engine, makes the car susceptible to load transfers, which can easily destabilize it and cause mistakes.
CH_GENERIC_RAIN_TARMAC_EVENT_DESC: Wet tarmac loses much of its grip because of the film of water that forms during rain. Grip progressively decreases as the vehicle's speed increases, requiring extra care when controlling the car and during braking and deceleration. Wet-weather tires improve water evacuation, helping to mitigate the loss of grip and ensuring better vehicle control.
CARSETUP_BUMPSTOP_DESC:
When selecting <StyleBold>bumpstops</> for a car, consider the type of surface and the jumps you’ll encounter. 

Longer bump stops engage earlier in the suspension travel, providing a more gentler and progressive cushioning effect. This helps protect the suspension from harsh impacts while maintaining control over rough terrain.

Shorter bump stops however provide a sharper and more consistent handling feel, ideal for smoother terrain.

Generally, the longer the bumpstop, the softer the ride when it compresses.
CARSETUP_HEAVE_BUMPSTOP_DESC:
When selecting your <StyleBold>heave bumpstops</> for a rally car, it’s important to consider the type of surface you’ll be driving on.

Longer heave bumpstops engage earlier during suspension travel, providing a softer response that helps absorb impacts more gradually.
This can be beneficial on rougher or uneven terrains, where cushioning is crucial for maintaining control and comfort.

Shorter bumpstops activate later, resulting in a stiffer suspension feel suitable for smoother surfaces.
DAMAGE_INTERCOOLER_DESC:
When the car is equipped with a forced induction system, the intercooler cools the air after it has been compressed. 
A damaged intercooler will be less efficient, compromising the forced induction resulting in a loss of power.

Like the radiator, the intercooler is generally positioned at the front of the car to make the best use of airflow. Frontal impacts therefore can easily damage it.
PACENOTES_TURNSDETAILS_DESC:
When the co-driver signals to the driver the approach of a corner, they often add several <StyleBold>details</> that enrich the description of that section of the road, to better help the driver prepare for and tackle the corner in the best possible way. Every detail can be crucial to signal a danger or a peculiarity of the corner; a wrong interpretation or the lack of knowledge of the meaning of these details can cause errors and dangerous accidents.

<StyleGray>Example:</> 4 Right <StyleBold>OPENS</> and 6 left <StyleBold>VERY LONG</> 80
In this case, the right corner of difficulty 4 tends to open its radius on the exit, allowing the driver to ease the steering and accelerate earlier, in view of the following very long left corner of difficulty 6, which ends with a straight of 80 meters.

Below are the most commonly used details to describe corners:

<StyleTitle>OPENS</>
A corner <StyleBold>OPENS</> when the radius of curvature, after the apex, widens on the exit, allowing the driver to ease the steering and accelerate earlier since the corner becomes easier.
A variant is <StyleBold>OPENS</> with a difficulty grade, for example <StyleBold>OPENS 4</>, indicating that a corner with a higher difficulty will become easier at the exit.
Another variant is <StyleBold>OPENS LATE</>, indicating the corner tends to open up in the last part of its length.

<StyleTitle>TIGHTENS</>
A corner <StyleBold>TIGHTENS</> when the radius of curvature, after the apex, tightens on the exit, requiring the driver to increase the steering angle and slow down, being aware that the corner will become more difficult.
A variant is, for example, <StyleBold>TIGHTENS 4</>, meaning a less difficult corner becomes more demanding on the exit.
Another variant, <StyleBold>TIGHTENS LATE</>, indicates the corner tends to tighten in the final part of its length.

<StyleTitle>OVER CREST / OVER JUMP / THROUGH DIP</>
These indications signal that the corner is located near or in the immediate vicinity of road irregularities such as <StyleBold>CRESTS</>, <StyleBold>JUMPS</>, or <StyleBold>DIPS</>, suggesting the driver prepare to face both the corner and the road feature at the same time.

<StyleTitle>LONG / VERY LONG / SHORT</>
A corner is defined as <StyleBold>LONG</> or <StyleBold>VERY LONG</> when the radius of curvature remains constant for many meters, forcing the driver to hold the steering and the car engaged in the corner for an extended period.
Conversely, a <StyleBold>SHORT</> corner maintains the radius of curvature for a very short time, suggesting the driver can soon change direction or straighten the steering.

<StyleTitle>EARLY / LATE</>
The indication <StyleBold>EARLY</> invites the driver to enter the corner as soon as possible, moving the trajectory towards the apex earlier than the standard line.
Conversely, <StyleBold>LATE</> indicates the driver can delay approaching and reaching the apex as much as possible.

<StyleTitle>NARROWS</>
A section is said to <StyleBold>NARROWS</> when the carriageway narrow, reducing the space available for maneuver. In such spots special attention is needed, as there may be walls or other obstacles that risk severely damaging the vehicle.

<StyleTitle>WIDENS</>
A section is said to <StyleBold>WIDENS</> when the carriageway expands, increasing the space for maneuvering. Generally, a widening road simplifies driving but the possible presence of obstacles or walls should never be underestimated.

<StyleTitle>SUDDEN</>
A corner is defined as <StyleBold>SUDDEN</> when it requires a very quick change of direction, often in situations where elements of the track impose a sharp entry.
CARSETUP_CAMBER_DESC:
When viewed from the front, wheels have <StyleBold>negative camber</> if the tops of the tyre tilt inward toward the centre of the car, and <StyleBold>positive camber</> if they tilt outward.

<StyleBold>Negative camber</> improves grip and tyre responsiveness , allowing the outer wheel during a corner mantain a better tyre contact patch.

However, too much negative camber reduces the contact patch on straights and concentrates stress on the inner edge, which can decrease acceleration and braking performance. It can also lead to situations, especially when the car is stiffer and has less roll, where the full width of the tyre isn’t used in a corner leading to a reduction in peak cornering grip.

It's important to monitor tyre temperatures, ensuring the difference between the inner and outer edges doesn’t exceed <StyleBold>20°C</> to maintain balanced grip and tyre life.
GROUP_RWD_DESC: With <StyleBold>rear-wheel drive</>, counter-steering is essential. Using the throttle controls the slide: accelerating causes oversteer, while lifting off restores grip and realigns the car.
PARTNER_DAVIDPRICE_PALMARES:
With a rallying career spanning more than 300 events across the UK and Europe, from grassroots club rallies to international competitions, Dave has consistently competed at the sharp end of the sport. His journey has brought him into contact with many memorable people, and several standout highlights define his career:

•	<StyleBold>Peugeot Talbot Sport GTi Challenge Scholarship</> – Winning a scholarship with Nick Elliott in the 1990s provided factory support to continue in the Peugeot 205 series. Competing head-to-head with Richard Burns, Dave occasionally matched his stage times, gaining invaluable experience alongside a future World Champion.

•	<StyleBold>Over 30 Overall Wins in the British Historic Rally Championship</> – Mostly in the Mk2 Escort and more recently in the Fiat 131 Abarth, Dave and Elliott became the benchmark crew in the BHRC, particularly dominant on gravel.

•	<StyleBold>Rallysport Development Fiat 131 Abarth</> – Helping to develop and compete in this fan-favorite machine has been a career highlight, with victories in the BHRC and appearances at international events showcasing the car’s potential and enduring appeal.

Today, Dave continues his commitment to the British Historic Rally Championship, while also expanding his horizons with new events abroad and fresh opportunities to experience historic rally cars. With decades of experience, a wealth of victories, and a deep love for the sport, he remains one of the most respected and recognizable co-drivers on the historic rallying scene.

OPTION_FREEDRIVE_DESC:
With the <StyleBold>Free Drive</> option enable the <StyleBold>Free Practice</> game mode change in the following ways:
•	Any time tracking is disabled.
•	Session Times & Telemetry are not available and are not saved.
•	The Co-driver is not present in the car and the Pacenotes are disabled.
•	It is possible to go in each direction.
•	In the Pause Menu are available the functions Reset Damage and Respawn in the Opposite Direction.
CARSETUP_SUSPENSIONS_DESC:
Without proper grip on the surface, it is impossible to fully harness the engine’s power.
Suspension adjustments allow you to improve the vehicle’s response according to the driving style and the type of surface.
In the suspension settings area, you can find the main adjustments that help balance the car mechanically. 
By using all available settings, it is possible to achieve the best performance from the vehicle. The goal is to closely follow the road profile while keeping the chassis variations as minimal as possible. 
Softer setups are preferable on rougher terrain, while stiffer setups work better on smoother surfaces.
PARTNER_YIPINGCHEN_BIO:
Yiping Chen was born in Chongqing, China, in 1983. He studied in Australia for university and later returned to Chongqing to found a car modification shop and set up a club team in 2006.

Since 2010, he has participated in rally as a co-driver. He participated in the World Rally Championship the same year and is still the Chinese co-driver with the most international events.

He has also participated in touring car championships and rally championships as a team manager. He also serves as a driving instructor in China for many top brands, such as Mercedes and AMG, Audi RS, Toyota Gazoo Racing, Subaru, and more.
PARTNER_YIPINGCHEN_PALMARES:
Yiping Chen was ranked 8th for the year in the PWRC class of the World Rally Championship 2010.

He was the Chinese champion of the 2014 FIA Asia-Pacific Rally Championship – Rally China.

He has won many events in the China Rally Championship as a co-driver.

As a team manager, he also has many championship titles, such as: FIA Asia-Pacific Rally Championship team and driver winner in 2019, 2015–2019 team champion of the China Rally Championship, winner of the China RallyCross Championship 2017, and more.

Yiping Chen is well-known as the best international rally co-driver and team manager in China.
CARSETUP_CENTERRATIOTOREAR_DESC:
You can adjust the <StyleBold>torque distribution to the rear differential</> by altering its ratio relative to the front differential.

Setting a higher ratio than the front shifts more torque to the rear, increasing rear bias.
However, this also raises the overall final drive ratio, which reduces top speed but improves acceleration.
To maintain the original final drive ratio, you can compensate by adjusting the gearbox final ratio in the opposite direction.

This asymmetric setup not only changes the front-to-rear torque balance but can also preload the center differential, allowing it to respond quicker to differences in axle slip, enhancing traction and handling in rally conditions.
CARSETUP_BRAKE_PAD_DESC:
You can select from various compounds for your <StyleBold>brake pads or shoes</>, each suited to different driving conditions.

For <StyleBold>shorter</> rally stages, you might prefer softer pads with a strong initial bite and better stopping power. This does come at a cost though, with faster wear and increased chance of locking on loose surfaces.
For <StyleBold>longer</> or low-grip stages, more highly durable compounds are generally better, as they last longer and maintain a more consistent performance.

Keep in mind that different pads or shoes can affect the brake bias at each wheel, so always check and adjust the bias accordingly to ensure optimal handling and safety.

CARSETUP_DIFFERENTIAL_RATIO_DESC:
You may adjust one or both <StyleBold>axle differential ratios</>; even differently one from the other. Setting a higher ratio at the front shifts more torque to the front wheels, enhancing front torque bias and viceversa.

However, this also raises the overall final drive ratio, which reduces top speed but improves acceleration. To maintain the original final drive effect, you can compensate by adjusting the gearbox final ratio in the opposite direction.

This asymmetric setup not only changes torque distribution but also preloads the center differential, allowing it to respond more quickly to differences in wheel slip between axles, improving traction and handling in rally conditions.
